THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION
Oral History -- Bud Freeman
Sides 1 - 4
Helen Dance, ind.

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
mt PROCEEDINGS
Bud, as I say, let us go right back to the beginning, and you tell me everything that you can think of about early days because we've got lots of time and we should hear all we can about that.

Well, I think that I was conscious of music at the age of eight, because first of all, my mother is a pianist and she had five sisters and two brothers, all of whom played the piano, and they were constantly visiting us, because we had this lovely old upright, a Kimball piano. One of the best of its kind, in those days, at least.

So, again, I was aware of music because that was all I heard. And then my father had -- he was not musically inclined but he loved it -- and he had in those days, the Victrola put out this big high standup player, record player, called the -- similar to the Victrola, and they gave a lot of operatic records. We had all of Caruso, they gave us symphonic records, they gave the old Paul Whiteman, Isham Jones records, you know, those were the big dance bands of the day, and I was constantly playing these things, you know, as I say, at the age of eight.
And I had a feeling that music came naturally to me, that I loved it, and, in fact, I had a difficult time in school because I was always thinking about music and couldn't

wait to get home to play my music." records. But there was an ambivalence there too, because I was interested in sports, and I would sneak out to play baseball and my mother had preferred to have me do other things. I became a runner and actually on the strength of my having been a good runner, I was in a field meet and won all the events at the age of 13 or 14. I was graduated from grammar school. I doubt very much if they would ever have gotten rid of me if I hadn't had that athletic talent.

And as a matter of fact, Dad got -- since I won this medal, Dad got a letter from some athletic society that seemed to have something to do with a thing called Junior Olympics. I am not quite sure of that now, because I have not kept notes on these things. This is all total recall with me, Helen

So I was to go down and be interviewed with a view to becoming some sort of serious athlete, and on the way down -- I was now 14 years old -- on the way down I stopped and I don't know if you have ever been in Chicago, but on Wabash Avenue there was a placed called the Lyon and Healy Band Instrument Shop and in the window there was a beautiful shined brassy C-Melody Saxophone, open in its case, with a lovely velvet case. So now I am on my way to this --
How old are you?
I was 14. On my way to this meeting

to be interviewed by the again these athletic people. Now Well, I completely forgot about the meeting, went into the shop and asked if I could just have a look at that C-Melody saxophone and the man took it out of its case and I put my fingers on it as though I could play it and I don't think the man knew that I couldn't, and I just loved the instrument. I said, oh, to myself, if I could only have this, and that was the end of the interview. I didn't get to the interview.

I went home and my father was brokenhearted -- because my father had been a very good athlete and he was hoping that I would get into some sort of career as an athlete. Well, so much for that. In fact, when I went into high school, I was in a track meet and I ran -- my running was so poor and I was so far behind the other runners that I had the feeling that I was running in the wrong direction. But anyway At any rate, enough of that. To get back to the age of eight again and my feeling that I understood music, they used to play -- Dad had brought out of the Spanish-American War a pair of old, very heavy old drumsticks. I guess he was a fair -- not really a good enough drummer to be a professional, but he could in the Army, in the drum and bugle corps, and he brought these heavy sticks back, I could hardly lift them. But there at the age of eight, I was just with no lessons, playing on a chair, to my mother's piano
playing and they all seemed to think I had a good beat. I don't mean that in any egomaniacal sense, but you know how flattering, oh, my boy has so much talent.
Yes.

Well, of course, it was not until I was about 15 that I was to meet at Austin High School, I was to meet the McPartland brothers, Jimmy who is still going very strong, of course, married to Marian Mary McPartland, who is by the way coming over here to England and had a marvelous musical career. I saw Jimmy at Nice last year and he was just as good as ever and in wonderful condition.

Well, anyway, it was through Jimmy's effort that (You know,) I got a saxophone because he went to my dad and he said, I think Bud, he sings and he dances and I think he might have a natural talent for playing and why don't you consider buying him a C-Melody saxophone. That was the instrument one started on, I was not to continue that. We didn't know whether I could really get into playing, so now in the meantime before any of this happened Dave Tough, the great drummer, later to become I thought the best, with all due respect to the other greats, especially Kenny Clark, Dave Tough came over to see his girlfriend who was attending Austin High School and every Friday they used to have a social hour there and it was an interesting thing about Austin High School, there were a we had half a dozen men who played professionally.
A most unique thing I think about a high school, having professional players in --
Instructors?

They were students. They were in their junior and senior years and professional players, playing maybe two or three nights a week and we sort of fell in with them. They knew Dave Tough and they idolized him, because Dave Tough -- I was 15 and I would say Dave was then about my age, but he had already been playing professionally a year and he just -- he came over and sat in with the high school group of professionals one Friday afternoon and I just moved right up on them as though I was one of them and I put my hand out to shake hands with the great Dave Tough, and he treated me as though I were one of the musicians. It was marvelous to me. And we became --
Let me ask you, Bud, what school was Dave going to?
Dave Tough was going to Oak Park High School. The same school Hemingway went to, of course, many years before us.
Yes.
And, incidentally, Dave Tough was one of the first people I ever heard speak about Hemingway. He idolized Hemingway and I remember that six months after
Dave Tough told me about Hemingway, The Sun Also Rises, H. L. Mencken in the American Mercury came up and discovered Hemingway.
Is that right?
Yes. Dave, you know, had this extraordinary literary mind and as you know, Helen, would have become a fine writer if he had lived.
Yes.
But he had the problem of drinking, I think he sort of just burned himself out.
Did Dave, that problem that Dave had when did that develop? How old was he when that developed?

Well, Dave Tough started to drink, I think, as did many musicians, at the age of 14. George Wettling the same. I say many, that isn't true, but I think there again, as I recall, there were about six different musicians I knew who started to drink at that early age and I think that they just burned themselves out. They could -- maybe a good -- Well, Condon, Eddie Condon certainly started to drink that early because he was a professional player at the age of 14.
There was an extraordinary thing about Benny Goodman that he never got into that. Benny Goodman started to play professionally at the age of 12. He was just an
extraordinary clarinet player.
Yes, in his short --
I knew Benny then, you see, all those years ago.
Well Anyway, to get back --
I will interrupt you once in awhile because I'd like to get just as much as you can.
Oh, sure.
So just because the whole historical picture is interesting, so if you don't mind, while you are speaking of that, you said, since you had musicians are you talking about Frank Teschemacher, too?
I don't think Tesh started to drink that early. I met him at Austin High School, and I think we were about the same age again.
Was he in that band?
I think I was 17 when I met Tesh. Tesh was in that band called the Austin High Gang, which I think is -- I think there are some words about it in the Library of Congress, I am quite sure.
And was he a little behind you then?
No, Tesh was ahead of me.
Oh, he was ahead of you.
I was a sophomore and Tesh, I think
was a junior.
I see.
He might have been a year older.
Now, where did George fit in?
We met George -- well, of course, this is a big step now from what you want, but I was not to meet George until I was playing professionally and had a tenor saxophone.
Now, to go back, if I may.
Yes, go back, please.

We will go now to where I am at Austin High School and I don't have an instrument yet, but the McPartland brothers talked to my father -- talked my father into buying me a C-Melody saxophone, which he bought at -- I think I was 16; yes -- the age of 16 and two years later, I played my first professional job with no study at all on the C-Melody and that was at a place called the Sheboygan Inn in Sheboygan, Wisconsin. It was right on the lake.

Now, there was a pianist by the name of Lyman Woods, who had a trio -- that is, he wanted a trio and he loved Dave Tough -- Dave Tough was his favorite drummer and he wanted an alto saxophone player, or a tenor, anything, a good saxophone player. Dave Tough told him that I was the best C-Melody saxophone player around and actually, I could hardly play. I couldn't play melody. I could play a few notes.
They always said I had a good beat. Well, that one beat and one note came out in everything I played.

So, this man said, 'Well, I'd like Bud to audition,' and Dave said, 'Oh, no, he's too much an artist to audition,' so the man, on the strength of Dave Tuff's praise, decided to take the chance and he took me into the group and when the man heard me play, he wanted to kill me. He was so furious, but he was frightened that Dave Tuff would leave.
So he threatened to fire me every night, and Dave said, 'Well, if Bud leaves, I leave.' So the man had to keep me there.
Now, when I tell you that I couldn't play anything, I am telling you the truth. This is just how it happened. And I was making a lot of money.

Bud, you know I must tell you, you see, I didn't meet you until a number of years afterwards because I was in Chicago, but you had already gone to New York. But, you know, I was always hearing about you and people like Jess Stacy, and people told me that and made me laugh and laughed when they told me. They all said, he couldn't play, he didn't know -- he couldn't play, but he just used to come in -- he played such good rhythm on the horn.
Yes. Yet on one note...
But we all knew he could sing and find out how to all he had to do was to blow his horn.
But when you say -- how did you learn to read, for instance?
All right. That then, is a big joke from where we were, because --
No, don't let me get you ahead, go right back.

All right. I would like to go into this thing, because now we're, as I say, in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, and I am getting about $40 a week and that was a tremendous amount of money in those days-- that must have been what, 1924 or something, and of course, I was living at home and Dad never took any rent from us, from -- when I say us, I mean my brother, who has become a well-known actor, and we could always go home, you know, when we weren't doing anything. Well, at any rate, the music was so bad, really, because of me that Dave Tuff decided he couldn't bear it any longer, either, so he got an offer to go to another place to play with some band from the University of Chicago and he took it, and the night that Dave Tuff left, this man grabbed me by the neck and said, 'You son of a bitch, if you are not out of town in an hour, I am going to murder you.' And that was my debut as a jazz player. Well, now, so much for that. We got back and we started to rehearse, and now again, I was 18, and we

started to rehearse a band and they said well -- the fellows in the band said, look, you are going to have to get a tenor, because C-Melody just isn't going to work and so about six months after that time -- and again, it's difficult for me to remember the year, Helen, but I should have thought it was about 1924, I got a tenor and now I was really confused because the few things that I had learned to play were now in another key. C-Melody being in C and the tenor being in B-flat.
So, I had to learn that. But we'd have jam sessions and I was now developing a pretty good ear so that I could play around. I didn't read yet. Now, I was about 19 years old.
What records were you listening to?

Well, that's the important thing. We were very much influenced then by the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, and I love that music as opposed to the very commercial dance music which I was brainwashed into hearing as a child.

And when Dave Tough told us about King Oliver and this wonderful band out in the black district of Chicago and where very few white people went -- only we went to hear this wonderful music and they were very nice to us. We would go out and you know, we were well dressed kids from school and they knew we were there just to hear the music,
and there was an unknown cornet player in the band by the name of Louis Armstrong and Lil Lowel Dutrey who was later to marry Louis, played piano. I think Duke Tray was the trombone trumpet player.
Where were they?
That was a place called the Lincoln Gardens on the South Side.
Yeah, right.
It was the most fantastic thing, and that, I think, is the greatest jazz band I've ever heard or will ever hear.
And it was in that band that Louis became the wonderful musician we were later to hear.
Well, King Oliver himself must have been very inspiring to hear, wasn't he?
Well, he was a marvelous -- King Oliver was the great first jazz trumpet player any of us was to hear.
Those things like Dippermouth and those things -- (unintelligible). He's the one that played them first, isn't he?

Yes, I think he was, there's no doubt about it, as far as I am concerned. I didn't hear all of the so-called New Orleans greats, but those I did get a chance to hear did not have the talent of King Oliver.
No. But I mean in that band, he

Well, it's difficult to know because I didn't have all the records, but I remember that King Oliver held Louis down. Not because -- he realized that Louis had this tremendous talent, Louis might have been a genius, but he was guiding Louis, because Louis was young and could have been wild, and King -- I think that Louis really did learn a great deal from King, but once he let Louis go, it was incredible to hear this remarkable player.

It's too bad that the young people today, Helen, do not know the true greatness of Louis Armstrong because they thought of Louis as Satchmo, an entertaining man, a man who just sang all the time and entertained. But if they could have heard the early Red Seal-Okay records, the Hot Five, Louis, and you hear those things today, Louis sounds as fresh and still far ahead.
No trumpet player, and I say this with all due respect to all the greats we have ever heard, no trumpet player has come up with that. The beat, imagination, sound.
And what he was playing was being played for the first time.

For the first time. There was no one -- of course, there was the great Bix and here unfortunately we did not -- the kids, and the young people listen to Bix today and even many musicians listen to Bix today,

and it is difficult to listen to Bix through all the other players because those players were not essentially jazzmen. They were men in the Whiteman band and in the Goldkette band who could read anything. They were fine disciplined musicians, but Bix out of a sense of loyalty, you know, playing with the men in the band used them on his records. They were not really, and I hope I am not being unfair when I say this, that they were not really jazzmen who lived the jazz music as did Louis and King and Bix and many of the greats, Dave and Kenny Clarke Tough, Benny Carter and a few people like that who were later to become --

I think that we then, as I said, never went back or as I meant to say, we never went back to the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, after hearing the King Oliver Band, because we realized that in hearing the King Oliver Band, we were listening to the real thing.

Now, we have -- you know, there is a tremendous amount of -- we have this controversy, whether the blacks were the only people who could play. And I would be very willing to say that's okay with me excepting that Dave Tough was white and was an absolute genius. Jack Teagarden was white. These were two very superior players. of course, Bix. There were many, and Bix, Again, I am And I mean
George Wetling was a good drummer.

Yes, there were many, many superior players who were white. Today you've got some of the finest drummers -- Buddy Rich. What's the chap's name who is married to -- Louis Bellson, people like this, there's so many great -- now I think and here is a very interesting thing -- I want to make sure not to get off the track here.

The man who published my first book called, 'You Don't Look Like a Musician,' a book of anecdotes and vignettes, is a black biochemist, a brilliant man, a genius at Fort Wayne University, yes, in Detroit -- is it Fort Wayne University -- Wayne State, beg your pardon. I am sorry. I was thinking about something about Fort Wayne. I want to tell you later.

But I mean of course Wayne State University and he again is a black man, a great biochemist and he asked if he could read the manuscript of my first book. Now, in the first book I tell this very story, I praise the black people and I explain -- I even go so far as to suggest the music might have come from Africa, well, this man, this black biochemist, Professor James, said no, I do not agree that jazz came from Africa.

So now, I was completely -- I began to think -- I was completely mixed up because I began to think because my goodness, almost every black musician I know thinks that the music came from Africa and thinks of the music as being his, and I am willing to go along with that since I felt

that way all my life, but the professor says no, you have all these different arguments about it. Well, I am not concerned with that. I am concerned with man as being a man, I am concerned with individual talent, because if we are going back to say it's the black man's music and again, I say, that's fine with me, how many really played it?

Of the hundreds of thousands of black people in the world, there were a handful who could play and that goes for the whites too and there were very few whites who could play, outside of Bix and Benny Goodman and Dave Tough and George Wettling, you named a half-dozen people.
Now, as I say, I don't get into these things, Helen, because I am just interested in individual talent.
Yes.
I couldn't care what the color of a man be, and if the black people want it to be their music that's fine with me, because I was very much influenced by all black music, as a child.
I think Davey felt the same way.
Dave Tough was the first --
He didn't care where the talent came from.
No, Dave Tough and Bix and if I may put myself in there, were the first whites, although Dave and Bix were ahead of me, and I think greatly talented men,
let's say we were the first white people to understand, have a feeling for the black man's music.

Now, Mezz Mezzrow had a great profound feeling and he loved the music, if I am not being too crude, I don't believe that Mezzrow had the, shall we say, the facility to go on and do something for himself, but I think he is to be given a lot of credit for what -- for the love he --
Well, Bud, Mezz, I can't help but feel that Mezz, although he had such small facility, what facility he had was authentic, and --
He had a marvelous feeling for the blues.
And his feeling and his sound were real and --
Yes.
So he has to be given credit for that, don't you think.

Yes, of course. Of course, I knew him a long time and I think the credit I would give him doesn't go in that direction. It's this; it has to do with the marvelous enthusiasm he had and how helpful he was to me when I made my first recording with the Condou-Carmen McKenzie Chicagoans, Nobody's Sweetheart, and incidentally, it was on the strength of that that I got an offer to go with Ben Pollack and got out of Chicago and went to New York,

which was the place to be in those days. Because of Chicago supported jazz for a few years, and then of course, when Louis and all the greats left, went east to New York, we followed, because we felt that New York was the place that then could afford to support jazz and one could actually make a living playing music, jazz. There were so many recordings.

Now, to get back to the black business again. I think that I learned more actually from the black dancers and black singers such as Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith than I did from black players, but the strange thing about it all was that I was not influenced by one kind of jazz. For instance, the first time I heard Coleman Hawkins play, I was amazed to hear the powerful authority this man had on the tenor because in those days, tenor was played as an accompanimental instrument. I was supposed to be the first white tenor player to play in a jazz band which simply means they threw out the trombone and put the tenor in. Jimmy McPartland, cornet, Teschemacher, clarinet and myself tenor and that was supposed to have been called later on Chicago Jazz.

But I would like to think that King Oliver and Louis started the so-called Chicago Jazz. Because what we played on those records was our, the white man's impression, of what King Oliver and Louis were doing.
They were the inspiration?

Yes. But to get back to Hawkins now, I could easily say that I was influenced by Hawkins, but not as strongly as I was by the black singers, the dancers and all the -- especially pianists, I was very much influenced by Lucky Roberts, the great black pianist, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller, Earl Hines. I was very much influenced by many of the great black clarinet players.
You didn't hear Lucky Roberts in Chicago, did you -- it was in New York...

No, I never heard -- these are records. I never heard Lucky Roberts in person. I met Lucky Roberts just before he died when Life Magazine came up to Harlem and had about a hundred of us, black and white musicians, and took this big picture up around 125th Street, and that was the first time I ever laid eyes on Lucky Roberts. I think he died not long after that.

But I used to listen to all of his records because, and incidentally, found out about these records through Bix because Bix told us about Ethel Waters and as you know, Lucky Roberts made all the Ethel Waters records, so but I never heard him play, in person.

But I heard James P., and in fact, I did a couple of concerts with James P. in New York, one of those Condon series things, and of course, played on a recording with Fats and never recorded with Earl Hines, but played -- did a long tour of

28 straight days with a band several years ago here in the U.K. called -- well, the band was from they were bands from the States and it was called Jazz of the Swing Era, but I have known Earl since I was a kid, because when Earl -- Earl joined Louis at the Sunset, say in 1925 or '26, I used to go there three or four nights a week to hear Earl and Louis. 'Cause This was a couple years after the King Oliver thing.

Well, I'll Bud, I'll tell you what. I would like to interject a question or two as we go along here because the whole Chicago picture is very fascinating, very interesting and I don't believe, though much has been written about it over the years, I don't believe it's been gone into thoroughly, and it warrants it by all means and there are few people in the position that you are in there to give that inside picture, which is a fascinating picture.
Yes.

And so, while we have got lots of time ahead of us, so while we are at this stage, let me, if you doesn't throw you off, ask you the occasional question because I know you have amusing insights, I know myself from being up there at that time, how many funny things happened.
What a family it all was, what a widespread family with all the different people, and the way they
talked and felt and the way they split up, I mean they did not fit in with the others or how there was the competitive spirit here and so on.
And so I will draw you out about that so we can get as much of an in-depth picture there as we can.
Oh, yes, I would like that.
So in doing that, we will put you right back where you were which I didn't mean to get you away from there. When you went back and then you said, you were 19 and you joined --
Well, it was a thing that we called -- we weren't playing quite professionally, or had that thing, that flasco...
Did you never have any instruction, ever?
Well, we are just going to get into that now.

When I was -- I took a few lessons from Jimmy McPartland's father, who was a music teacher, and I didn't seem to like the lessons because that was -- I didn't like the discipline, you know, of sitting down and reading music at that time, and so I became bored with that and just went on my own way, which was sort of slow, but eventually I did learn how to improvise and did learn how to play the melody with the beat I had, and Dick McPartland,
Jimmy McPartland's brother, was a fine guitarist, taught me chords, and we just called them chords in those days. I didn't go very deeply into (unintelligible) studies until later.

And so that I could -- I knew what key I was playing in and I could -- when I improvised, I had an idea what the chord changes would be. Well, now at the age of 20, it appeared that I was going to have a serious music career. I wanted to be a jazz soloist because I was very involved and I was still listening endless hours to all of my jazz favorite records, of course, being Bix, Louis, Fats, James P., as I mentioned all the names, Ethel, and Bessie, and I found that I was learning more about jazz just through listening to records than I was occasioned to learn by going to the clubs, because in a nightclub atmosphere, your attention was not always on the music; being young one, we were always, our attention was drawn to a lot of interesting things we had never seen before.

Here we were in black nightclubs where white people didn't go, and usually when a white man was out in a black nightclub in those early days, he was there to get a woman, I suppose or to get some booze, but we were there solely for the music. But not only did I witness something --
We were just talking about when
you were down on the South Side and what life, what you all saw there and the life that you saw.

Yes, well, as I say to repeat, because we had to change the tape, I saw this freedom of spirit that we whites didn't have. Now, of course, it's an easy thing for me to say that because these people were having a difficult time getting hold of money and they weren't given -- they weren't allowed any of the privileges and life could have been difficult for them but when they were out in the night life, out in a nightclub dancing, they just appeared to be so free in spirit and so happy.

Now, there again, the word happy, you know, it's a difficult word, because a lot -- many, many years ago when the whites, the majority of whites who did not understand that black man to say nothing of today, they could easily say, oh, they are all so happy and always smiling. Well, that's a cruel, stupid view to take. I don't mean that view, I only mean that they were free of spirit. They were not brainwashed by many things that we whites were taught to believe that aren't true of life.

These people had their own culture, and their own way of thinking and were forced into a culture that had nothing to do with their heritage. And so I just learned so much from watching their pattern of life, and I got to
know Louis very well, I got to know Earl well -- I didn't get to know King Oliver.
He was a little bit older than Louis was. older.

Yes, and he was going -- of course, poor King Oliver stayed around Chicago a couple of years and -- well, you know more about this because you have gone into research, and then went down south and the last I heard he was working in a poolroom racking up balls. It was sad, this great genius who had given America so much beautiful music.
And died before all the boo-ha-ha and --

Yes, because you see in those days one couldn't make a living as a soloist. We had now to get back to what I had to do, I began to realize, as I said a few minutes ago, that I was getting in something deep, and that I was going to become a serious musician, that is, a jazz player.

But in order to make a living in those days, one had to read and one played in a big band. So I went to a clarinet player, the first clarinet player in the Chicago Symphony, Duke Real and I told him, I said, I would like to learn how to read music, because I know that I am going to receive an offer in about a year to go with one of the good bands, they want me for my jazz solo work and the

first thing Duke Real said to me, or asked me, where did you get all that technique and I said, well -- he said you must have studied, and I said, no, it's just comes of playing naturally and having listened to music since I was eight years old, and feeling that I understood it, and he said, I think I can teach you how to read in six months and he said with that technique, you will have no problem executing anything you read.

Well, in five months, I was reading all the best studies we could get, all the different books and when I got my first job in a band where I had to read the music, it was so simple compared to the studies I'd had.
How much time a day did you put on your --
Well, of course, this was a labor of love in those days. I used to play that horn all day long. I didn't realize I was working hard.
I had the books and I would practice out of the books and then I, of course, didn't want to spend too much time at that, but I had to learn just enough about reading to please my teacher.

And after awhile we played duets and he used to invite his other pupils, who were younger people, amateurs to come and hear us play duets, because I could play all the best studies with him, and I don't mean that in any
sense to boast, but that is just simply realistic. How it was.

And on the strength of, there again, of a record I was to make a year later --now, I was 20, playing tenor and at the age of 21, Condon and McKenzie had the record date in Chicago, and I had played a lot of different things around Chicago.
That was the Blue Blowers. Mountain City-- Mound
Mountain City--
Well, I never played with the Mountain City Blue Blowers, but McKenzie was there with them, and McKenzie was the kind of man who could sell things.

Musicians were never people who could go -- jazz musicians could never go call up a man who ran a recording company and sell themselves. Condon could do it, McKenzie could do it, as they were later to prove.
But anyway, here now was my first record, as I mentioned --

But, Bud, really we have gone too fast. First of all, I am interested -- you know, you never told me, what about your family background. What about your grandparents, I mean, what kind of an ethnic background.
Well, I must explain I didn't really -- my mother came -- my mother was born in Chicago, my father was born in Pennsylvania. My father's father
was born in Germany and my mother's father was born in the French part, I think, Montreal.
And then my great grandparents came from Russia, Germany and on my mother's side of the family, came from France.
Well, you see, you have a multi-ethnic background. Isn't that extraordinary?
Yes.
Of course, you would have a very big musical heritage, coming down both sides.
Well, I just don't know. The only thing I can say, Helen, was I was aware of music at the age of eight.
Well, now, you see, there you are and there's Arnie, your brother, both of you extraordinarily talented, so now where is this^-- you had no sisters.
answer going to be pinpointed
I had one sister who studied piano for a few years and I don't think she can play a bar, a note of music today.
Is she still alive?
Yes, she lives in California.
That's nice. Well, now you and Arnie, you were talented -- you were personalities, both of you, I suppose he was too, as a young -- as he grew up. Is he older or younger?
My brother is two years and four months younger than I and he has become a very successful actor.
He has. You told me he is in the Barney Miller Show now.
He is in the Barney Miller Show.
That's very exciting.

He lives about six months a year in Hollywood where he does a lot of television and films but he would prefer to do a Broadway play, and he loves London, by the way. When he came over, as I told you earlier, he was here ten days and we saw nine plays. And this ambivalence that has always existed in my life, that I didn't know when I wanted to be an actor or a musician, so my agent just recently having seen me at a concert, said, 'Well, you can become both.' Because I like to tell the anecdotes which people like to hear, you know. Well, look do you think all Now, where does this sound comes from? Is this partly your father's or your mother's or did it come from nowhere or what?
Did you say --
Your talent.
Well, it's a difficult thing to know. You see, I was environed luckily with this group in Austin High School, the McPartland Brothers and Dave Tough, and they got me
Well, : That's your career. That wouldn't account for what's within in, though, Bud.
Well, yes, we knew of no musicians or actors in our side of the family.
What kind of a personality had your father?

My father was a lovely man who worked as a cutter of ladies garments and he was very good at it and managed to make a lot of money at it and he adored people who were talented. He was not a talented man; in that sense.
Oh, I see. But he was a --

He just loved -- my father furthered all of this by wealth. There's a very funny story that goes along with it all. We lived in a community in Austin where people were always butting into other family's business and they had meetings. They noticed that my brother and I never did anything, because so when my brother was readying himself to become an actor and I was getting ready to become a professional musician, so we were out till all hours, listening to either Louis or Earl Hines out in the South Side and my father was a hardworking man. He would get up at 7:30 in the morning and work all day and come back and there we were maybe still in bed.
And, so, the people would have meetings and say, Mr. Freeman, why don't your boys do something? Why don't

they go to work? And my father would say, 'You don't understand, my boys are different. They're crazy, but they are different.' So now having after been brainwashed by the community for several months, Dad dared to come into our bedroom at 7:30 one morning, the cardinal sin, since we had just got to bed probably from having been up all night, and I pretended to be asleep and he shook my brother and he said, 'You boys are going to get up and you are going out into the world and you are going to get jobs and you are going to amount to something and live normal lives as do other normal people.

Whereupon, my brother said, 'How dare you wake us before the weekend!' Now, the beautiful thing about all this, was that Dad never bothered us about that subject after that and he was to live long enough to be very proud of us because Newsweek -- well, it wasn't Newsweek at that time, it was Time Magazine and Life Magazine came to interview about his two, if I may say, famous sons.
My brother became a wellknown actor and I became, I suppose, a wellknown musician.

Now, when my brother -- the first thing my brother did, he came to Chicago from New York in a play called Streetcar Named Desire, of course, the great Tennessee Williams play, and my brother had a walkon part

of about four minutes, extraordinary thing, and my father said, and my father alerted the community, they all came and took about four rows in the theatre and they all came to see this thing, and my father said, 'My Arnie is the star of the show.'
Now, my dad was not to see me do anything or hear me do anything until I joined the Ray Noble band. You remember the story of the Ray Noble band.
No.

Which I would like to get into later on, and we made a film called the Big Broadcast of 1935 with Amos and Andy, but we made our part of it, not in Hollywood, but I think Astoria, New York, and we were playing at that time at the Rainbow Room till 3:00 in the morning and then we'd get in bed at 4 or 5 and we had to be on the set at 7:30, and we worked about a week on that film.

Now, there was I -- as you know, in films the band were set up and you didn't see all the musicians. Some were behind posts and there was I being in the saxophone section, the tenor man, on the end and you couldn't see my face at all, my body, but you could see my foot and my dad said, 'You see that foot, that's my son's foot.'
Anyway, we will get into that. Ray Noble comes on much later, but we will get into that.
Now, that's very interesting, and
now tell me, what about your mother? How did she feel about you both.

Well, mother unfortunately died when I was 16. I already had the C-Melody saxophone but she knew nothing about my becoming a musician or my love for music. She only knew that I liked to sing and that I could play the drum, but she loved -- she had a lovely voice and she was a good amateur pianist.

But she had been ill -- oh, she took ill -- about a year before she died, she spent that year in a sanitarium and then they realized that she wasn't going to live much longer and they brought her home where she died. As I say, I was 16 and she knew nothing about my brother becoming an actor and nothing about me become a musician, which was sort of sad, because she would have been so happy and proud of that.

Mother was never very well, but quite a lovely woman, of course, and just adored the theatre. That was another thing, you see, we were always going to the theatre, going to see films, always there was with this constant music, and I think if I hadn't become -- and this pertains to your question, Helen, where did the talent come from, I think if I hadn't become a jazz musician, I would surely have become an actor, or maybe a writer or story teller or
something. I was involved with the arts.

I will never forget, 15 years old, as you know, Helen, the Louvre rejected all of the early Cezanne -- I don't know all, but they did reject, and the Chicago Art Institute bought all of the Cezannes they could get hold of, and to this day, the Chicago Art Institute has the best collection of Cezannes in the world.
I didn't know that... They have a very good director.

Yes. And Dave Tough called me, I remember I was about 16 years old, and he called me up and he said are you familiar with the painter Cezanne and I said, I am sorry, I am not, I wasn't into painting at all. Well, he said, look the Louvre has rejected his works and the Chicago Art Institute bought them and let's go down tomorrow and have a look at this, and so we went down and I looked at this one beautiful thing, the first Cezanne I had ever seen and I said to Dave, 'I wish I could say something about this magnificent work.' And Dave said, 'That's the best thing you will ever say about it.'
But Dave was the one who got into love for theatre, into books, into painting, into all the arts.
We can't say too much about Dave.
It would have to be about me.

Oh, no, what I was going to say was as much as you want to say about Dave, it's great, because there isn't anyone here to speak for Dave, and there are not so many people today who really knew him. Unquestionably he was a wonderful guy, so please state all you want.

So I can say this -- very good. Before I met Bix, before I ever knew Bix existed, Dave Tough told me about King Oliver and Louis. He was way ahead of his time and he was just super drummer. In the beginning he was influenced by Baby Dodds. Let's see, there was Johnny Dodds was the clarinet player and his brother was Baby. They were in the King Oliver band, and Dave was very much influenced, by him. Of course, MS. DANCE: George Wettling was too. MR. FREEMAN: Yes, Of course they were. I say this with all due respect to the great drummers today, all the great soloists, I thought that Dave Tough knew how to play more behind a soloist solos than any other drummer because today of necessity, maybe, drummers have become soloists, they become their own individual people, like Buddy Rich, I think, is a great artist and there are so many great drummers who become soloists, I suppose, because well, in order to get a name this what one has to do. And the times. is one way to do. But Dave Tough was the greatest, to me, band drummer
I had ever heard, and of course, Sid Catlett and Dave were considered the tops of their times.

Bear in mind that Dave Tough influenced people like the so-called modern drummers. Now, we in jazz, we musicians in jazz do not use categories. We do not put people into categories and I will go into that in a few minutes. We don't call a man a modern drummer or an avant garde drummer or a dixieland drummer. A man can either play or he cannot. This is what it's about and only musicians know this. Not critics, I am sorry to say, with the exception perhaps of a few, such as you and Stanley Dance, Leonard Feather. All right.

Say that musicians never called the music jazz, but they knew what they were hearing and what they were feeling. It was the only kind of music they could find wherein they could express their feelings, because they worked all day in studios or theatres and all night in night- clubs, playing dance music or playing other people's acts, but why did they want to play this kind of music? Because they had a chance to express what they felt about music.

And to go back to Dave Tough, Dave Tough was the first man to introduce me to this new sound. Now, when I say new sound, Helen, you know, I am 71 years old and jazz then, all those years ago, almost 60 years ago, was a brand new sound and when I hear Louis Armstrong today on the old

Red Seal records that I mentioned earlier in the interview I hear a brand new sound, since nobody's touched it. Many, many white players and many blacks have tried to play like Louis but they never had the sound, they never had the beat. Certainly they never had the beat. Louis had the greatest beat of any trumpet, any cornet or trumpet player I have ever heard.
Of anybody I guess.

There is no doubt about it. Maybe with other players, and I say this with all due respect to them, maybe they sound a little old-fashioned, but Louis still sounds way ahead. There is no one, and I say this again with all due respect to Dizzy and Miles and all the great players, never had the beat that Louis had.

And again, I want to cover that by saying that I have -- that people like Dizzy and Roy and Buck, you name it, all the great players around today, are dear friends of mine and they know, they will vouch for what I say. We discussed Louis many times, they have tremendous admiration for this great genius.

But, again, Dave Tough was to introduce me to all of that. I owe a great debt to him and I never -- not only that but he was to teach me -- he was to make me understand that I understood a lot of things about the esthetic life, that I might certainly have missed. I might have gone
just into music and become --
As most of your musical contemporaries, most of the musicians weren't into anything else.

No, I want to say particularly if I may, that I have tremendous respect for Jack Teagarden and there was a story about him that -- I remember that I was playing with the Pollack band, in New York, and Glenn Miller had given his notice and so Ben said & well, we will be looking for another trombone player to take Glenn's place, and I got a call about 3:00 one morning, one of our nights off and the call was from Pee Wee Russell, and he said, <Bud, about the greatest jazz trombone player in the world is blowing into town and he wants to say hello to you and we are going to meet over at a this saloon, at [Randy's], this was during prohibition and the saloon ran 24 hours a day, a speakeasy, we called it.

So I went over to hear this great player and Pee Wee was at the bar and we waited about a half hour and there appeared at the door, the speakeasy door, a man with a little cap, a button cap, a corduroy Norfolk suit, shoes -- trousers halfway up his legs -- I can't remember the shoes now -- but anyway, I think they were suede shoes and he had a trombone, not in a case, but in a little velvet bag. He took it out of the bag, put it together and played with no accompaniment, some of the finest music I ever have heard in

my life. I absolutely flipped over hearing him and I went back to Pollack that night, and I said, I heard the best jazz trombone player in the world. Well, But, of course, Glenn Miller wasn't I don't think too happy, I don't think, having heard me say that, but anyway, -- although Glenn and I were good friends and we were later to play with the Ray Noble band. Pollard heard Jack Teagarden play one chorus and hired him. Bud,
Incidentally, I remember riding in the front of the car with Jack doing the same thing on his mouthpiece in the back of the car.

Oh, yes, in a glass; he was a great natural talent. And Teagarden could read anything you know, he played in the Whiteman band where you and we had to read some heavy stuff. Well, anyway, Oh, I wanted to say about Teagarden that although we were good friends and he seemed to like me very much, musically and... we got along reasonably.

In fact, I recorded with Jack just before he died. He hired me for the record date. And I think the sad thing about his life, or maybe it wasn't a sad thing, was that he never, although he enjoyed listening to intelligent people talk about the theatre or books, he never got into that himself. He was not what one would call a social kind of man.
No.
His life was all music. I think on
the days that Jack didn't play he might have been terribly miserable.
He wasn't an introspective man.
No, not at all.
He was a man that just operated on instinct.

Yes, exactly, and I think it was he made a sad great mistake in having a band, because if he would have remained a soloist, he might still be with us, but the headaches of an artist like that trying to keep a band going were are just too much.

I was always amazed that people like Benny Goodman, especially who was is a great artist, and Tommy Dorsey, could have a band and still play as well as they did. But they were hard men. They had to be.
They were ambitious men.

They were ambitious men, but they were hard men, because, you see, in the few times I tried to have a band, Helen, I realized it was not for me. That I could not be custodian over other people's live, that I had all I could do to handle myself.

And if the players in the band didn't like me, I couldn't play, where Benny Goodman and Tommy Dorsey didn't give a damn what anybody thought of them. They had this strong ego plus the talent and they were hard men. But I
will say that off the bandstand they were pretty nice people, especially Tommy. He was a lovely fellow off the bandstand.

Now Benny was always very nice to me. I think he might have been not knowing this, not being aware of this, he might have been a little unfair at times with different people, but he was always nice to me, but there were many musicians who complained that he wasn't the most lovable character in the world.

But I think that we have to understand that for a man of that great talent to try to run a band as successfully as he did, I think it takes it toll in some way, you become hard and selfish and completely impervious to the feelings of others.
But to get back to what I knew about Benny, he was marvelous to me, I must say, especially when we played in the Pollack band together as kids.
He's --
He was a magnificent player.
He's an odd person. I mean he's a person unique.

Well, if he were cruel, excuse me. I doubt very much that he is aware of it, because I have known him to do some very kind things. But I knew Tommy Dorsey to be -- really do some lovely things for people

and he was a hard, cruel man at times.
On the bandstand, get him off the bandstand, again he was very -- if he loved a band's playing, he would do anything for them. There is a marvelous story about this. Bunny Berigan was playing with Tommy Dorsey and one night he got terribly drunk and they were playing at the Pennsylvania Hotel and there is his music, strewn all over the bandstand, his stand is over, and he is lying there completely passed out.

Tommy's manager came up to Tommy and said, 'Why don't you fire that son of a bitch' and Tommy said, 'I can't fire him, he plays too good.' So you see, he had this wonderful -- he had wonderful respect for people who could play. Jazz soloists. Tommy is not a jazz man himself, but he did play some pretty nice things. He was a magnificent trombone player.
Yes.
In a dance, solo sense. And --

Well, if it's all right, let's go back to Dave again. Davey. Because I would like -- well first of all, on the subject of Davey, I mean people like Chick, I mean drummers that appreciated Davey so much and this was in the days before white drummers were really drumming.
Well, what I was going to say before
and I got off the track, but I knew we would get back to it and you have just taken me back to it.

I remember running into Max Roach who we'd say is the father or grandfather, so-called of avant garde drumming and I don't, although Max himself wouldn't use that category, but that's what the critics called him.
You are going back to --

Yes. I ran into Max. I had never seen him before nor had he ever seen me, but we had seen each other's pictures. And it was a cold February day in Chicago and I was playing the Blue Note, and I think Max was playing at the London House, and the wind was up about near the north side of so 45 miles an hour, Michigan Avenue, and we were both -- he was coming -- he was walking south and I was walking north going our different ways, of course, and we were really, you know, holding our coats, because it was terribly cold, Alaskan weather, in February, he looked at me and he said, 'Bud Freeman,' and I said, 'Max Roach,' and we got into a doorway somewhere and what do you think we talked about: in that cold for 35 minutes. Dave Tough.
Max told me how much he admired Dave and how the ideas he got...
Dave had gone then.
Yes, Dave died in 1948, didn't he?
Something like that, yes.
I think That would be the year, and there
were Max and I talking about Dave for 35 minutes and just a marvelous -- too bad all the avant-garde other drummers who copied Max didn't know that they were really copying Dave Tough.
Did he say that?
Well, no, he didn't say that in those words, but I know how influenced he was by Dave Tough.
Is that so?
Oh, no doubt about it, and Max and I on the strength of that, have been very good friends since. I ran into him in Italy a couple of years ago. Nice guy.

Oh, I am glad to hear that. And the one thing I wanted to bring out about Davey. Davey's concept was the same as Chick's or people like that, you know. His concept was that drums were the heart of the band. The heart of the band. Correct?
Yes, there's no doubt about it. If the man were the artist Dave Tough is. Chick Webb who is a super drummer.
And should be the heart of the band, is really Davey's concept.

It takes a man who doesn't get a noise out of a drum, but gets a sound. It's like another -- it is like part of the harmony, another note. Dave chose not to be a soloist because his whole understanding was --

he knew more about this music than any drummer I had ever heard. I am talking about the music, the thing we call jazz music. Dave knew about it, he knew -- he was the only drummer who studied the soloists and knew how to play.
For instance, you listen to him on a record date, from one soloist to another, he changes his style of drumming. Not style, but changes the background. He was one of the greatest --
That's what I meant, when I say the heart, I meant the heartbeat. So that whichever man will alter the heartbeat, according to the voice that it's accompanying.
And Dave gave the band a sound.

For instance, after all those years when Dave Tough went with Woody Herman and changed the whole thing around, gave Woody Herman a band that Woody was never to have again, although I respect Woody. He's a fine guy and he is over here in London appearing at Ronnie Scott's. And Woody would tell you that himself. Dave came in, and he made the, I think, the Four Brothers never sounded like that before or since, they played with Dave Tough.
And these young musicians to come on, knew of one drummer, Dave Tough, which was most unique, when you think that Dave Tough had been playing that way for 50 years. Just think, for 50 years.
Yes, for 50 years.
But that developed as he went on.
That is how long it was, 50 years.

Yes, he had been playing that -- Dave Tough, as I say, played professionally at the age of 14 and when you think of this great mentality he had, you can say a man could be an illiterate man and still be a great drummer, but I like to think that Dave Tough's great mentality made him the great drummer, because he was so interested in the -- he was a sensitive artist, he knew about improvising, he knew about composition, he knew the music he was playing.
That took some mentality. He knew every player he played behind.
Did he read, incidentally?
Yes, he was a marvelous musician. Dave Tough was reading music as a boy scout, as a child. He was reading music at the age of 14.
Oh, he was.
Yes, he was.
Did he pick up at the piano at all, I don't remember.
Oh, no, he used to with one finger, had to be fun kind of like that. Lionel Hampton's.
Yes. But Dave also, in his own personality, I mean he blended with people personally on
the whole.
Dave Tough was one of the most delightful you would ever want to meet, and had a brilliant sense of humor. I will never forget, Dave Tough was having an affair -- is this okay?
Yes.

Having an affair with in those days, a corny bandleader's wife, who was sort of nympho-manic, and her husband -- the bandleader came in and found Dave and his wife together and Dave looked up at the man and said, 'Thank God, it's you.' And you know, when you think of this, this man was so --
(Laughter)

Helen, I want to make a correction here. At that point, I said that Dave had been playing 50 years and that of course was a great mistake. What I mean to say was that he played, talking from this day and going back, he played that way 55 years ago. I have been playing 54 years and I think Dave played long before I, but he played really that same beat that same wonderful way, some 55 years ago.
So at that point, I think -- Dave died at the age of 48, so at that point, say, 1946, he had been playing then about 32 years. That would be right, he started at the age of 14 -- some 30-odd years.
That's right.
HEMLOCK

And when you think of that alone, or even if it had only been fifteen years, that is still a long time, still way ahead of his... And I think that when you suggested earlier that there isn't enough said about Dave, I certainly must agree with that, that I would like to suggest that fans go back to an album that Dave and I made, it's called from -- I think it's called From Austin High Comes Jazz or simply called Comes Jazz, and we used the Condon, Pete and Russell, group: Pee Wee Max Kaminsky, Eddie himself, we had Jack Teagarden, because Jack sings that thing, 'Jack Hits the Road,' blues, and if you just listen to Dave Tough on that, that is the finest -- I mean, how they managed to get it recorded so beautifully. John Hammond handled that date, tape, by the way.
Where, in Chicago?
No, it was done in New York, about 1938 -- the end of '38, and maybe into '39. It was a marvelous album called Jazz Band Tunes, and the way Dave Tuft plays drum on that --
What did that come out on, was it Columbia?
I think it was Columbia. I am not sure.
I am glad you mentioned that.
HEMLOCK BRASSABLE
I think it is called Comes Jazz. And it is fronted by me, although it had been Condon's group which, I fronted.

A very interesting thing, to get away from Dave Tough Tuft a minute, a lot of people think that the Summa Cum Laude band was my band. Well, of course, it wasn't. I had just left Benny Goodman and I hadn't the faintest idea what I was going to do. I knew I didn't want to be a band leader and Ernie Anderson, who now handles Charles Bronson and he is sort of a genius at publicity, was handling Eddie Condon, and as I say, there was a lot of publicity, Tommy Dorsey and Benny Goodman had this little war on and I got a lot of publicity out of that and so Ernie Anderson came to me and said, Bud, would you want to front the Condon band that's playing down at Nick's? and I thought said, Well this will be ideal because they had -- Dave Tough was later to come with it. He played with it from time to time.

Dave Bowman, a Canadian pianist who was one of the finest I had ever played with; Brad Gowans, the beautiful valve trombone player; Pee Wee Russell, of course, who became a world -- I want to talk about Pee Wee later; Max Kaminsky was still going very strongly; and then Eddie on tuning what Eddie called the pork chop, ukelele guitar; and myself on tenor.
And we went in, we were playing at Nick's and it became the place to go, all people from the theatre, writers and everything came to hear this wonderful band and as I

said, it wasn't my band, I just fronted it, and the name Summa Cum Laude, meaning I suppose of the highest laudatory monetary praise, was given to us by Eddie's wife, Phyllis Condon, who was quite a brilliant woman, good copywriter, I think, at the Darcy Agency, or Young and Rubican at the time, and no one to this day, knows what Summa Cum Laude means. In lauda, Latin, the summit; laudatory.
It's your highest degree, as far as the universities go

And so any way, people would say, what does that mean, they love that -- and you know, that band was catching on. We started I think, the first album job we made was for Victor. Leonard Joy was an A+R the man there who knew me from the Dorsey-Goodman days, who of course both recorded for Victor, and he came down one night, and said, I would like to record this, this is a nice little band.
Now this is before anybody felt that jazz bands were --

Of course, strangely enough, Bud, you see, well the name of the band, it ties up with you, because you always were a very much word man. You had that feeling for words and to my mind, I didn't know fronting it; you were just -- I just said, 'Oh, typical Bud, you know. thought, Typical Bud.
Actually, we never made any money with the band. I just loved doing it, as I say, when I left

Benny Goodman's band, I was so disillusioned, I didn't really know what I wanted to do. I know I didn't want to be a band-leader, not after having worked some 11 and 12 straight years with big bands, and worked-- you know.

I will never forget, when we were playing in theatres, we played --with Benny Goodman, Dave Tough and I now, and we played nine shows at the Paramount Fairmont Theatre, of a given day, and then we'd run out, get into a cab without putting our instruments away, run over in time to rehearse the Campbell show, which was a great radio program at that time, then do the show and run back to the theatre and do a show, and then at the end of that, we'd go back to the hotel, and finish there, at 1:00 in the morning.

On this particular day, they threw in a record date, so we were working; out of a 24-hour day, we were working about 18 hours, and Dave Tough said the following day, he said, 'You know, every time I sat down yesterday, I was playing the drums.' He was fantastic.

Well, Listen, Bud, let's just go back to Davey one more minute. I mean, so many wonderful people you've been close with and created together with, going grown up with, that there are one or two others that we do want to talk about at length, because I don't think anybody else as you are is as qualified to do so. But let's just talk about Davey about this one thing. I myself don't know, now where did
Davey get this feeling and taste for the things he loved and appreciated. What was his family like?

Well, Dave Tough came of a learned father. I don't know very much about his mother. I am almost reluctant to say, but I think he saw his mother die in a certain drunken fit. As I say, I don't like saying that, but then you are looking for the truth in these things and to lead you to -- to shed a little more light about what made Dave Tough tick. Dave Tough, who knows, maybe in a Freudian sense, all of these things started in our lives when we were about three years old. We don't really know, do we?
No.
But Dave Tough was purely an artistic man, a man whose mentality was way ahead of his time, a profound guy who was very learned, about the best read man I have ever met.
He must have been reading from his childhood, I guess.
He started to read, I think, at the age of ten, I mean, reading stuff that may have been over his head but still he understood words.
What did his father do, do you know?
I wasn't too sure about his father.
I just met him a couple of times. His father was a highly educated, sensitive man, who was --
Was he a teacher?
I am not sure. I am sorry to say, but I didn't know --
But that is where it came from really.

You see, I saw Dave's father twice I think and he was quite ill at the time, but I remember that he was -- he reminded me of Bertrand Russell, the same stature, same, I'd say -- well, from what I can remember of Bertrand Russell, who was one of my idols, he always appeared, although he might have been 90, he always appeared to be in his sixties. I would say Dave Tough's father was very much like that.
And has this poetic quality about him and was very soft and sensitive.
Dave must have related more closely to you than any of the others, I expected, didn't he?
I think that's true.
Because you shared that together, which neither of you really shared that with anybody else.
No, I think that's absolutely true. Of course, you know, I didn't know what he was going to become of me.

I was around Chicago during the bootleg era and I could have easily gone the wrong way, because I knew many of the people that were to later get involved in that and get killed and go to jail for the rest of their lives, and I feel that I was very lucky to run into Dave and that he did influence me a great deal, with books, with painting, music.

I am just wondering what accounted for Davey's compulsion to drink. I mean, he had a terrific joie de vivre, he had a greater appreciation of life than most anybody of his contemporaries, I should think. Whether it was -- he surely should not have suffered from a sense of inadequacy since he was tremendously talented. What do you think drove Davey to that?
Well, with all due respect to your question about the drinking, don't you think, Helen, that it doesn't really matter much what a person is, men don't drink because they are musicians.
No.

There are hundreds of thousands of people around the world of whom we shall never hear, who are drunkards and addicts. We will not hear of them because they are not in the limelight, so that all people in the arts who become famous are considered to be either addicts or drunkards, which isn't true, really. If you look --Dave Tough and Bix just happened
to be dipsomaniacs. Now a dipsomaniac differs from a drunkard, doesn't he?
A dipsomaniac is a man who can smell a cork and go completely berserk. Dave Tough was not a big drinker. He would take one drink and he was gone, out of his mind. But let's --
Well, would you say any of that is hereditary?

I just don't really know. As I say, if we could only know, so much of this may -- the child's mind is like a camera, it photographs pictures that can neither do well for it or destroys it as it goes on in life.

And at the age of three, we might make all our decisions. I don't know. But Dave Tough was just another profound guy and I found with profound people -- Bix was a profound man, with profound people such as poets, sculptors, sculptures, painters, writers, whatever the case may be, if I may say all sick -- we are all sick, aren't we?
Yes, there's a little imbalance.

When I say we are all sick, I think that I was very much influenced and frightened by my father who was an athletic man, and thought it was a thought it was a sin to drink sin to destroy oneself. He loved Dave Tuft and Jimmy Tough McPartland. They were at our home all the time, but he
felt very badly, he could not condone their drinking habits. They were not addicts ever. Never got into that. But a very interesting point, that our era had none of that.
I know it.
It was an thing to know,

Incredible. But we were all drinkers. I was not -- I never really got into drinking a great deal because, by having been an athlete as a child, I loved the idea of health and my father instilled this in me, and kept -- my brother to this day is a health nut or a nutter as they say in England, and I suppose I am too. We don't overeat, we don't eat a great deal, we are not big drinkers, although I do like a couple of drinks every day.

I am a golfer, my brother is very active in what he does. He takes long walks. We're really concerned with health. But I don't think that Dave Tough and George Wettling and many of the musicians we were raised with were concerned with that and they thought it was kind of corny. Although Dave Tough did play a little golf.
Oh, did he?
But, I think, to get back to your question, what made Dave drink. I don't think that Dave ever enjoyed drinking. It drove him crazy, but it was a way of escape for him, because he was so bright.
A relief from intensity.

Yes, certainly from tension and I must say that I enjoy drinking. I got a -- here am I at the age of 71 and I take two or three drinks and I feel marvelous, but I don't drink enough to get the bad hangover which I could not bear, because when I get a hangover, it's as though all traffic is directed at me and the world is against me, and in the Freudian sense I really suffer. But Dave Tough, you can imagine what Dave and Bix and those people went through when they woke up, it was incredible, and they had to have a drink immediately.

Bud, I don't -- in the sense we are sidetracking a little bit, but I feel pretty certain that J. R. will be interested in this, just as I did Red Norvo recently and we talked about a good bit about Mildred, because it was interesting, and I think J. R. will feel the same way, because Dave was one of the greats. So I just want to ask you, see, when I knew Davey, he had his -- I believe it was his second marriage in New York. Well, I knew him in Chicago, but when I saw more of him, it was in New York.
Davey was capable of tremendous strength in his attachments. Now, am I right in thinking he was married first in Chicago. Did he have a first marriage -- He was married --
Yes. I don't know where. I should have thought it was Chicago, and then he went to Paris and
took his wife to Paris and then she -- here we go again, talking about other people's lives, but I think it might be important.
I think it's very important.

But I think it brings in Dave's great sense of humor again. She had an affair with one of the members of the band, and so Dave found out about it and was brokenhearted, because he truly loved her, and he came back to New York.

I was staying in a big flat with Jimmy -- Jimmy McPartland, and we were doing rather well financially. Dave came back and stayed with us for awhile and in those days, many musicians stayed, maybe seven or eight musicians could stay in a big flat together, you know, we were always running in or out of town and call up and say, 'You got a bed or can I sleep under the bed?'

And so Dave Tough came back and stayed awhile and then a month later, his wife came back from Paris looking for him, and she came to that address and the day she came, Dave Tough was drunk and I thought, 'Well, I would let them have the flat for a couple of days, I think Jimmy was away on the road with a show, so I went away for about 48 hours, so that they could be together and I came back and she was now gone and Dave was still drunk and I said, 'Dave, what do you think of your wife now, after having seen her
for two days. And he said, 'I don't like her; she cheated on the piano player.'
So you get an idea of this man's great mentality.
Well, Bud, Dave's second wife --

Yes, he was married. We were playing with Tommy Dorsey, this was now 1937 and we were playing at a black theatre called the Nixon's Grand Theatre in Philadelphia and in the chorus, it was a black chorus, as you know, and a black pit band, marvelous band and of course, marvelous black dancers, but we were the attraction because Tommy had become a big thing and we sold the theatre out, and there were great comedians like Pigment Markham and he and I became friends and there was a little gin mill that we used to go in a back alley behind the theatre the whole show would go every day.

Now, I went to the bandleader of the Sunset Royal Band and I said, 'Would you mind very much if we dated the girls. We're going to be here a week and we'd love to take them out.' And the man said, 'Go ahead,' there was no jealousy, he was so nice about it, and he said, 'Go ahead, it's cool, great, we're glad,' because there wasn't too much of that going on and it hadn't really begun, so we, Dave Tough and I fell madly in love with two lovely girls in the show, and Dave married his lady friend and my lady friend later was to marry and Englishman and I think she is living somewhere here in the U.K.
I don't think London, but I think she is living somewhere in the country and it was --
What was Dave's wife's name?
Casey Majors. She was a darling little girl. And she was so marvelous for him. He quit drinking for three years because of her, because she straightened him out.
And I remember later when Dave was in terrible trouble, Casey would go all over the city and find him and rescue him.
She was marvelous. She was a lovely little thing.
She really loved him, didn't she?
She really loved him and he loved her.
Yes, I know that.

You know, in those days, I don't -- I think I prefer life today because I want to go on and I love life, I have so many things I can do, but I must say that that could well have been the best period of our lives, because we were -- Harlem now had become the place to go -- we are skipping a lot, but I am getting into that because that particular anecdote about Dave takes me into Harlem, where we were to hear the greatest pianists ever in history, Willie The Lion Smith, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller, Lucky Roberts. You name them.

And there was a way of life in Harlem, it was a marvelous village in those days. You could walk around there at 4:00, 5:00 in the morning and nobody would bother you and word was out that the white musicians were there to hear the music and everything was fine, not that they would have bothered us anyway. It wasn't that kind of place. There were some lovely places to live on the Hill. Duke Ellington for many years, had a beautiful apartment on the Sugar Hill.
St. Nicholas Avenue.
Yes. And there were so many marvelous places to go, there was good food, and people were marvelous to one another, the different races.
There was a feeling that is just gone.

It's gone, it seems to me because we have so much racial misunderstanding today and I think it's a shame really, because we got on so beautifully. All musicians, all white musicians, were color blind anyway. We weren't raised that way. My father never had any of that prejudice, you see. And we were, for instance, you know the old-fashioned business well, what's it like to sleep with a black girl. Well, what the hell is it like to sleep with any girl, you know, it's -- this is ignorance to ask such
a question, but people didn't really know.
No, you're right.

For instance, white people aren't as much to blame as it would appear. They were just simply ignorant about black people. They didn't understand them. They didn't know them. They weren't around and having been brainwashed all these years that a German was different than an American was stupid, really, because we are all really simply people.
They were much narrower worlds.

Yes, Just misunderstanding. I remember we were talking to a wonderful black old man, out at the sitting out at the ballgame in Chicago, Cubs game, sitting out in the bleachers park and Jackie Robinson had just broken into baseball and he as you know was a superstar and he was having a fantastic day, his first day playing with the Chicago Cubs, and Jackie was the only black man in baseball and of course, he was a big star and a big attraction and he had sold the place out.

And I am sitting out there and loving this so, because we had been through that years ago with musicians, I mean, we were always -- record dates were always black and white, and we were always trying to get together and we were always having jam sessions and respecting one another. Good, dear friends.
Now, I looked at this old black man, I think he

was about 80 and he and I seemed to get along well and he was very nice and he seemed to accept me as one he could talk openly to, as a white person. That is rather my being a white person, and I said to him, 'Sir, you have seen so much of life, what is all the racial misunderstanding about, why all the trouble?' He said, 'Son,' and I was proud to be called son, I was in my late thirties, he said, 'It's only one thing and it all goes back to -- you can go back as far as you want and read your books, but there's only one thing that covers it all. Misunderstanding.'
And I thought that was the most profound thing I had heard. He was not an educated man, but he saw it all and was 80 years of age.
And oddly enough, I think it applies more today than it ever did.

Well, it's a shame really to see what is going on. I don't get into these issues because I know what my life has been. I know that I can honestly say that my prejudice never went to anything racial. I think my prejudices were always personal. We are all prejudiced in some way and about something, obviously, but it was not possible for me to have it since I admired the black musicians so much and loved the music so much. And made a life -- you know, I didn't really know, Helen, when I first heard this beautiful music that
I was going to be able to make a living trying to play like that. It was such an esoteric kind of thing, you see I never dreamed.
So wildly exciting.

I have been so lucky really, in and all the good white players who were later to become famous soloists, were very lucky that they had this music to use because without it, it might have gone into the studios where they would have become old and not wanted. There's a beautiful thing -- I do not think this has been said before, Helen, about becoming a jazz soloist, that if you are real, genuine, the older you become, the more regard the public has for you, and I am seeing that now at the age of 71, living here in Europe, I have never known nor did I ever know that I was this -- I mean I had never known that I was this well known.

I am based here in London and the work I do is all on the Continent. I do Holland, Italy, France, Germany, Switzerland, Ireland, there is no end to the work, if I want to look ahead, if I am going to live another ten years, I will be booked up another ten years. There is no end to the work, as opposed to , and I say with all due respect to the United States, which is certainly a lovely and great country, because they are a great people, I doubt very much that I would have this sort of success in the
United States. But there again, I don't know, because Dexter Gordon the great tenor player, went away all those years, and now he has become an idol in the States.

Yes, but he has done something a little different than what you are doing. He had -- he's adopted a commodity in a sense. I don't know, I may be wrong, but I think so in a way, he's adopted a commodity, which is hogging the market, so that instead of you are always Bud Freeman and it is Bud Freeman that you are doing and that is who people are hearing, he is now doing something that's a little different from what Dexter Gordon stood for.
I think I am right, I may not be right.
Well, I heard Dexter Gordon one night at a concert, we were on the same show in -- it was in Verona, Italy, of course, and he --
When?
Oh, it was, I would say, back four years ago.

And then I ran into him on a bus, in fact, and he was -- I didn't get -- you know how it is when you are on a show, on a concert, you are in a dressing room with your horn waiting to go on, and if you want to hear that player, you have to leave your horn, which you don't like to do and go out and sit in the audience, so I didn't get
a chance to hear him. But I understand that he's playing better now than he ever has. I don't know. I have not heard him.

Well, I am not equipped to talk about it either, because I am not that familiar with what he is doing now, but I just had gained the impression that what he is doing now, very successfully, is something that belongs with the times today that people want to hear, and therefore, I just thought well, it isn't exactly the same thing.

So, I don't know. That's only sidetracking there. Your point about being yourself. He is probably right. I think there is a more limited public in the United States for a person doing what they do best.

Well, the only thing I know about this, you see, I have not given the United States a chance. Maybe I could do very well, because my name is bigger now, you know, being over here three and a half years has gotten me more published in the United States than I would have got being there.

I can only tell you that because now the world is so small and we have all the jazz journals and what not, and there was a show that I made over here called -- a film it's seventeen episodes, called All You Need is Love, and my episode was the swing episode. I don't know if it's hit the States yet, but it's

got a tremendous amount of publicity around the world, around the Continent. I suppose it will be coming. It's Tony Palmer's production, and mine is the swing era and in mine, are Artie Shaw, Benny Goodman, Cab Calloway opens it and Bing's in it, oh, there are all kinds of people and I have three little spots in it, talking spots, and then I close, they got me in a concert in Switzerland, with the Dutchmen College Band.
But I want to say that I never know with whom or with what I am going to play so I play with all kinds of different styles, you know.
So I have -- it's very interesting for me. I would not try to carry a group myself, I couldn't take the headaches.
No.
