I get on a plane -- just recently I played a concert in Munich, and I was on a plane in the afternoon, played the concert which was early and caught a plane back to London that night, an hour away. Takes an hour to get to Switzerland, an hour to get to Holland. Fantastic.
I know when I was talking to Red Norvo the other day, he does exactly the same thing. He doesn't even carry a bass player or anybody and Red is working steadily and doing very well and playing with
anybody, you know, I mean, they are booking him where people want to hear him so they are trying to put back of him the kind of group that will suit.
But, as you say, he's blending in with a lot of different --

Well, Red, of course, was always a fine musician. You know, people ask all the time, how does it happen that you can still play at this age and so on, well, I remember a few years before Coleman Hawkins died, I had an apartment in New York and he -- I didn't know this -- all these years was living just around the corner from me, and I saw him at a newsstand and I said, you know, we used to call him Bean, I said, Bean, why don't you come up to the apartment and have a little chat and have a drink. So he came up and he was drinking vodka and a sort of fruit juice, apricot juice, I think, and we finished the whole bottle. He stayed all day and we had a wonderful time.

I remember asking him -- Hawkins was sort of a loner, but he was very nice to me. We got along beautifully, and I remember asking him, how does it happen that you and I, after all these years, are still in demand today.
He said, well, it's as simple as this. He said, we are in demand today because we knew our instruments
when we were young. Isn't that interesting?
Yes.

I never heard anybody put it quite like that, and it held up. But, of course, I don't mean in any sense to compare myself to Hawkins. I think Hawkins when all the history is written and all put down, you would have to say that Hawkins was the father of the tenor saxophone-soloists. But, although I was a great -- although Lester Young started playing ten years, eight years after I played, when I heard him play I realized he had something all of his own that was -- I hate to use the word taste because taste means something different to all of us, but I thought that Lester had the best taste of all of the tenor players. And I loved Ben Webster too.
But to get back to Hawkins, he was a great musician, there's no doubt about that.
This is tremendously interesting, and we are just coming to the end of the side, so we will switch over, because it's a tremendously interesting subject that we're on right now.

But, I don't want to lose any of this as we begin. I think it tremendously interesting, especially to me when we are talking about the tenor saxophone players, we mustn't skimp words when we are talking about Hawk too. There again, Hawk's gone, and we ought to, you know, from
somebody who is eminently qualified to talk about Hawk, we should.

But, on the subject of Lester, It's funny, I told you I was a fan of yours long before I met you. When I was still in Chicago, and really before you had become any sort of a household name. What you were doing meant a great deal to me and I was a close friend of Jess Stacy's and you know, you were filling a role there that nobody else was filling. And, as a matter of fact, you were the only white musician I think we can say, perhaps, tenor saxophone player, that was blowing like that.

I don't think -- not that I can think of were there white tenor saxophone players in that category. Of course, plenty they came later, one way or another. Bud, you had have something special which I always heard right from the beginning, and when Lester came along, now, I couldn't say and you'll tell me about, you know, what Lester -- perhaps, what relationship the two of you had together or how much Lester may have heard you and when and how much you heard Lester, but I always heard something and the people admired you very much.

But I always felt that I was hearing something that other people weren't putting their finger on the same way. They all liked it, but I heard something else there. And later, of course, as people realized what Lester was

doing too, and loving Lester. Like, For instance, how Billie Holiday, above everybody, Billie interpreted Lester, particularly felt what he was doing. But it was something unique and different and in after years, as one hears the various records it becomes clear that there is a relationship between you two and I am not talking about one playing like another and or one having heard the other, but it's you might say in the same family.

Yes, well, that's very true because many people have said that we play a little alike. I am not too sure about that, but I only know that we were influenced by the same people. You can hear -- in fact, I have written about this in the first book called You Don't Look Like A Musician -- I was very much influenced by Louis and you can hear that Louis beat in Lester.
I never thought of that.

Maybe Lester wouldn't have thought of it as being a Louis beat, but you see, the difference between Lester Young's playing and all the other tenor players was that Lester swung everything he played. He never played a phrase to show off technique. He had the facility, he was a brilliant musician, but he played -- he was probably the most honest tenor player I have ever heard, because he just played what he felt and he had that -- now Hawkins had the great big sound that all

tenor players at that time were trying to copy. Lester came in with that little tiny sound and took over the whole world and when I heard it -- now, again, I had started to play eight years before this -- when I heard that, it reminded me of something I had heard many, many years ago in Chicago, that wonderful beat and the conservation of notes, the wonderful taste, and in my view, and it's just my opinion, having been there, Lester Young was the most interesting tenor player.
Now, again, I don't mean to say that I didn't admire Hawkins, which I did, and I thought really that Ben Webster was the best ballad tenor player I had ever heard of.

Now, there are many tenor players I admire. I admire Stan Getz, there are so many different players that I have tremendous regard for. Eddie Miller who played in beautiful taste, lovely sound and all that.

But I think that Lester Young had the thing that no one else had, and he was not frightened to come out and play that little tiny sound when everybody else was blowing his brains out. And Lester also had -- he had a marvelous sense of the ridiculous, not in his music, but in his way of life. I will never forget. You see, when the jazz solo thing started, we now left the bands, and I was the first one to go into this. Hawkins was in Europe, mind you, doing
very well, and I had just left the Goodman band, and the people who owned Kelly's Stables in New York asked me if I would want to come in as a soloist and they would put a band behind me.
I remember that.
I was the first one to do this.
I was there.

Forgive me, when I say the first one. I don't mean that I am looking for any credit. I just mean that it's interesting because then Lester Young was later to leave Basie and he went into the solo field. Hawkins came back, he went into the solo field. Webster left Ellington, he went into the solo field. Roy Eldridge left Krupa, he went into the solo field. All this started and we had a thing called -- we called it tenor parade.
There were about half a dozen tenor players and they all went up to play George Wein's place called Storyville in Boston. So we had the same rhythm section, we traveled alone.

Now, I followed Lester Young into Storyville and I used the same rhythm section. There was a black drummer by the name of Marcus Foster who had just adored Lester Young. Lester Young was his god, and so I told him that I was a dear friend of Lester Young, and I said, 'What was the first thing Lester Young ever said to you?' and Marcus

said, 'Well, I asked Lester how I should play behind him, as I am asking you.' I said, 'Well, just play.' Lester said to him, 'Man, all I want you to do is just tiddy-voo,' which to me, you know, this wonderful sense of humor.
And he said it was the most delightful thing.

Well, now, I am going to tell you a story that may sound to many people to be egomaniacal and God knows, I don't mean it in this sense, because I would like to try to live a gracious, humble sort of life if I can, and I don't always succeed with that. Evil gets ahold of all of us.

But this is a beautiful story about Lester Young. There was a critic whose name I shall not mention. Back some 30 years -- let's see if I am right, we are going into '78, so, yes, -- who refused to have a Bud Freeman record in his home. He loathed my playing and he idolized Lester Young. Now, he had invited Lester to his home for supper. His idol. And he wined and dined him and now, after dinner, he said, 'Would you want to come into my music den, I would like to play some records for you.'
They get in there and he gives Lester a cigar and some brandy and black coffee and he said, 'Lester, what would you like to hear?' And Lester said, 'You got any Bud Freeman?'
Now, I have to tell this story only because the

interesting ending of the story is this: that just a few years ago, I was to meet that same critic in London and he volunteered to tell me this story. Just some five years ago. I was over here on tour with the World's Greatest Jazz Band. He said, Bud, I owe you both a compliment and an apology, and he told me the story as I told you, He Said, I wouldn't have a Bud Freeman record in my home and when Lester Young said that, you got any Bud Freeman, it changed my whole attitude, and I said, Well, you didn't have to tell me that but that was very gracious. You have your right to dislike players as we all do, and what are all these things based on but opinion anyway.

So I learned one thing from that, Helen, that people have to be told what is good. A critic idolizes a certain artist and that artist can get away with murder. He can tell that critic that some non-entity is a genius and the critic will have to believe it.
Well, Bud, let me, since we are talking honestly and everything, let me take issue with you in a way. And that's simply this: Isn't that too sweeping a generalization?
No, no, I am just talking about the misinformed people who have written about jazz and made money. You know what I am talking about, because you and I have been friends for some 30 years.

Well, I have a tin ear in lots of places which I recognize. When I find myself not appreciating something in a certain area and I know where that is appreciated, I know that I have a tin ear in that respect.

But, excuse me, dear, I am only speaking of one incident. I am speaking, how was it possible for this critic to have loved my playing because Lester Young wanted to hear it. That's not possible. The critic was just being polite.

No Well, surely not, perhaps he actually -- I will tell you something, though, when I listened -- take sometime ago, listening to Charlie Parker who, after all, I preceded that generation, so Charlie Parker was not a musician who, his style, when he altered it, was not -- to me it was somewhat esoteric and it didn't register naturally and immediately with me.

And it was something that grew slowly on me, but when Dizzy would sing to me, what he was doing and what Charlie Parker was doing, I heard it then, where I didn't hear it instantly when Charlie Parker was doing it.

You have got to understand something. You have lived this music, you see. I am just talking about a man who idolized one person. He didn't idolize Duke Ellington and Louis. He idolized Lester, that was all there was to it, and everything he ever wrote, if he wrote
it was about Lester Young, a short story^A everything he wrote was about Lester Young.
Well, that is a bit off.
I loved Lester Young.

something about Lester: Let me ask you^A It's funny, I've got Lester on tapes and anytime I go out to the supermarket or anything, I shove my tape on and I am listening to Lester all the time. It just so happens that I have those at this time, and I will be just living with Lester daily, as I go in and out. It just so happens that I have those tapes.^A And Irv Goodman sent them to me and I have been playing them all the time.

And I've been thinking -- you know how it is when you hear something over and over and I have been thinking to myself about Lester. It seems to me that the gift that Lester had and what Lester does and it's what you had said in a way, what he's doing all the time is singing music and he's not selling sound. It isn't how he's presenting it and it isn't the total effect of what he's presenting, although it's there in almost a negative way, you might say, but it's the way his musical imagination and creativity and flow went all the time.
When you say he's the most interesting saxaphone player, that's because of the -- that's the kind of creative gift that he had, isn't^4 it?
Yes, as I said earlier, he dared to

come out and he wasn't frightened and play this little sound, which was a lovely sound, of course, and just went on, and incidentally, if you hear the records that he made after he played with Basie, he became a better player.
He learned it all perhaps in the Basie band, because he was originally an alto player, an alto saxophone player.
Yes, I know that.
But when he went on and became his own man and, therefore, had more freedom, you heard the real Lester Young.

Now, here's what his playing does to me. As you know, I live halfway around the world in my work and people invite me to their homes for record sessions and they say, what would you like to hear and there are always three people I ask for.
First, I ask for a pianist, because piano has always been my favorite instrument.
Is it?

Yes, I've never played the piano but it's my favorite instrument. I could listen to the piano for hours on end, and never get tired of it. So I ask for that. And then in horns, I ask for Louis, Bix and Lester, and Ben.
And Ben, did you say?
Oh, yes, very much so. I got to
know Ben, too, very well.
Wonderful guy.

Marvelous man. But, anyway, to get back to Lester, I find that in listening to many players -- I say get back to Lester, I want to talk about other players, but in listening to many players of that instrument, I get a sort of nervous feeling, but when I listen to Lester, I am completely relaxed.
Why do you get a nervous feeling?

Because I know that what they want to do, isn't going to come off -- I can say that about my own playing, I suppose, too, but when I hear him, it is just so soft and lovely. And then of course if you knew the man, you see him.
It's Just so relaxing, not trying to prove anything.
That's right, because that was the man himself. He was that way, wasn't he?
He had no axe to grind. It appeared to me in his playing.

And I would say this, I don't know whether you would say this, but just as Louis established an alphabet for jazz, almost, not only for trumpet, but for jazz, Louis did really in a sense establish the alphabet, didn't he, in a way.
Yes.
He used letters other people used before, but he stuck it all together and there was the jazz alphabet, from Louis. Well, in a way, you would say that Hawk did this with the tenor saxophone.
Yes.

So in a sense you might say that the tenor sax was influenced by Hawk, that came after Hawk, they all used that alphabet and more or less used it the same way. Developed it in different areas but used it the same way. So that in a sense when you hear those players, you are more often hearing usage of the alphabet as you are accustomed to hearing it, as you have heard it before, but when Lester played, he may have started with Z and gone on down to A, I mean, it was a different --

If I may say this, and I trust that all the tenor saxophone players who or read this, understand that I have tremendous respect and regard for all the great players of that instrument, but when Lester Young played, he told a story. I don't think that very many players really do. He told a story, whether he be short or long, he told a lovely story about his life, about his life, you see.
Lovely, Bud, okay, thanks a lot.
Give me that story.

Well, again, Helen, may I preface this by saying I am always frightened of talking too much about myself -- I don't mean to, but just to tell it because there is a relationship [between Lester and myself.]
This story about Lester, speaking of the nature of the man. He was very deep and very bright and conserved words as he did notes, to make beautiful sentences, and he -- I had made -- now, let's see.

I had left Goodman and Lester had left Basie just about the same time and I ran into Lester in 52nd Street, Gabler had the Commodore Music Shop, and I ran into Lester and I said, 'Would you come in and hear a Trio album that I just made -- it was the one I made with Jess Stacy and George Wettling and Three Little Words was on the album and so we played it, and Lester said, 'Oh, could I hear that again, and I said, 'Thank you, I am very delighted you like it.'

So we played it all over again and he started singing and whistling phrases from it. Now, I was not to see Lester again until -- let's see, that would have been I think I left Benny, about the end of '38 maybe '39. I hope that is the right year, although I don't think it matters too much.
I was not to see Lester again until I went to Chicago and got lost in the war and I came out of the war

and I came to New York and that -- I got out of the war just about a month after it ended, August of 1945, and I ran into Lester again in '46 and of all places, would you believe it, 52nd Street. He's going the same way. He was going toward 6th Avenue, I was going towards 5th, and before he said, 'Hello, Bud, how are you,' he said, 'That Three Little Words was a bitch.' Now, you think of the memory of this, again not because it was about me, but the lovely thing to remember.
I told that to -- who is the bass player who has such a marvelous collection of Lester Young stories, is it Gene Ramey?
Ramey, yes.
Well, I remember running into him at one of those jazz festivals in Colorado and I told him that story about Lester and he just fell out laughing and then he told me a beautiful story about Lester.

When Lester and Bud Johnson and Buck Clayton and some people were down in the Deep South, they went out on a party and the band, the Basie band left without them, the bus left, so they were on their own, expecting to catch a bus or a train since they knew where the next date was to be.
Well, in the Deep South this white bus driver refused to let them on the bus and Bud Johnson pulled an

instrument, and put it in the man's face, and said, 'listen you so and so mother, you are going to take us on this bus.' The man said, 'All right, you can go and sit in the back,' because the man was terrified. So they sat in the back and Lester -- here they were, everybody was tense and frightened and Lester Young claps his hands together like a little seal and says, 'Shoot your pistol, baby, shoot your pistol.'
Ramey Rainey told me that story, and it is just like the man. He refused to be frightened and always had this wonderful sense of humor, yet very deep.
I don't know that I should take the liberty of telling these stories.
Oh, they are wonderful.
Whatever they want to do about it, I would hope that if they don't use the story, you know, they delete it completely.
They won't, they will be very glad. What we are getting is very precious, but perhaps I am a little guilty. I have got to get you back, we have gone a long time.

So let's get right back to -- we still will digress a little bit because, let me ask you, if you agree. I mean, there are other -- it would be nice for you to say more about Bix too and possibly about Jack if you feel like it, and also maybe you -- well, we haven't even
mentioned Jess and what about Tesh. I mean, were you close with any of them?

Frank Tesch Teschemacher and I were close, we went to Austin High School together, and we had -- I was still playing the C-Melody saxophone and we had a sort of sax team and we would do -- were playing professionally now and getting as much as we could, we weren't really good enough to get -- to demand work, but Wingy Manone came to town and Wingy came right from New Orleans and he was the bandleader.
Wingy, you know, an interesting thing about him, he could get jobs, you know, he was a fairly good businessman, and terribly funny man, certainly one of the funniest men I have ever met.

And he heard our sax team and he liked us, and he took us out of high school -- well, I mean, we were in high school -- we worked on Wednesday nights, Saturday nights and Sunday nights at a ballroom called the Merry Garden Ballroom and we had a good little band and everything Wingy we played swung. You know, he was a very good player for that time.
Of course -- I will tell you about Wingy later. I saw him in Milan a couple of years ago, on a record date.
Did you really?
Yes, but we will get back to that.

Anyway, we loved Wingy because we weren't enough advanced to play with anybody that could play that well, and Wingy could play in very difficult keys and really get around the horn and had a narvelous feeling for the blues and a good beat, and he was a great singer, and of course, Wingy was solely influenced by Louis. Louis was his god.

And so, to speak, you asked about Tesh. Tesh was very much, probably more influenced by Bix Beiderbecke than I was and very strongly influenced by Jimmy Noone, the great New Orleans clarinet player, who had a most unique style, and Tesh and I would just play together because we seemed to like each other's playing. We could play phrases together. There wasn't much music to read in Wingy's band, we had to know the charts.

And I think that if Tesh had lived, as you know, he was in an automobile accident and was instantly killed, if he had lived, he would have become one of the greats. Because he lived his music, he had a great talent for it and was also a great musician, could read anything in sight and could write and knew composition.
Is that right?

Oh, yes, you know, in those days, we listened to music that had nothing to do with jazz as many of the great players had, black or white. We listened to people like Stravinsky, Jacque Ibert, Ravel, Debussy,
Scriabin, Honegger, Scrivener, Hunager, Gustav Holtz (phonetic), the lot and we

were introduced to this music by Bix, and played it all, who could play much of this music on the piano. You see, people don't know -- they think of Bix as being just a great cornet player, but he was a marvelous pianist.
I know, Jess was always saying what a marvelous pianist he was.

You wanted to talk about Teschemacher, I can tell you that no one lived jazz music more deeply than Teschemacher. He really loved it and his whole life was music, and I think that he, as I say, had he not been in that accident, I think he died when he was about 28 -- I am not sure of that age, but it seemed to me he was in his late twenties -- he would have gone on to become one of the greats.

Although he had a great regard -- he idolized Benny Goodman, he was not influenced by Benny Goodman. He was influenced, as I said, by Louis, by Bix, by Jimmy Noone, by many of the great black players of that day, by Omer Simeon who was a great clarinet player with --
With Earl.
With Earl, but before that, on the records of Jelly Roll Morton.
Terribly sad, Bud.
Well, it was sad, but Tesh, I think

really in the short time that he lived, lived a beautiful life in that he just lived music and you see, he idolized - as young people, we had a tendency, we were naive and instead of just idolizing the musicality of our idols, we wanted to live like them and I think that was a great mistake, because in following Bix' life, I think that most cornet players, trumpet players were ruined by him because they all became drunkards, you see, Bix -- it wasn't music that made Bix a drunk. Bix was just a dip-somaniac, as I said earlier, because Bix was also a very profound man.

And Bix was an educated man and he had great regard for the theatre, books, for anything artistic. It wasn't just music, but in the short time that Tesh and Bix were to live, they lived full lives, if being dedicated to music can be considered a full life, and I certainly would agree that it can be.

I always think of this analogous thing that Somerset Maugham wrote about a man who lived as a beach-comber on a beautiful island and when someone asked the writer how the man died, or why he died, he said, 'I think it was the beauty of it all that killed him.'
And, you know, there is much to be said for that line because I have seen that happen to people. They just die from living perhaps too beautiful, too dreamlike, too

fantastic a life.
But Then again, that could sound a little naive.
Who knows what prolongs a person's life, who knows what
cuts a life short, excepting that these men burned them-
selves out at an early time, just staying up all night
drinking.
Did Tesh drink very much?

Yes, he did, he became -- well,
I think he was -- oh, I wouldn't have called him a drunk,
no. You know, we used to drink some pretty bad stuff
during prohibition, homemade gin, and all that.

Tesh was a strong boy, I think he might have
lived, gone on to live a long time if he hadn't been
killed in an automobile accident.
Were you there?

He was riding with Wild Bill and
they were -- it was on the near North Side of Chicago and
they were struck by another -- sideswiped by another car
and Tesh went through the windshield.

I wasn't -- Wild Bill would remember more about
it than I, because after all --

No, that's beside the point really.
What we are really talking about was the musicians.

Well, good, I think you ought to say something
about Jess, don't you?

Well, Jess, there's a marvelous thing to be said for Jess. You know, in all the years, Jess and I had a job -- now, we had both been with the best bands. I was with all the top bands, Dorsey Brothers, and what not, and I would go back to Chicago every once in awhile, because I would see my dad and stay at home for awhile, and Jess had a job at a summer resort called -- it was near Dowagiac, Michigan, and I can't remember the name of the lake now -- it was on a lake and we were to play for dancing.
Jess had the job and he heard I was in town and he said, 'Come on up and we will give you your room and board and we will pick-up what we can.' I think we made about $2.50 a week apiece.

We had an absolute ball. We would play golf and baseball in the daytime and would be out in the sun all the time, having a very healthy life. We didn't really need any money, and we were playing together which was what we wanted to do.

Then I got a telegram -- my father got a telegram in Chicago from the Dorsey Brothers again and so I went back to New York from there and then I was never to go back. I went back for short spells with different groups and all that, but then I stayed -- No, I think I went back one more time when Mezzrow was getting a black
and white band together, that was long before Goodman and John Hammond gave the idea to Benny Goodman, as you know.
That's not the one he had in New York.
That was the band that Mezz had in New York, and so we sent for Floyd O'Brien and then we rehearsed --
That was a beautiful band.

Yes, remember we played just a few gigs engagements. Too bad that it didn't come off, but it needed financing. It was way ahead of its time because I think Benny was not to -- Lionel and Teddy were not to join Benny Goodman until --
The later thirties and then this band was being organized around '32, wasn't it?
Yes, yes.
So maybe three or four years later Teddy and Lionel went with Benny.
Right.
So Mezzrow was really first in that, I think.
Yes, I think he was, too.
And we had wonderful people like Benny Carter writing for the band, just to help Mezzrow
and doing wonderful things, coming to rehearsal and sitting in and Alex Hill, the great writer-composer-pianist was writing for the band, and he was a marvelous arranger.

And, of course, it was a labor of love sort of thing. I think I played about three or four dates with the band and that was the end of it, and then Joe Venuti came by Mezzrow's apartment and asked me if I would do a record date and work started to open up for me and I left Mezzrow's thing -- of course he had no work to go on and branch out and then I went from one band to another.
We will get to that --
Yes, but to get back.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

Well, let's talk about Jess. That is what we were starting about, so let's talk about Jess.
Well, we were talking about playing for $2.50 a week and having a marvelous time because we wanted to play together.

Now, Jess had never -- he too was very much influenced by Bix, very strongly influenced by Bix, played all the Bix compositions, you know, In a Mist, Candlelight, and played them very well and later was to make a record I think of some of these things.

Now, Jess went back to Chicago where he went into a Chinese restaurant, and I went to New York to do some freelancing with the Dorsey Brothers and I did not to see Jess again until I'd say about 193 -- it's so difficult for me to remember the years, dear, because after '32 I did stay in New York, but I think it was just before that, I went back to Chicago again, and Jess had a job at --
The Subway.

No, at a place, again, the Merry Gardens where they were having a dance marathon, and it paid very well, and he asked me if I could work with him for about a month. Just played for this crazy dance marathon where people danced for days on end without any
sleep, and who do you think won it, Frankie Laine, won the dance marathon and was to go on to become very famous. He was a very nice guy, by the way.
Isn't that amazing.
Yes, and then, I left that -- that ended and I went back to New York, where that now with Mezzrow and I was to stay on in New York and as I say, go from one band to another.
I was not to see Jess or do anything with him again until I joined the Goodman band and that would have been in 1938.

Now, Jess Stacy was a far more brilliant soloist than people ever realized but he was willing to just sit back, always in the background and play the accompaniment, play the band piano, never received the recognition he should have received, because he was a super soloist, having his own style.

Because Teddy Wilson, a super pianist, and a great guy, was the big thing in the Goodman band, being featured as a name and playing in the trio and quartet and what not, so Jess was always in the background, but since now we are talking about Jess, I want to say that he had a beat.
Again, that Louis-Bix beat that Lester Young had and many other great players, that very few pianists had and Jess was to influence many pianists without realizing

that he had influenced them and you must realize that after I left the Goodman band, I was with Benny a year, I did not see a great deal of Jess because he too left and went, I think, out to the Coast and then was to get out of music and work for Max Factor in the mailing room or something, I am not sure just what.
You remember he did -- he went with the Crosby band and he did do things like that.
Yes, he did. But I was not to see him because I was going off to South America and going to Europe.
You know, it's funny, when you spoke of those records, it was when you made those Trio records, that I was able to proclaim --
Yes, but we were still working.
-- you and Lester where it became were at the King (unintelligible) that there was that relation because it was right there. I think those Trio records were absolutely superb.
Well, those trio records are going to be put out here again.
They have already been put out in America, you know.
Yes, I heard. I have been over here three and a half years, as I said, but they are going to be put
out here very soon and it's all I think on the strength of Jess's playing. Of course, George Wettling played beautifully on them.
And those -- I would like to feel that those records have held up.
Oh, they have held up, they're marvelous.

Now, most interesting thing, I don't want to dismiss talking about Jess, but as you know, I did not see, over a period of years, I did not see too much of him and didn't have a chance to work with him. But this is the thing that happened, George Wein gave me a 50th anniversary concert, I think you were there, or I think Stanley was there, at Carnegie Hall about four years ago, and Jess came from the Coast and played on the show.
And while he was there --
Did the interview with Whitney Balliot.
Yes, while he was there, we made an album for O'Neal, for Hank O'Neal and Whitney Balliot came down to the record session to interview Jess and that became --
Part of the album, article.
Yes, it was in a profile in the New Yorker. Yes, well, on the strength of that, Jess was now an idol again after all these years and I wrote a

little piece because Jess and I had a wonderful talk, he brought a tape recorder and we had a wonderful discussion about the days, and I told Jess -- Jess said to me, 'You know, for the first time in our life now that I have become a free soloist,' he said, 'I feel that I am doing something worthwhile.'

And I said, 'Jess, you always were doing something worthwhile, but you have now become your own man. You're Jess Stacy and the whole world knows who you are and why do they know who you are, because of your unique style.'

So now after the profile broke in the New Yorker, Jess had become an idol and I have heard, since I have not seen him, since I have been over here, that he has had to turn down the work, there were so many offers. He and his wife had been very happy together and living a quiet life and he wonders if he wants to get back into the rat race of the music business.
So I just don't know whether he's taking all of the work or not.
Say that again, will you, Bud, because it's so nice to think of that happening right now.
Well, the marvelous thing, if Jess could get to know, and this eventually he will, I suppose, hear this and read it, he's -- all the pianist I have
played with in Europe, say in Holland, Germany, the U. K. especially, Ireland, did I say Switzerland, Italy, are trying to play place that Jess Stacy style.
Bud, wouldn't it be nice if Jess did come over --
I think it's a shame that he doesn't come over. He would be a big thing over here.
He never really had it on his own like that. If he did it with you...
It might be a little frightening. Well, it's difficult -- my agent handles about eight big American stars, such as people like Teddy Wilson --
Who is your agent?
Robert Masters -- he doesn't handle Teddy but he handles Benny Carter from time to time, Buddy Tate, Lockjaw Davis --
Not Robert Patterson.
No, it's Robert Masters, and he would love that idea. He brings Ralph Sutton over.
Oh, does he?

Yes, and what's the other pianist's name, Dick Wellstood, they have been very successful here. And he would love to bring Jess, I know, but he couldn't couple Jess with anybody else because it would be too expensive. But Jess could do very well on a tour,
it would be a very big thing, because his name is big now.
Of course, he may --maybe his personal affairs will be such that -- it's a great pity not to.
Yes, it is.
Well, anyway, I think we have given enough time to that, Bud, and actually -- in actuality we really have brought ourselves to the point of where you're --

Yes, excuse me, dear, I want to get this added thought in and perhaps it's a redundant thing to say and maybe it's an original thing to say, but as regards one becoming an idol after he dies, I think the amazing thing that there are men still playing and playing well in their seventies and eighties and perhaps nineties which history never realized was going to happen.

Because history seemed only to tend to idolize the man and make of him a great figure after he died and now what is history going to do about the guys who are still alive and what is history going to do and what is it doing. It is bringing the men back to a musical life the man could never had before he became an idol and Jess Stacy now is a living legend. It's a marvelous thing.
But does he know this and is he willing to give the rest of his life to the dedication of playing
around the world. I just wonder because --
No, I don't think he is --
He would rather have the peaceful life.

I think he is probably torn and possibly, you know, possibly, he would like to be flashes of something, you know, but I don't think -- I really don't think he is prepared to sit down and maintain a standard which he would need to maintain, his own standards, to work rather steadily professionally.
But I am sure that he would be very tempted if he actually realized and knew that the things were at the stage that they are, I think he would be tempted.

Yes, just on the publicity he's gotten, you know, making a comeback and of course, the New Yorker article, which is a tremendous piece. That is big international stuff, I think he would get the greatest surprise of his life, because when we played in the trio, we played -- we did a duet date since we were recording a duet, we had Cliff Leeman on drums and Jess and Cliff didn't hit -- they didn't get on too well together, so we decided without offending Cliff, who is a super drummer, that we would do a session with just piano and drums -- and George Wean heard about this and so he put us on to Carnegie Hall and we played two num-

bers, we played Don't Blame Me as a ballad and some blues in F in a fast tempo, and I couldn't -- Jess got a standing ovation and I couldn't get him to stand up, he was so scared, but he played beautifully.
From that time on, Jess Stacy could do no wrong, He was now becoming an idol--
What year was that, do you remember?
Well, as I said, I think we did the concert -- I had been over here three and a half years, so that must have been four or five years ago.
Not even that long.
Well, I have been over three and a half, so let's say it's a little over four years.
Because I was still with the World's Greatest Jazz Band, and we came back here -- You see, I left the World's Greatest Jazz Band here.

A very, very funny story, if I may throw this in, speaking about men who are still around playing well in their eighties and maybe a couple in their nineties, there was a bass player from New Orleans that was doing a show with a New Orleans band and I think his name is Russell, I am not positive of the name now, because I did not meet him, but this was the story I heard.
He was here in London, and I think he was in his

nineties -- would it be incredible to say he was about 96 and he was doing some one-nighters with this band and the English road manager, when they got to London, may I help you into your hotel room and the guy said, 'Oh, thanks, man, but I'm okay. I got my chick with me.' His chick is 78.
Gives you hope.
I am terribly sorry, I can't remember the man's name. Garland or something, oh, dear.
I don't know.
I am that way about names. I must tell you, Helen, a funny thing about names. I had an uncle who had the same name as I and I remember I was introducing him many years ago and I forgot his name.
That's hard to top that one.
Well, listen, we've got you out of Chicago. So, all right, --

I wanted to add and I think it is only fair to add, if I did not say this, that Jess was not only influenced by Louis and Bix, but certainly by Earl Hines, as I think we all were. Earl Hines had a style of playing -- now, here, it was Earl Hines who told me about the James P. Johnsons, the Fats Wallers, the Lucky Roberts and the Lion, because he knew, he was from Pittsburgh. He was in the east. He came out to Chicago
Yes, I think it should be said, too.
Of course, it's great to see Earl -- Earl has become an idol now and he's busier than ever he would want to be.
Yes. It's there to hear. You can definitely hear that -- it isn't anything that he's -- anything that he has physically picked up from Earl but it's in that rolling style --

No one had played like that before or since, and of course, Jess became his own man after many years of listening -- there's a little thing I say about myself when people ask me if any saxophone player influenced me, I say with all due respect to the great Coleman Hawkins, I was influenced by so many different things, the black dancers, the black singers, the pianist, the clarinet players, the drummers, that I like to feel that all of this and here I go with the again mania has rolled itself up into a -- sort of a Freemanistic ball in music. Does that make any sense?
Very good.
Yes, and that is what I think happened to Jess. I think his playing became his own.
Yes, and he always did like singers
Take all of the influences of Lester Young, yet look at how much his own man he became.
After all, that's the proper thing for evoluation, isn't it?
Yes, of course. We are all influenced by somebody and we always will be and we need to be influenced if we are going to be working.
And it's like growth, it's how you develop--
I think Eddie Condon said a very funny thing once, 'Can you imagine music that doesn't sound like music?'

Good. Well, listen, Bud, there is just one other person I do think we ought say a word for, because he was a talented guy and a wonderful guy and I think in fairness I think we should say something about George Wettling, too, don't you?

Yes. I don't mean to plug my book but in the -- this is the second book of anecdotes and vignettes that I had published in Ireland and it's called If You Know of a Better Life, and then the page turns over and the title goes on, Please Let Me Know. And it opens up with a story on George Wettling, the great

drummer. Now, George Wettling and Dave Tough were contemporaries, had tremendous respect for each other. George Wettling was one of the greatest snare drummers ever and had very profound wonderful feeling for the black man's music, was a great Louis fan. I think he idolized Louis more than anybody.
And Baby Dodds.

And Baby Dodds of course, and to George's dying day, he still had that Baby Dodds in him, and stayed so honest to jazz. He was a true jazz drummer and a wonderful guy, but unfortunately, at an early age, started to drink the bad gin around Chicago and never got away from drinking and he too -- he was a lovely fellow but when he got drunk he went sort of berserk.

He didn't really need very much. He like Dave Tough and Bix and many, many others didn't need very much to set them off. And they went completely out of their minds and didn't know what they were saying and what they were doing, and I write this story in the book, the book published in Ireland, which I just mentioned, opens up with a George Wettling story and I tell about the time George Wettling was playing with Paul Whiteman.
Now, when Paul Whiteman went on a drunk, it was a big, and he was a big, strong man and they were out in Texas and when you were honored in Texas, it was usually,

you were made a sheriff, they gave you an authentic sheriff's badge and they gave Paul Whiteman and George a complete set, a cowboy set, a complete outfit of cowboy clothing, the ten-gallon hat, the dungarees, the boots, the belt with synthetic bullets and a gun that actually worked, but with no real bullets, and a holster for it.

Now when George Wettling went on one of his drunks when he didn't know what he was doing in New York, he would go around, he would put this outfit on and go into these tough bars that were gangster-ridden and take out his gun and say, 'Why don't you so and sos go back west where men are men?' He was completely out of his mind and if it hadn't been for certain of these underworld characters who knew him he would have been killed. They would have really given him a terrible going over.
But this was George Wettling. Of course, it has nothing to do with the music, but this is what happened to him when he drank.

As regards his music, he was a true artist all the way and he spent, you know, he became a session man, as we call it here, a studio man in the States. Did very well, but he had the drinking problem and then he did want to play jazz and of course, he worked down at Condon's for many, many years, but he was one of the funniest people I had ever met. He could make up things -- he
wrote a beautiful piece, you remember, that was published in Esquire, called A Night Before Bopmas, which was a satire on The Christmas Carol. You remember that?
Yes, I remember that. And he painted, too.

And he was a marvelous painter. He was a pupil of Stuart Davis, who became -- you know, Rockefeller paid $80,000 for a Stuart Davis, which is just as you walk up into the Museum of Modern Art in New York, I think the painting is still there. It's not exactly a painting. It looks like a rug.
Is that right?

Yes, and it's a Stuart Davis and I think given to the Museum by Rockefeller and anyway, Stuart Davis used to -- Stuart Davis taught George Wettling art, taught him how to paint for a short while, that is, he was with him but they were very close friends and Stuart Davis used to paint to jazz records.
Did he?

Oh, yes, you take all the painters who knew -- I met all these painters through George Wettling, there was Pollack, there was the great Dutch-American painter who got, I understand a couple of years ago over $100,000 for a painting. I don't think any American painter ever received that. That was William De Kooning and I know his cousins who lived in The Hague, a
lovely house in The Hague, where I go to play.

Anyway, to get back to George, George was a very good painter and did some marvelous things. He would have gone on, I think, as Pee Wee Russell did, and we will talk about that later, to become a fairly good painter, but time was running out on him. He didn't take very good care of his health, and at the end, I went to see him -- his wife called and told me he was in the hospital --
Helen.

Helen. I went down to the hospital to see George and he was under sedation and he looked terribly thin and I remember going out to get him some magazines, and he wasn't drinking of course, but he liked chocolates and I got him some cigarettes and when I was out, I called up his wife and I said, 'Jean' -- you said Helen, but her name was Jean.
Oh, yes, it was.

And I just remembered that now. I said, 'Jean, I am terribly sorry to tell you this, but you should know, George is dying, and I doubt very much that he'll live the week out.' Well, as it turned out, I am sorry to say, George died three days later in the hospital.
But, I remember saying one thing to him and it broke him up, made him laugh, I said, 'George, I think

you are going to be okay, because I just heard the doctor say you were merely critical, and that broke him up. He laughed and then I told him -- 'Oh, yes, George, how do you feel being here in the hospital?' He said, 'Well, you know, Bud, it's not really bad at all,' he said, 'And furthermore, I don't have to carry those damn drums around any more.'

So you see, he was going out not really suffering. I think they had given him -- put him under sedation to take the pain away. I don't know just -- I think he might have had cancer of the throat or something like that, I am not sure. But he died laughing.
He was a very lovable guy.
He was a lovable man, but when he got drunk he was -- in a schizoid way, so to speak, he was another person.
One thing I loved very much about George, do you remember that he was tremendously devoted to his terrier, his fox terrier.
Oh, yes, and then of course, he had the cats he adored so much. The day one of them died he was so sad.
But I loved playing with George and of course, those Trio records speak for his marvelous talent, and --
You keep giving these wonderful
insights into wonderful people and I feel guilty, because I so love to hear you do it, but I must develop you in depth here now.
So all right, you are going to be leaving Chicago now. Now, let's stick with your career and digress just a little bit perhaps with Bix and Jack as we talk and Pee Wee.
Yes, we got the telegram from Mezzrow. I mentioned this earlier. It was forming this black/white band, and of course, we wanted to be in it.

So, Floyd O'Brien and I got on a bus, you know, the trombone player, and came to join Mezzrow. And we stayed, he had a house up in the Bronx, or up near -- yes, the Bronx, I was going to say near Harlem, but it was way up 167th Street, I think, and he had this big apartment where we stayed, we had no money or anything and we were just rehearsing, and Mezzrow was feeding us and what not, and as I say, the thing didn't take, I mean, with all the help of people like Benny Carter and Alex and what not, the thing didn't go and so I got offers to go with other bands.

And I think the first one was with Roger Wolfe Kahn. Now, as you know, Roger Wolfe Kahn's father was the famous financier, Otto Kahn, and every time we got a job the owners of the club found that Roger was the

son of one of the richest men in the world, Otto Kahn, so they would try to get Roger to buy the nightclub or restaurant which Roger refused to do, so that would be the end of our job and I said that being this wealthy was an obstacle in the way of getting work, because I was only with him about six months and we had about three jobs in the six months.

And it was a marvelous band and all the best arrangers in the field were to go on and become composers out in Hollywood and it was beautiful music to play, Of course, it was dance music, and I was just a jazz soloist in the band, and Roger was a marvelous guy to work for.
It was sort of like Isham Jones.

Well, it was better -- if I may say, the musicians were the top players, session players in New York, and they would be sending in substitutes like Manny Klein and all the great -- who I just saw recently in Holland. He was a super session man, as you know.
Anyway, that went on for about six months because we couldn't keep a job once they knew Roger was so wealthy and business wasn't good, why you know, buy in or get out.
From there I got an offer to go with Joe Haymes, and I don't think enough has been written about Joe Haymes,

who was a marvelous arranger and pianist but then he stopped playing piano and just wrote for this band and we worked at a place called the McAlpine Hotel in New York for about 18 months and in that band were such great players as Pee Wee Erwin, is still on the scene today, playing very well.
I saw him recently.
Toots Mondello, the great -- now, he has become quite a composer, having studied some 20 years with Creston, I believe.
Toots just died not long ago.
I didn't know.
Well, I think so. Benny and I talked on the phone not long ago and I think Toots just died.
I didn't hear a word about it.
Now, don't take that for gospel, but I am almost sure.
I am sorry to hear that, I didn't hear a word of it. Because he was a brilliant musician.
Yes, simply gorgeous sound.
Toots was not a jazz man, but a marvelous session man, beautiful musician and had studied all those years to become a composer.
Had he? I didn't know.
Well, I am quite sure he had
written several things years, but I did not see much of Toots, you see, after I left. I saw him a couple of times --

I may be wrong and you must might check with somebody, but I think I heard it this year, because I said to Stanley, 'Oh, that's very sad,' because he is a wonderful musician and then Benny and I were talking on the phone the other day, about something, and Benny said to me, 'You saw that didn't you?' I think Benny went to the funeral.
Now, I could be wrong, but --
Are you speaking about Benny Goodman?
Yeah.
Oh, well, then if Benny went to the funeral.
I cannot think I would confuse Toots with anybody else.
There was only one Toots Mondello
I thought you might have seen that in something, but you might check.
I hadn't heard a word about it.
So just don't take it for gospel, but I think I am right.
I hope you are wrong, but anyway, so let's see who else was in the band. I don't think there

was anybody -- oh, yes, Johnny Mince was in the band before I got in it, but that was the band that Tommy Dorsey was to take over, Joe Haynes is a very sensitive sort of guy, but he used to wish that he could stand behind the band, he was so frightened of the public. But He was a marvelous talent.

Then, from that job Toots Mondello and I got an offer and Pee Wee Erwin, the three of us got an offer to go with Ray Noble. Now, as you know, Ray Noble was a fine musician who had made a lot of recordings here in England and was not allowed to bring the whole band in to the States because of some labor law condition that existed or may still exist and so he brought Al Bawly, who was a very good singer in those days -- we are not talking about jazz now, we are talking about dance bands.
Yes.

MR. FREEMAN: And he brought his drummer-manager, Bill Harty, who was a damn good musician and we played in a place called the Rainbow Room. Now, in those days, it was white tie and tails, tiara and slippers, very posh and we worked in tuxedos, and we had in that band Claude Thornhill on piano, who was later to become a famous bandleader. I cannot remember the name of the bass player. Bill Harty played drums. We had Wilbur Schwichtenberg, who later became Will Bradley, the bandleader, a fine

trombone player. Glenn Miller, Pee Wee Erwin, Charlie Mince, Spivak, Toots Mondello, myself, Johnny Mince, who is very much on the scene today, fine clarinet player and George -- oh, dear, the great guitarist, George Van Epps, a super musician.
Yes.
I cannot remember the other players in the band, but we had a ball and --
(Unintelligible)
Now, if you are going to change this over, do it now, because I got a wonderful story to tell you about Ray Noble.
Really, when you called the lineup on that band, there'd be few bands of anybody's band that you could call a lineup like that. I don't think the Goodman band would be any finer, would it?

Well, of course, Benny was in another type of music and we were -- but it was dance music, of course. Our band was not -- Noble's band was not a jazz band in any sense, excepting that he allowed me to play and he allowed Pee Wee to play and so --
What talent.

And Johnny Mince, of course, and so I say we were with that for 18 months, but when you turn this over, because the story I tell will take a few minutes. Ray Noble was not aware that English and American were
two different languages and actually I became interpreter because in my travels, I was sort of an Anglo-philé and I used to go. --
All right, Bud, you try this and we will get a shot on this.

I used to go see a lot of British plays when I was a kid and I got to understanding the language pretty well and liked English. So Ray would talk, you know, he was a Cambridge graduate and we had a radio show, the Coca-Cola Hour, which was quite a big thing in those days and Ray would get into the control room during rehearsals and give orders, talk out to the fellows, and he would say, 'Fellows, take the last eight bars and (unintelligible). They couldn't understand him. They'd come over and they'd say to me, Bud, what the hell did he say.?' So I would interpret. Ray, of course, and I became very close because he used to say to me, Bud, did you ever go to school in England?' and I said, 'No, I have seen a lot of films.' You know, when Hollywood got going in talkies, they sent to England for all the best theatre actors of course, and we were all brainwashed pretty much by the British speech, Dave Tough and I, you know. So anyway, a funny thing happened, Ray -- I think

it was Wilbur well, I didn't want to mention his name, I might say that one of the men in the band was having an affair with a married woman, and it was a habit every Tuesday morning to show up at the rehearsal at such and such a studio at CBS at 10:00. No one had to say the night before that we have a rehearsal tomorrow, you just automatically went there.
But he didn't show up for rehearsal because this woman's husband came home unexpectedly and she locked him in a closet -- her lover in a closet where he lay for about nine hours.

Luckily the husband left in the morning without finding the man, so he came out and he called the studio and now, the rehearsal is all over and he meets Ray somehow, he said, didn't know there was rehearsal so now Ray, threw his pen down and knocked the music over and said very angrily, 'Didn't know, my ass.'

Now, the Americans musicians had never heard that word used with a broad A and there was a sort of double take of thought and they fell on the floor rolling and laughing and Ray looked at me and he said, 'Buddy, what are the chaps laughing about?'
So it was really quite an hilarious experience being with Ray, because as I say, the musicians just could not understand him. And there was the proof of the two

different languages.
Another marvelous thing happened with him. As you know, musicians were always through the years, pretty much treated like waiters, and they should have been treated like artists, you know, so whenever you played a swanky party, you always went through the kitchen and I wrote a story about this called, 'We Don't Go Through the Kitchen Any More,' and it has to do with this. We were playing in the Rainbow Room and some debutante was coming out and she hired -- her father hired the Ray Noble band which was the band they talked about in those days to play at this townhouse in New York, and we couldn't get there before 4:00 in the morning.

So we came in the front way and surely enough, we were greeted by a British butler, of all things, and he said, 'Oh, around the back and through the kitchen, fellows,' and Ray and Bill Hardy said, 'Out of the way,' and just pushed him aside and we went in and sat in the drawing room and just sat around and waited for the debutante to come and she came and was very upset and she said, Mr. Noble, I hired you for 4:00 and I think we should have some music immediately,' and Ray said, 'The boys haven't had a drink yet and we got to have some champagne,' and as incredible as all this seemed to be to the girl, they sent down to the cellar and we got some champagne and we came up and were sitting around drinking and

then we started to play. Now, we had a contract for a lot of money, maybe two or three hours, and we played about one hour, and then she came and she wanted the band to play later and Ray said, 'Oh, no, nothing doing, we're very tired.'
Then we left. And I thought to myself only the British could get away with that in the States so I called the piece "We Don't Go Through the Kitchen Any More."
That's very good.
But I must say, it was a great musical experience, Ray was a fine musician and he was a gentleman.
How long were you with him?

I was with him 18 months. There was a very funny story about the ending of that. You see, the main number of them were being let out, or were a group leaving for other offers and Glenn Miller got very drunk one night and he said, 'You know, Ray, if you're not careful, they are going to be saying, here come the British with a [bad, bad band.']
That was a funny thing to see, you know, when Glenn Miller got his own band, he completely stopped drinking and became quite the disciplinarian and of course, became a tremendous success.
I knew he did, but I didn't know he was a very heavy drinker.
Oh, he was a big drinker in those days, oh yes, [good heavens, oh many years.]
Is that right?

Once he stopped he was able to go out and become a big success. But there are so many funny stories of course to tell about the experience with Ray Noble, as I say he was a great musician and he wrote some beautiful songs, but he and Claude Thornhill didn't get on too well and I will never forget the night Claude left. Now In the Rainbow Room you had a big stage like in the back, on either side of the platform stage were two flights of stairs and the acts would or were run up under a spotlight, They would come out of a velvet curtain and down the stairs, running down and on to the dancefloor to do their acts.

Some of the best acts in the world and it was so funny to hear Ray Noble introducing these acts, 'Now, ladies and gentlemen, from the continental (unintelligible) we have so and so, and the people didn't have the faintest idea what he was saying. It was all a lot of fun.

And the night that Claude Thornhill decided to leave, he got up -- now, in those days, we had these sort of plastic-paper combination like music cases and they were very fancy, with our names on them, Ray and his orchestra, very expensive, and they were paperweight without

of course, music in them and Claude got all of those and Claude had this sort of straw-like, sandy-like hair, and he combed it all down to the sides and was monstrous looking and he was the funniest little man in the world, anyway, being the fine musician he was, he was crazy. He got up on the stage and the spotlight is on him because somebody in the house thought it was an act, and he's going to leave and he has all these music cases, all over, like a -- like stocks of bananas, you know, and he's looking down at the people, all laughing like hell, and he said, 'Ladies and gentlemen, I'm going to leave and this is the last time you'll ever see me. Goodbye.' And he left and we never saw him again.
And an hour later, Ray Noble looked at his watch and he said, For God's sake, where's Claude? Well, anyway, that was it.
The next time I was to hear of Claude, he had a big band. Writing serious music.
Ray didn't realize what was going on.
Ray didn't have the faintest idea that Claude was leaving. But that was Claude's crazy way of leaving the band, instead of going through the two weeks' notice -- pardon.
And then he had that good band.
Yes, he had that band that played some very serious music, if you listen to Claude's compositions, they are beautiful.
Very fine musician.

One of the funniest people I ever met. In those days, the musicians all roomed together -- a big flat -- and you took a very expensive place and roomed together to save the rent. And I will never forget some of the funny things he used to do, not realizing that he was being funny. Just -- we used to go down to the bar, as you know, the Rainbow Room was in the Rockefeller Plaza, NBC, of course, all that. And there was a bar called Hurley's, sort of a hangout for all the well known people in for radio, radio being a big thing in those days, so we were always there, seven nights a week, always drinking, but I don't recall having seen Claude drunk. He was just crazy, did some wild things.

But a great guy, and he -- you would never think of him as being a very serious musician. He wore a hat. He just never thought about how he put the hat on, he just slapped it on and his hair would be falling down from his eyes and his tie to one side and his clothes never seemed to fit him. He had no regard for that. It was just so funny. He was very intelligent, very deep, and had a great feeling for music and many artistic things.
So then what happened.
You mean, in what band.
Yes. (With you.

I got an offer then to go with Paul Whiteman just for a short spell. Carl Kress, the guitar player who died a few years back. I joined a little band in the Whiteman band. We were doing the a program which was called the Woodbury Soap Hour, which was a big radio show, and as a matter of fact, Johnny Mercer was writing material, songs, and singing in a group on the show, and in the band were Jack Teagarden, Charlie Teagarden, his brother, a marvelous trumpet player, let's see, Frank Trumbauer, C-melody saxophone. I am trying to think, Carl Kress, I played tenor, Carl Kress guitar and it seems to me the pianist was Roy Bargy from time to time. Remember the name, he was a fine writer, wonderful musician.

And so we had that little band and that was all we did, and then we made a few records with Whiteman. I was only with him maybe a month. And then I got the offer to go with Tommy Dorsey and went with Tommy.
You were with Tommy a good while, weren't you?
I was with Tommy at least two years. It's difficult to remember because I think I joined him
in 1936 and I remember Dave Tough was in the band, Max Kaminsky, Tommy --
How long was Dave in the band?
Dave was in the band before I got into it. And I was with Tommy about, certainly two years, and I think Dave was with him a little longer.
Were you happy in that band?
I was happy because --
Bud, you were just telling me that you enjoyed it in that band, but you hadn't yet told me why. Will you go ahead from there?

Although it was essentially a dance band, and Tommy had to feature his beautiful solo playing, he loved jazz soloists and whenever he could get one, if the price was right, he would bring them in the band.

I think if Tommy had had his way, he would have had a complete 18-piece jazz band, but he was selling dance music and of course, his beautiful melodic trombone and dance music was the thing in those days. But, again, to answer your question I was happy most of the time because Tommy let me play almost every tune we played that he wasn't featured on, he let me play several choruses.
When we played in theatres, I'd get out in front of the band for maybe 10 or 15 minutes and play. It was incredible, maybe 20 or 30 choruses on a song and

it became very exciting and Tommy loved it and I think that that and recording with Tommy gave me the name that perhaps I have today. It's difficult to know because I think essentially we all become our names through our recordings, don't you?
Yes, but then you were doing broadcasts too, weren't you?

That's right, but of course, I am not too sure that our names were mentioned on the broadcasts in those days. When I stood up to play a solo, I don't think the man said, now this is Bud Freeman on tenor. I am quite sure that he didn't, because we used to hear them all.

For instance, we were getting -- as early as 1937, we were getting residuals, you see, from the broadcasts. I remember we got residuals for a whole year of broadcasts we never knew we were going to get, but the union had passed the law that if things are rebroadcast, we then get a residual. That to a person who may not know, is like a royalty, but you actually got paid for the complete show. You got what you originally got for the show.
And I remember we got a whole year's, that was 50 weeks, residuals. It was quite a sum of money and a few drinking musicians disappeared for awhile.
But Tommy, as I said earlier, Helen, in order

for people like Benny Goodman, Tommy, highly talented people, to run the bands and take over custodianship of all of these people they had to be hard men. What do I mean when I say a hard man? If I were to have a band and God knows, I never tried, except I will tell you some very funny cases where I did try to have a band -- if I were have a band, I couldn't play if I thought that one guy in the band disliked me.
And how would he come to dislike me, by my being a hard egomaniacal leader as one had to be. Do it my way or else. God knows the things that Tommy --

So, I would say that with all of that, Tommy and Benny were pretty nice guys. Of course, when most people hear this, they are not going to agree with me that Benny was a nice guy, but I knew Benny as a kid, as I said earlier on the tapes and we don't have to go over that again, but what you want where I am going and what the next band is.

Well, I would say the best time I ever had, the most freedom I ever felt in a band, essentially a band of regimentation, I mean, you had to play in the section, you had to wear a tuxedo, you had to do -- be there. You were, in a sense, almost in jail, and the music -- if I had not been a player of improvised jazz, I couldn't make take it. I loathed the idea of having to do what somebody wants

me to do. Music should be a freer thing than that. But, again, in all realistic remembrance, it wasn't a bad deal for me, because I had a chance to play. But I often wonder about the guys who had to just sit back there at the back and play and take Tommy's insults and all that. It must have been pretty rough.
Now, later on, well --
Was Sy Oliver in that band?
No, Sy came along much later than that. You see, Tommy always admired the Lunceford band.

The one thing that Tommy loved in a man's playing -- just playing jazz was not important enough -- that jazz had to have showmanship in it. Therefore -- well, a perfect reason for saying that is that he absolutely idolized Charles Shavers, and Charlie Shavers was a brilliant player but he was a theatrical player -- everything was done for an effect although he was a highly talented guy and I loved him, you know, but Tommy thought that Charlie Shavers was the greatest thing that ever happened, because Charlie Shavers would make up all kinds of contrived little phrases in a given theme.

Like, he would play other songs in a theme, anything to be tricky and clever, you see, and Tommy ate that up. Tommy didn't see through that as being kind of synthetic jazz, but Charlie Shavers was a great trumpet player. Don't understand, nor do I want anybody who hears
this or reads this, Charlie Shavers was a very talented guy. But that was the way he played and Tommy thought it was great.
I don't think Tommy would be a great admirer of a guy like Buck Clayton, who was a pure player.
I mean the point is it comes out in taste, and if you got that kind of taste, you got it. It's not what you call good taste in music. It may be good taste as far as selling a product is concerned.

And so the Lunceford band, although it was a super band, was a pretty commercial band. The guys with the horns up in the air, all done beautifully, and very swingingly, but that was what Tommy's idea of a great jazz band, you see.
And so he loved Sy Oliver's arrangements, thought Sy Oliver was a genius.
Sy's arrangements did swing.

Oh, Well, Sy Oliver is a highly talented man from way back. But I was speaking specifically of the style of the Lunceford band. I don't think it was built [unintelligible] around Sy -- one of the powerful writers.
But Tommy loved the musicality of the band also and that would be Sy Oliver's -- so when he got a chance to get Sy, he grabbed on fast, and I think Sy -- of course, Sy is a big success today.

Well, Sy is operating on the same principle today. Sy is selling a nice musical product. He plays waltzes, he plays rhumbas or what have you, Latin American things, and he's very smooth and he's very nice and it's musical. It's very nice but, of course, it's a musical product.
Yes. But the thing is that Sy, I think -- it's difficult to say, but I think Sy's arrangements gave Tommy a whole new life.
Maybe he kept him going, and it's difficult to say because Tommy's name was already established and he liked Guy Lombardo.
You see, once a thing was established in the dance music field, there was not -- that was it, you were there and you were there to stay.
If Lombardo had lived to be 1000 his music would still have sold.
Sure and he wouldn't have altered it.

He would be an institution. Take the case of Woody Herman today, he's an institution. He can go on as long as he wants to work. Because he's done it. He has done a great job. He's a lovely guy and he is marvelous -- I saw him the other night on unintelligible show here. He's an institution.
Benny Goodman is an institution. Tommy Dorsey, Glenn Miller, they are institutions. So it didn't make much difference what they did, but I think that Sy Oliver gave Tommy a whole new life.
Well, something in the sense of Fletcher being Benny's -- gave

Well, there is no doubt about it. You see, Benny Goodman started a long time before I did and of course, Benny Goodman compared to me, I mean, Benny Goodman was a true genius, at the age of 12 he was a superb clarinet, and I remember -- he was not as involved in jazz as I was, and I remember one time playing with the Pollack band in New York, and we were all sitting around, Glenn Miller, Benny Goodman, Ben Pollack -- But Ben Pollack knew, and I happened to say -- we were talking about a player and I said, 'Well, I don't think he understands how to play the blues,' and they all broke up laughing, because Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller didn't understand what I meant by the blues. They thought that the blues was Ted Lewis and they thought that was a corny remark that I made and years later they were both to come back and apologize to me. They said, 'We didn't know what you were talking about when you said blues.' Glenn Miller specifically; he said, 'Yes?' And I was only quoting Jack Teagarden who called and said, 'let's play the blues,' man, and we knew that the blues but

was something. But Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller didn't. This is 1928 I am talking about. They were putting me on because I mentioned the blues, because they were identifying with something Ted Lewis did, Blues My Naughty Sweetie Gives Me.
The white man's blues, you see, and anyway I don't know what brought that to my mind. Tributaries of thinking.

Well, I will tell you what, I think we ought to go back a second there, because actually from a jazz point of view, you pardon me, we take all the misery out of that word. It's got to be used, you got to express yourself for what you mean.
So, forgive. So, from a jazz point of view, Ben Pollack is a lot more interesting to me. than Tommy Dorsey.
Oh, Ben Pollack was a marvelous drummer, and he was one of the first people to understand jazz and he was one of the first men to hear King Oliver and Baby Dodds.

I remember one night he was telling -- just happened to mentioned to Glenn Miller that he thought Johnny Dodds was a great clarinet player and Glenn Miller was insulted. He said, 'How dare you say that in the presence of Benny Goodman.' They had a big argument and I wanted to break in, but I was new in the band, so I didn't.
And Glenn Miller just stood there -- he was a Denver guy, he didn't know anything about the early jazz.
He thought that Benny Goodman was the first jazz clarinet player that ever lived. True enough, Benny Goodman was a great artist, we all know that.
That is needless to say, but God, there were guys that played clarinet before Goodman that really --
Well, I am surprised Benny didn't speak up because he knew about Jimmy Dodds -- Johnny Dodds, and Jimmy Noone -- the same thing.

I never wanted to talk about these things. I never thought I would write about them but they are things that should be perhaps -- that might be of some interest to people since they are true. That it was not until Bix took me and Jimmy McPartland up to Harlem to hear the Lion that the rest of the white guys in the Pollack band started to go up to Harlem, Benny Goodman being one of them. Long after us.

Naturally, Benny Goodman's background was a disciplined background, beautifully trained clarinet player, a genius, having played again as I say professionally at the age of 12, and he was not grounded in the jazz that we understood as kids. I lived at the Sunset where Louis Armstrong and Earl Hines were playing.
Benny might go out there once a month or something because is different. which is his background was Mine is a raw uneducated musical background whereas Benny's was a highly musical background,

from a Let us say from a symphonic point of view, but I started out just loving this new music, and frankly, I doubt very much that I would have become a musician at all if I had not been interested in jazz.
I would have done something else because I never wanted to be a studio player. I never wanted --
You weren't thinking of a career.
I didn't want to be a slave. Jazz music was a way out, finding freedom of expression. I may not have thought of it at the time but now in retrospect, I know, that is right.
That's what your instinct was, and you knew.
Of course, Benny could have gone on for the rest of his life, going into symphony or doing something with the clarinet, because he had the education in musical background.
You didn't say -- you talk about Mezzrow sending for you and about it not really coming off, but you didn't say -- we didn't get to Pollack, we missed that.
Now, how come Pollack asked you to go to work and when did that happen?
Well, I thought I mentioned it earlier.
You did mention that, but we did not go into it.
You see, when I made the Condon-McKenzie record on Okay, it was on the strength of the solo that I played there, when I got into the Pollack band - you are right, I didn't say that.

And I must say, Glenn Miller, Benny Goodman and Jimmy McPartland spoke up for me -Fud Livingston was leading the band and they wanted a tenor man right away and they were going to New York on this new job. We were then in Chicago.
They were passing through Chicago?
No, they weren't passing through, they were playing at the Black Hawk, where Crosby was later to go.
Oh, I see.

Fud Livingston got a fantastic offer from a fellow by the name of Nat Shilkret, Nap Shokert, who was a big figure with Victor Records, fine musician, and Fud was to arrange to come to New York and freelance and I don't know that he was going to play, I think he was going to write.
Well, poor little Fud -- he had a drinking problem and when that fell off he went back to playing for awhile and went with Whiteman where he played, but Fud Livingston
was a marvelous saxophone player, tenor player and clarinet player, and he had a great love for music, especially jazz music.
What happened to him?

Well, he died. We were playing -- let's see, what would the years have been, in the fifties, maybe '53, '54, we were playing the Metronome -- the Metropole, you remember the jazz spot where we played up on the little stage, and Fud came in one night wearing a big Halloween nose, one of those clown's noses, and came in one night, and I thought, oh, poor Fud, he's gone, and he was standing there and he was almost out of his mind with drunkenness and not long after that they found him down in Skid Row in New York, found him dead on a stairway. But what a super talent. We are not talking about Fred Livingston, but there was a guy who burned himself out. He started out at the age of 19 and was on the top of the music business and then ended up. . .
Sad, isn't it?
But I don't think he knew it because he was pretty much gone, I think the last ten years of his life.
But we were talking about the Pollack band, and you said, why did we not get into talking about Pollack.
Yes, that's right.
Pardon?
That was your first experience in a big band with wonderful guys at that time.

Yes, a big band in those days was ten men, and I say, Glenn Miller, Benny Goodman -- and Benny Goodman was so nice to me. I had never sat next to anyone that played that marvelously. And Pollack played the drums.
And Benny was very nice to you?
Oh, Benny Goodman was a marvelous young man.
Is that right? So he wasn't as standoffish and he wasn't --

Oh, Benny Goodman was the finest man you would ever want to meet until he got into the big band thing and had all that pressure on him and nervousness, and I say it is an amazing thing that a man that is as great an artist as he was, could have managed to run a big band, which he did.
I mean, he knew what he was doing and he knew what he wanted and he was like a machine, but when he was cruel, I doubt very much that he was aware of it.
