No. Benny lacked and does to this day awareness of what an ordinary guy feels and thinks, an
ordinary musician I should say.

I have said many times and now we are on this, we got into it and we may as well go all out, Benny lives in an egomaniacal shell that prevents him from -- well, I think, instead of being a part of the world, he thinks of himself as being apart from the world. I think the world is built -- Benny's world is built around Benny.
Perhaps that's true of all of us, but I think that if you go as far as he's gone, you are bound to be cruel to people.
I don't mean to imply that he is cruel, because I didn't play with him when --

We weren't going to talk about Benny Goodman at this stage, but since we got into it, I would like people to know something they may not know about Benny Goodman. I think Benny's father died when Benny was very young and Benny supported a big family, I think of which is some 12 people, which I mean, was quite a loving thing to do, and let's give the man credit for that.

I must say that he was far less selfish than I might have been in the same -- you know, I would have just run off and just gone amuck or something, but Benny stayed and supported them and saw them all through and gave them a lovely life and ended up, and one had to work pretty damned hard to do a thing like that, so I think that in finality we could not call

Benny Goodman a selfish man. I think that being a genius and being -- having begun music so early in his life and having lived music and thought nothing but music in his life, he might have tended to become completely impervious to the needs of his fellow man, needs from a social point of view. And that many times when you talked to him, he seemed to be off in space.
Well, of course, he was. But I had known Benny to do many kind, loving things, so I could not judge, from my point of view, I could not judge Benny Goodman as other people have.
No.

What I talk about is only hearsay, which perhaps shouldn't be talked about, but I wrote a little piece in my first book about, I say, in defense of Benny Goodman, that when one hears the pernicious things he is supposed to have done, one readily wants to hate him, but Benny Goodman came in to the Roosevelt Hotel about six years ago when I was playing with the World's Greatest Jazz Band and he was absolutely charming, you know, just another guy, that but I never knew.
And another thing about him, Bud, do you know he goes to -- I mean, when people go, Benny is there at that service. Billy Strayhorn, no matter who. I mean, if he's known them, he's there.
If there is something to hear in music,
he'll be there. He's all music.
And God knows the man -- I don't think that there was any luck in his career at all. It was all talent and hard work, a true realist. I never saw a man work as hard as he did. Never.

Bud, one thing I think that should be said in fairness to Benny and I'll see if you agree with me, and that is the way he was endowed made it hard on Benny because it came naturally, he studied hard and worked hard, but the gift was there and in all fairness to Benny, he never -- I don't think that Benny really recognized the size of his gift, he thought that this is what is meant by saying you're a musician, and he judged people by what he had. He wondered why people -- he wondered why guys were slow.

I will tell you something analogous to that, very interesting. There was a great, to me, the best saxophone player I ever heard, not jazz, but a great musician by the name of Max Farley. You wouldn't have known about him because he goes way back to the early Whiteman days and Whiteman used to say about him, I never saw him sober but I never heard him make a mistake.
There was a marvelous thing. Max was my saxophone teacher -- I studied many times with different people and he was a beautiful musician and I remember one-- we were playing
Wolfe Kahn Wolfe Kahn

with Roger Wolfe Kahn -- he got me in the Roger Wolfe Kahn band and he played something so beautifully that it brought tears to my eyes, the sound. He was the first man to get a singing sound on the saxophone, like a violin or a cello, and he played it so beautifully, I was in tears and I said, I don't mean to embarrass you, but that's the most beautiful thing I have ever heard played on a saxophone, and he turned to me, and said, 'Isn't that the way it's supposed to be?'
So there's your answer. The guy says --
That's it. That's absolutely it.

So, you know, Tommy Dorsey was the same way and expected everybody else to have that, so perhaps in that way, they were cruel but they had this great gift, but don't think they didn't work terribly hard.
Right.

You remember when -- well, you wouldn't know, but when I was very young, there was a great critic by the name of James Gibbons Huneker and he wrote all kinds of fantastic books. He wrote a novel about Mary Garden called The Painted Veil, I think, and he wrote about some beautiful things about Caruso and he wrote beautiful stories about Chopin and just a great theatre critic and I remember a line when he first heard ragtime and he said, 'I don't think anything's going to come of this.'
And starting to think of this one beautiful thing he
said about talent or about genius and he said, 'The piece was called How Not To Be a Genius, Just Don't Work Hard at It.' Isn't that lovely? How Not To Be a Genius was the name of the piece.
Yes, excellent, awfully good.
Benny Goodman and Tommy Dorsey were the kinds of guys, you know, worked on their horns all the time and there was no -- with all their success, they tried to go on and play better.
Well, then, of course, Benny -- Bartok wrote for Benny and I mean, that was a serious step for Benny to try to move into that, wasn't it?

Well, I wondered, because, you see, his background was that. They don't know, they think of Benny Goodman has having been a jazz dance band clarinet player, but Benny Goodman was schooled in symphonic music.

I mean, he could play the clarinet backwards at the age of 12. When I say backwards, I remember we were talking earlier about Toots Mondello, the great saxophone, flute, clarinet player, and when I asked Toots how -- Toots Mondello played with Benny long after I did, for a short while, and I asked Toots how he liked Benny and he said, he knows that clarinet backwards. Very few people you can say that about.
Toots played with Benny quite a long time, didn't he?
He was with him about a year, I don't know.
Oh, no, longer.
Because that was after --
I think --
He took Hymie Schertzer's Hiney Shirts place (phonetic) didn't he?
Isn't that funny, I thought it was vice-versa. Maybe I'm wrong.
No, I think Hymie Hiney was first -- I am not sure. I am not very good --
Well, it doesn't make any difference. It's immaterial.
Well, let's get back to --
We're talking about Pollack.
That's what we're talking about.
I think -- and I was so saddened by the way Pollack emoted headed. I doubt that it makes a great deal of difference how anybody dies.
How did Pollack die?
Well, he hanged himself.
I never knew that.
This man with this marvelous talent, but I did not see Ben for many years. I went out -- there was a big jazz concert, I think the first of its kind in Los

Angeles at the Shriner's Mosque, and oh, my God, there must have been 150 musicians, California jazz musicians, Eddie Miller, Pollack, Mugsy -- well, Mugsy wasn't a California musician, but we're all out there and I came from -- I went there from Chicago, I was in Chicago at the time, and it was such a thrill to see all these people and Pollack played drums on the thing. At that late date, that was about 1950, yeah, -'51, he was still playing marvelous drums.
You wouldn't believe the talent this man had, that was, but there again --
He didn't get his just desserts, did he. You know, he really didn't.

No, well, of course, there are many things -- you see, I don't want to get into the personal things here. I don't like -- I haven't liked too much talking about Benny Goodman as a person, because I don't think really that it's any of my business.

Well, the only thing is this, Bud, this is history in a way, and you know, when you see a biography on anybody, if you were to try to divorce their life from them - themselves, you are getting half a picture.
As you said Lester is telling his own story when he blows --
Yes, but I think if Lester had been an unkind man, I wouldn't have said anything. I would have just told you about his playing, but there was an element there
I liked to talk about.

Now, if you want something again analogous to this idea, there is a marvelous book written by two psychiatrists, a man and wife, and I cannot think of their names, but the book was called Beethoven's Nephew. Now, just go and listen to music. Get the nine symphonies and listen to them all -- I have them all -- and you just wonder where this heavenly music could have come from, because Beethoven was a monster as a person.
I know, yes.
And it's about well, he drives his young nephew almost to an asylum and the monstrous things he did, but look at the music.

So is the man his music, I doubt it very much, or is the music the man, you see. So what right have we really, I think it's best that we think of Benny Goodman as a great artist, having given a lot of great music to the world and forget what he was like as a man, with all due respect to what you are looking for in the interview, Helen.
This is my view and --

All I was thinking is a positive aspect, what I was -- now, when we said about Benny, we all know that there have been some odd things said about Benny so when we say that we think it was the size of his talent and so on, that made it difficult for him to relate to the way ordinary people were, to me that's a positive statement to make. But
perhaps you feel differently.
Well, let me say one simple thing here. Let us try to find out about the wonderful things he did for people.
Yes, sir. right.

Which no one has ever written about and talked about. It's very easy to dislike a man who's made it, not that you -- you and I are not speaking of that sort of thing, nor am I saying anything original, especially to you, Helen, you know much more about any of these personalities than I because I have been all over the place. I rarely read jazz books with all due respect to the people who have written them, because I was there.
That's right.

If I am going to spend time reading, I have so much I want to read -- I went over to the Isle of Man not too long ago, to do a couple of shows, radio shows and I did a couple of concerts and I was there about ten days and I read a book a day. I am a great one on paperbacks because they are easy to get and you don't have to lug them around, and when you are finished with them, you just give them to somebody.
And I just love to read, so if I am going to spend all that time reading, I am not going to read about something I have already lived.
No, I quite agree.
I suppose I am an omnivorous sort of reader --
People who like to read are.
Anyway, to get back and finish off with Benny --
Well, we're not, we're on to Ben Pollack.

We are on to Ben Pollack, of course, but I was thinking for a second, as you said that, as regards Pollack, I think the things that caused his unhappy ending are not things that I want to talk about. They could certainly easily offend people who might be related to him. The only thing I know is that Pollack was a wonderful man --
(Recording interruption)
We did talk an awful lot about him.
All right. Good. Do you want to say anything more about the Pollack band, anybody in it, or --
I was only in the band about, I think, less than a year certainly. Only in the band about a year and then I had a chance to go to Paris and I went over and I was very disillusioned with that.
Why, this was what, in the 30 whats?
That was in 1928.
Why were you disillusioned.

Well, I over to Paris -- Dave Tough, my good friend was over there and I went over to have a look at it and then found that the bands -- the music would be bad, so I came back and went right out to Chicago and got a job with Zez Confrey. That was kind of a funny thing because Zez was not a jazz pianist, but he was a good composer, he wrote all those, Kitten on the Keys.
I'll tell you who we haven't talked about, the Chicago musician. You mentioned him a moment ago. We never talked about that beautiful guy Muggsy Spanier.
Well, I wasn't very close to Muggsy.
Oh, weren't you.

I only played a couple of concerts with him and I think I made one record session with him and that was on A Good Man Is Hard To Find, on that Condon thing, but I was not very close to Muggsy. We all loved his playing of course, and I -- Maybe over a period of 30 years, I saw Muggsy maybe a dozen times.
Is that right?
Yes. And he went out the Coast. I saw him just before he died on the Coast. You see, his whole influence was King Oliver and Louis.
He brought to his music an extraordinary authentic feel and style.
Oh, yes, he never changed. He believed
in that way of playing and stayed with it all his life and I suppose you might say that it paid off for him because he had a long career.

You see, he was another guy who -- it's so silly really to talk about -- I am speaking of myself -- to talk about why people die, because you can be the healthiest person -- the old remark, here today, gone tomorrow -- you can be the healthiest person in the world and then be gone, I think perhaps longevity of life is inherited. There is something in the genes, because I have known people --

When you think of what Eddie Condon did to his body and yet managed to lived all those years. When you think of old drunks, for instance, the wonderful old saying of Joe E. Lewis the great comedian, he said, 'I see a lot of old drunks around, but I don't see any old doctors around.'
You know, and --
I have seen that in the doctor's office.
So it's sort of foolish really to talk about why a man died or how. It's just that I think there could be one good way to hang around and that's just to keep moving.
That's like Ellington and guys like Hines.
When you think that Ellington lived
75 years and maybe 80 for all we know, he just was a remarkable man. He refused -- he never stopped creating, he never stopped working. His life was his band, and I think he had a fine life.
Yes, he did.
He just went to sleep.
Life wouldn't have been life with him unless he had been working.
What I think we should do from now on -- what time is it, dear?
Well --
(Recording interruption.)

I think from this point on what we should do is, instead of determining where we'll give a lot of time or a little time to that, we ought now to just the follow the career, as briefly or at whatever length you want to do, and then when we have done this and we know we have covered it all, and we bring ourselves right up to date, then perhaps you'll just digress on various thing.

You'll probably want to talk about some length about how you feel today, why are you living in England and all this sort of thing, so let's see to it that we have covered the career, so how good is your memory? I may be able to help you a bit.

All right, you want to go on more with the career. We are through with Benny Goodman. We are through -- we went into the Condon thing. I told you why I fronted the Condon band, ERnie Anderson, Charles Bronson had me front the Condon band, because I was the name and there was a lot of controversy.
Was PeeWee Russell in that?
PeeWee Russell was in the band.
Is there anything you want to say about PeeWee?
You can just ask the question and we'll -- you ask the question when we're on.
We're on, Bud. I said that what we would do, is we would start to cover the career.

I think in talking first about PeeWee Russell, most people don't know, they judged Peewee by his records, which were fine with me, but I think you had to -- PeeWee Russell was a photogenic player. You had to see him, to see the suffering that the man went through to get those notes out and how marvelous he was, because PeeWee unfortunately had been a heavy drinker all his life, and he came to a stage in his later life where he was very, very nervous. He was always nervous anyway as a child.
PeeWee was a very articulate man but nobody knew this because he was so nervous. Now remember that towards the
end of his life, he became a painter. Now, here's the most incredible thing.

PeeWee was also a very good friend of Stuart Stewart Davis and was very much influenced by Stuart Stewart Davis' work, which showed up in PeeWee's paintings and PeeWee painted some 55 things, and I was not an agent, but as a friend I was selling paintings for PeeWee. We got not less than $700 a painting and I remember getting $3000 from Princeton University for two paintings and oh, when a millionaire, some patron of the arts would come to town, I would tell them about PeeWee's painting and they all wanted them.
Now, there was a crazy thing here. People around the world began to identify more with the idea that PeeWee was a painter than with the idea that he was a fine jazz clarinet player.
When did this happen, starting with (inaudible) period.

PeeWee started to paint about three years before he died, and -- no, I think it was less than that. I think -- all right, let's say three, I could be wrong about the time, but certainly two years. I remember once calling up PeeWee to tell him-- no, PeeWee called me to thank me for getting $3000 for two paintings from Princeton University and it seems to me he died not long after that.
How simply extraordinary.
Yes, and PeeWee, now think, PeeWee -- Rutger*s University gave PeeWee a show, now we got a call. Before Mary died, Mary died about a year before PeeWee.
Yes, nine months to a year.
We all went to Mary's funeral. I didn't go to PeeWee's, I was away or something, but went to Mary's.

Now, Mary called me and told me that she got a telephone call from the Australian Ambassador who was in Washington and he wanted to put on -- he was putting on a show of painters from New Zealand, Tasmanian and Australia and they wanted to include PeeWee's works. And would he come. It was to be a black tie affair.

Now, I wrote a short story about this, called The Black Tie, and so Mary said 'I don't think PeeWee wants to go,' and I said, 'Well, let me talk to him.' So I got PeeWee on the phone and I bawled him out and I said, 'PeeWee, you have got to go to that thing,' and he said, 'Bud, I can't. I haven't got a tuxedo.' And I said, 'Well, for Christ's sake, get one, do you realize this will launch you into becoming a world renowned painter?'

Well, alas, PeeWee did not go and the final line of the thing, I say, I think truly that PeeWee did not think of himself as being a painter and I said, 'He could have fooled the Australian Ambassador,' and that's the tale.
That's nice, Bud.

It was said, because he would have had this luxurious life. Of course, he was doing well, making money and just picking his jobs and getting well paid. He had become an idol, you see, around the world. PeeWee Russell, the world knew him backwards.
George Wein, of course, was devoted to him.

Well, he was, yes, so anyway here was PeeWee now a painter. Now, isn't it interesting that this transference of -- remember, Ernie Anderson said, 'What do you think it is?' I said, 'Well, it's a transference of intelligence and talent into another idiom of art.'

Because through all this haze of being -- all the years of being drunk and falling down -- not falling down, but just being so nervous and you never knew that the man was seeing things, and here he was, not knowing that he was so aware, and we didn't know that he was so aware of this art, because some of the paintings are excellent, or maybe many aren't.
But at any rate, I think that people were, as I said, more interested in the idea that a jazz musician could become a painter than anything else. This was a big story to them.
Now, there's a very funny thing that happened here pertaining again to Benny Goodman. Benny Goodman was doing -- he was giving a lecture at the Juilliard School of Music to a

woodwind class, very young people, and a little kid in the back put his hand up and said, 'Hey, Benny, what do you think of PeeWee Russell?' and Benny said, 'Well, Pee Wee is a great artist, but if you want to play like that, don't practice.' So there you are, I don't think Benny meant to be cruel, but you see, how words come out. And he was capable of saying these hilarious things, without meaning any harm.
Well, he was absolutely correct. Correct advice, in a sense.
Yes, being natural. Meaning Pee Wee was -- he didn't mean anything disparaging, I am sure. But it is so hilarious as it comes out because Benny was perhaps not a word man.

But to get back to Pee Wee, I want to tell you that when Pee Wee began to paint -- you see, Pee Wee, I am sorry to say, was pretty much smashed most of his life playing -- had to, he was terribly nervous, and he could manage to play, but when it came to painting, he realized that one had to be cold sober in order to paint and he was, and I called him up one day not knowing that he was painting and he was so articulate and lucid that I thought I had the wrong party. I thought I had the wrong number.
He said, 'Oh, hello,' because he was a very bright guy, very sensitive, bright guy. It was a pity, but there again was a man who burned himself out, lived a thousand years in
the sixty-odd years he lived, you know.
I wanted to ask you something about it. Say, Oh, no, I only wanted to isn't it funny about -- Duke was a painter too, did you know that?
I didn't know that.

Well, he was a painter in his teens. He was offered a scholarship by the Pratt Institute and there are paintings that he did in those days, and he didn't go back to it, but he could probably have been considering what kind of a genius he was, I should think he could have been a genius painter, too, and it's a bit strange in a way, maybe it isn't strange, but in other words, it's as you say, there are different -- there's your perception and the channels you may choose through which you channel your perceptions. But of course, I don't know. I guess there are the facilities --
Well, we have said this so many times that if we hadn't become jazz musicians, we would have become some other kind --
Other interpreters.

Yes, I think so, because this was our rebelicus nature, rebelling against a given societal structure that we didn't want to live in perhaps and this was a way of escaping, when I mentioned the letters of Gauguin and how he was more interested in not having the obligation than anything else, at that time, and then went out to become the great artist

he was, but I think oh, I am sure I would have done something, maybe been a dancer or maybe a ham actor or maybe a writer of -- I don't know, when I say writer, you know, I may if I had not got into this field, I would not have the anecdotes to tell, really, because I might -- I remember I had a job in an advertising agency once. I was about 17 years old. I hadn't begun to play professionally yet, and I spent all my time -- it was on Michigan Avenue overlooking the Chicago River and there was this lovely Wrigley Building at that time.

And I spent all my time dreaming and looking out the window and I suppose somebody was watching me, because after a month, they just told me my services were no longer needed. But it seemed to me it was one of the big agencies, like J. Walter Thompson, and that was Chicago. I am not sure of the name.

And I knew that that sort of work, any work of that nature of being inside of an office, would not have been what I wanted to do. I think I might add that I was just a natural born bum, you know, when I say that, I mean to say that I didn't really want to work at anything, only to find that when I got into music, which I thought was all romance and fantasy, just -- I admired people who could play, what a lovely life they had. It never occurred to me that it could be the most difficult life in the world, because when you think we used to play eight and nine shows in theatres, as I mentioned
earlier in the tapes, it was no different from being in a factory because you cannot play music all day long and love it. It was like pulling teeth, you know.

So we, who thought we were going to escape into an easy life, found that we might have picked the most difficult life we could. But I am very happy that I got into it, because now I have things pretty much my own way. I have stopped -- when I left Benny Goodman, I vowed that I would never work again for another bandleader and I never have. I went out as a soloist and there were many lean years, and I just managed to survive and then I finally, I think the last band I played with, I am sure it was the last band I played with, was a band put together by a rich man from Colorado and it was an ideal setup, we were all paid very good salaries and we worked in the beginning a few months a year and then we were able to free-lance doing our other things.

I stayed with that thing for six years, because in that band, I was -- the band was built around ten soloists in the beginning and then went to nine and later to seven, and we had all the freedom we wanted. We could play -- I was there because I was a soloist. I could do anything I wanted. We made plenty of money. We had a very good way of life and we didn't work hard. There was a lot of traveling and a lot of sleep lost different days, but I -- we came to Europe a couple of times and I got a picture of London and the U.K. and
I wondered if I shouldn't try living in Europe for awhile and then I got a --
(Recording interruption)
Then you were approached with this offer and --
And so I took the letter, it was an offer to do a tour with the College Swing Band, incidentally, I go out with them very soon and do a tour of Germany in October.

And they offered a tremendous amount of money, there was no jazz player getting that kind of money playing in a band, and then I wanted, I thought for some years, going all out and become just a soloist and not being in a band and not being regimented any more, although the World's Greatest Jazz Band was a great band because Bobby Haggart was a beautiful musician and arranger, he wrote for it, and Yank Lawson, who was the other leader, was very nice to me and it was quite a nice thing and you had these marvelous players in the band and they did the best work, around the world.

We never spent a winter in the north, it was either in the Islands, or Mexico or Hawaii, California, wherever, so anyway, I showed to the letter to Bob and Bob said, 'See, Bud, we're just about to make the turn into success, I wish you'd stay and turn it down.'
You wish you had?
He said he wished that I would. Well,

I did, on the strength of what Hag said, he sort of persuaded me, I stayed on. I did turn it down, but then when we came to Europe the next time, I told Hag, 'Well, we have no work for a month, and look at the scene and see -- I will just stay over, I didn't say I was definitely going to stay and we're in the Rotterdam Airport and most of the guys in the band -- we had finished the tour in Holland and the guys are going back now to London and then the States, and I am just going to London, where I have been now for three and a half years.

And a Dutch impressario came running up to me, all out of breath before we went in to get on the plane and he said, 'Mr. Freeman, would you want to stay over here and do some work in Holland? There's a big festival coming up called the Brada Festival, and he offered me a tremendous amount of money for -- just to play one hour, and so the agent, Robert Masters, who was handling us on the road, said, 'My God, how are you that they would offer that kind of money, because he had never been in the solo field, he had always been in the band field, so on the strength of that again, I decided to stay and I asked Robert to handle me.

He had never handled a jazz soloist before and now he's handling a dozen people and he's a tremendous success and everybody's doing well and it appears that the jazz soloists are outdrawing many bands. You know, they go into a

small room and it's just fantastic, so as I say, I have been here three and a half years, and I have always wanted to live in England, always loved London, although London has changed a great deal in the last 16 years, and it's a fantastic life really, because -- I think I might have mentioned this earlier in the tapes, Helen, but I -- it takes me an hour to get to Holland, London is my base. It takes an hour to get to Switzerland, an hour to get to Germany.

I've made a little error here in allowing you to carry me on almost to the present here and I want you to have plenty of time to talk about the present, but we don't want to skip any part before that, so what we really want to follow is not only the development of the musician, the career, but the development of the musician and the artist. The conclusions that you really -- you really became very, very successful, moved climbed to the top of the ladder and you were conditioned in various ways and your thinking was affected and I would be interested to know what -- the trend of your thinking at that point and where it carried you to, from there.
You're on now, I have put this all on and this is the point now where you'll carry over.
Let's see, what year are we in now?
Well, let us mention a few days. As we said, you left Dorsey in '38 and Benny in '39.
And then I fronted the Eddie Condon Band which we talked about some time ago.
That's right, so would that bring you up to about 1950 -- '40, I mean.

That would take me to '40, and then I went off to Chicago. I stayed with my brother for awhile and then I got an offer. Wingy Manone was playing in a place called The Brass Rail and I went in to hear him and the boss came over and said, 'Are you Bud Freeman?' and I said yes, and he said, 'Would you like to bring a band in here?'

I said, 'Well, I'd like to work here, but I wouldn't want to front a band, I don't want to have anything to do with that,' and he said, 'Well, we will get the people for you,' and so I said, 'Okay,' and so I fronted the band. It was some very good Chicago musicians and --
What musicians, Bud, do you remember?

Well, there weren't any names in the group. Bill Doler was a fine alto player and a very funny man, he was in the band, and I'll tell a story about him later. It was in many of the papers as a feature story about the musician who wrestled a bear.
Well, of course, we'll get into that in a minute. This was Bill Doler and this wild saxophone player who too when he got drunk went completely berserk.
Now, we're playing in this club, we used to start about

nine at night and go until 4:00 in the morning. Incredible, the hours, six and seven hours, and the men noticed that I was easy-going, I wasn't a leader, and although they were good friends, they tended not to have the respect for me that men have for a hard bandleader, you see.

So they started to come late. They would be a half hour, an hour late, and I would never say anything to them, but the bosses would get on me and so I had a meeting one night and I said, 'Fellows, you know I am not a leader and I would like to keep your friendship but the boss is getting on me. Do you think that we could start coming on time or I am going to just quit, and you can do what you like.'

And they said, 'Oh, no, please don't quit. We promise to come on time,' so after about a week -- they came on time for a week and then they went back into their habit of taking advantage of me, so I went to the bosses and gave them our notice. I didn't want to stay on and fire everybody, because I didn't want to live that way and I didn't want to be a leader anyway. This thing was foisted on me.

So I went to the men, we had been there 14 weeks doing fantastic business. Every big name in show business and all the bandleaders used to come in, it was quite a lovely little hangout, you know -- I mentioned the Brass Rail in Chicago -- now, I went to the men and I said, 'Fellows, we have just given our notice, and we left in two weeks. But you
know, maybe they learned a lesson from it, and I said to try to behave with an easy-going guy who was trying to be a leader.

I didn't want to be a leader, I just wanted to do my thing and hope that they would go along with me, because it was a very good job and it paid very well and the scale in Chicago for sidemen was very high, you had a strong union there.
And times weren't that wonderful then.
Well, it wasn't too bad then. That was about --
-- '42, yes, because a year later I went into the Army.
Well, that's another thing, we haven't talked too much about.

Now, in this band, I had a close friend, Bill Doler. Bill Doler was a very wild guy and as you know or may not know, in those days, there were bars in Chicago, that were open all night, they never closed. There was a place called the Ohio Inn that was open 24 hours a day and made their political payoffs, of course, and we used to -- we'd get through about four in the morning and we'd go over and have a drink and a little bite to eat or something, and sit around and talk, So we lived near Lincoln Park and now, one Saturday -- Well, let's see, on Saturdays we played over past

midnight into Sunday about 5:00 in the morning. So now we're over in this bar, drinking and suddenly it's starting to get light, it's about 7:00 in the morning, and Bill Doler said, 'Oh, I have a wonderful idea. Let's bring some cheese and nuts and things up and feed the bears, the polar bears come out about this hour.'

So we walked up there and surely enough, there was a polar bear out, so Bill put this food on his hand, put his hand in and the polar bear ate the food off Bill's hand without scratching his hand, but I was scared to death, but in the next cage was the grizzly, a female grizzly and Bill tried it with her and she grabbed his hand and just slit three of his fingers right down, and it was a terrible thing, and I had to walk to the hospital and luckily he was a strong guy and luckily he healed in about six weeks, his hand healed.
But can you imagine, he nearly lost it. He nearly lost three fingers.

Well, anyway, he got drunk again -- he was a golfer-- and he got to thinking about that polar bear -- that grizzly bear, and he wanted to get even. He got his five-iron and he went over, terribly drunk, went over in the morning and when that grizzly bear came out, he hit the grizzly bear over the head and as the grizzly bear was going down, Bill said, 'Do you know, she had a guilty look on her face.'
When you tell these stories, they are so incredible
you don't expect people to believe them, but there they are. There's no reason to make up a story unless it actually happened.

Well, Bill was -- we were now not getting ready to go in the Army and Bill got a -- we used to call it greetings from Uncle Sam, meaning we'd like you to come down and see us, he got his before I got mine and he went down and he was interviewed and Bill did everything -- oh, yes, when we were children, Bill was -- I think we were about ten years old, Bill was riding on a motorcycle and he was -- an automobile ran over and he had a big dent in his leg. Never grew back right, had quite a big dent in his leg and so he thought, 'Well, now, what I'll do is use that to keep out of the Army,' so he took his golf club and he got drunk and he closed his eyes and he banged himself on that and his leg went up to about twice its size and then he went out and got a crutch and he went down for his physical examination and they took him in.

They took him in the Army and there he was. You probably don't know that when you go in the Army you go through a lot of different offices and there are a lot of questions and as you go into each office, you take some clothes off, so finally the last person you see is the psychiatrist and there you are naked.
And Bill is sitting there doing everything he can to get out and he's naked and the psychiatrist is asking him all

these questions. The psychiatrist says to Bill, 'Did you ever have an affair with a man,' and Bill said, 'No, did you,' and the psychiatrist says 'Now, listen, just answer the questions and don't get smart with me,' and Bill said, 'Well, look, if you were sitting here naked and I was sitting there dressed, you wouldn't be so damn smart,' and the man threw up his hands and said, 'Get him out of here.'

But they took Bill into the Army anyway, and he ended up with a wonderful deal. He was in Florida for four years in the Army playing in a band where he played golf every day and he was worried about me. He said, 'Bud, as neurotic as you are, you'd better do something because if you go in the Army -- I practically enlisted. I went in and I ended up in the Aleutians Islands, fronting a band for 22 months. Fantastic thing.
But we were both lucky. I didn't --
Very rough, wasn't it, Bud?

Well, the climate wasn't as bad -- it rained a great deal, but it wasn't terribly cold. Sometimes about 3:00 in the morning you'd get sort of a tropical breeze in that part of the ocean, it's the strangest thing in the world. Almost warm, and then of course, it got never too cold really, but it snowed -- it rained most of the time.
Because when I was reading that Yehudi thing I told you about, he said --
He came there when I was there, played for us.
He said those wonderful guys that were stationed there.

Well, of course, what we had to do, you see, the worst enemy for us was boredom. We never saw any action. The Japanese was out of there maybe at the end of '41 or early '42, and so we played -- we got together a show called Take A Break. That was an Army expression, take a break from you --
I was in the Army too.

Oh, excuse me, well -- so we were able to tour the Islands, not that there was much to see but then we were doing a great thing for the men who were stuck out there. We went to Atka, Shemya, Atco, Semya, Amchitka (phonetic).
You had the band, Bud.

Well, actually, there again it wasn't my band. I just fronted the band because I was the best known person, and the band was put together by some very fine arrangers and we -- I knew a Colonel in Washington and we requisitioned a lot of men who were coming into the service, they that probably have never forgiven me, because they had all hoped to go to Europe and there they ended up in the Aleutians. But actually, we were in good health there. The air

was clear and the food was good and we just had to wait it out but we were lucky that we could play, and as I say, we toured the Islands and then for a little break, we were allowed to go to the Mainland where we did some concerts, but we went to Fairbanks, where it was about 50 below 0 at times and Mt. McKinley and Anchorage and Juneau and Nome.
I will never forget what a dreary place Nome was. But as I say, we were there 22 months, which seemed like 22 years, but still came out without a scratch.
What did you do about reading.
Well, we had wonderful libraries there. We had a wonderful library there and everything --
Why? Were they able to really requisition a wonderful library.

Oh yes, we had all the lovely conveniences, but there were no women there, which of course, is the first horrible thing to happen, and so Dashiell Hammett, the great detective story writer had the paper called the Adakian, which he edited, it was his paper, and he and I were very good friends and he was so funny.

I will never forget as long as I live, his attitude. He was a buck sergeant and he could have become a general, you know, he had big connections but he didn't want it. He just wanted to be a sergeant. He just wanted to be one of the boys, and I remember -- Russia was our ally and he used
to -- he was quite an authority on Russia and he used to give lectures on China. We used to go twice a week to his lectures.
How did he know so much about --

He was just very learned in many things, and he used to write about the progress of the Russian armies in the war thinking that would be okay since they were our allies and the commander of the Alaskan -- well, the general of the Alaskan command came down to visit him one day.

He said, couldn't we have -- and he asked Dashiell, you have a fine newspaper, but couldn't we have more talk about the progress of our own American armies, and Dashiell said, well, I am sorry, sir, but this paper has a policy not to publish any ads.
You know, it was a funny thing, and the general just didn't know what to make of it, because they need Dashiell Hammett because he was doing a great service.

But, of course, again, what the hell, the Russians were our allies, weren't they. So anyway that was the end of that, but Hammett was very anti-officer. He was going a damn good job. He was a pro-American. He was in the thing doing his best. Doing a big job, and he enlisted you know, because he wasn't well. He was the original thin man, you know. He had tuberculosis when he was in China and cured himself.
And, you know, when Hammett came back and he was involved in the McCarthy interviews, you know, the blacklisting

business, he just refused to give names who were involved and so he went to jail for six months and he didn't have to but there he was, he was a good friend and didn't want to give names to people and --
Did he really, I didn't know that.
Yes, went to jail for six months and came out and it must have been a horrible thing for him because he wasn't well -- and he came out and it seems to me he died not long after that.
Oh, isn't that disgusting.
But, I thought -- he loved humanity. He was a lovely guy and a damned good writer.
That was very nice that you were close to him there, wasn't it?
Well, I wouldn't say that I was close, but he liked the band and I used to talk a lot to him and I used to go to his lectures on China.
How old was he?
It's difficult to say, but I think Dashiell must have been in his fifties then.
Was he really. He wouldn't even have been --
Well, I was 36 when I went into the Army and so I think -- let's see, I went to -- I was in the Army 28 months, I came out when I was 39 and I was in the

Aleutians Islands 22 months, so I knew Dashiell for about 22 months and he came to see me when I was playing down at Condon's when Condon opened the club after the war in 1945. Remember, the club in the village, and he came down with the famous Helen --
Keller.
No, Lillian Hellman, you know, that was his ladyfriend.
Yes, of course, she has just published her memoirs.
I got a call from her, not from her, I think her secretary. They wanted some information on Dashiell but we never got together, but I did --
You mean recently.
When I was in New York about five years ago.

I got the call out in Detroit, but anyway, I had -- I did know some things about Dashiell that a lot of people didn't know, because, you know, when you are thrown together with someone for 22 months --
And under those conditions.
I thought he was a marvelous guy and a lot of people said they thought he was a communist. Well, that was ridiculous. Well, he wasn't, he was just a humanitarian. He believed in people and he --
In later years, people realized how savage and uncivilized it all way anyway.
Oh, sure, and in my view Hammett was a fine guy and he cared about people and he had a lot of courage to do what he did.
Yes, to go to jail to not involve other people is --

Yes, of course, because as you know, like Dalton Trumbo and of course, John Bright, who wrote Public Enemy, they had to get out of the country, went to Mexico, I guess, and ruined their careers and I think Trumbo died not too long ago.
Yes, I believe he did.

I knew these people because they were all interested in jazz music. I never got into any of these political issues. I escaped all that because I was so involved in music and I don't know -- I don't think I would have got into it anyway. I have never been a political man. But one might say, well, to not be political is being you know, not being a part of what's going on in the world today. But I think being involved in thearts is doing enough.
Well, Bud, I don't think -- I mean you just really have a hard job to try to think of artists who are actively politically. It doesn't go together, does it?
Not in my view. I just think that jazz
music is political enough.
Take somebody like Casals, after all he just stood for what he stood for, but he was --
You mean Pablo, about Spain, getting out.
Yes. I mean he took his stand and so on, but music was his -- he was first and foremost the musician that he was.

Well, truly, one of the great cellists in the history of music, but you know, I remember when we lived in the Village, all these very political people who were -- many went over to Spain to fight, and they'd invite you to their home to hear records, and all you'd hear is this talk about well, let's help Spain but I always ended up by saying, I am sorry, gentlemen, but my interest is music. Whatever I can do to help -- well, I don't know if I ever helped anybody by playing music, but I was in love -- and in a way, when you think of jazz musicians they were taking a risk because -- jazz is still to this day not a very commercial music.
Oh, no question.
And there are many fine players who have to sit around and wait for work. But we did what we wanted to do.
But to get back to Hammett, I never witnessed an unkind act on his part. A very kind man and he was so nice to

the people who worked on the paper for him and if a man wrote something he didn't approve of, he was so polite and said, 'Well, don't you think it ought to be this way,' and it was a most interesting paper. It talked about books and it talked about --
Did you write anything for it?

No, I wasn't into writing then because I didn't really know I was going to write the first book that I mentioned, You Don't Look Like a Musician. I was playing out in Detroit with the World's Greatest Jazz Band. We were playing at the Detroit Athletic Club and I met Nancy Kennedy who was the women's editor of the --
When was this?

That was in 19 -- oh, it's not too many years ago. I have been over here three and a half, so I'd say about six years, and I met her at this party. Nancy is a food editor, a world famous food editor. You might see her things in many magazines. She got an assignment to go way off, go anywhere, Spain, you name it and she finds a restaurant she likes and does a big piece on it and suddenly that restaurant is doing a tremendous business.

So we became very good friends and I had a lot of anecdotes to tell her about music and musicians and she said, 'Why don't you write some of these things down,' and I said, 'Well, I don't have the motivation to write a postcard.' She said, 'I think you might be a good writer, the

way you talk, so she said, but down a dozen things, just write them in longhand, which of course, I had to do because I don't know the nomenclature of a typewriter, so I wrote a dozen pieces and she read them and she said, 'You know, there are no ambiguities in your writing, this stuff doesn't have to be edited.' She said, 'You are a good writer,' and I said, 'Well, if you say so.'

So I went on and I took -- as I say, I wrote in longhand, it took me about 20 months to write this first book and got a couple of offers, and then a bio-chemist, a black gentleman by the name of Dr. James at Wayne State University, asked for the book. Because he got a big kick out of the things I wrote about King Oliver and Louis Armstrong, and the black music movement of those days and the book is still selling, in about half a dozen countries.
That's wonderful.

And from that, I got an offer in Ireland and I had one published there about a year and a half ago, about a year ago, and now I have just finished. -- there are just short books of anecdotes and vignettes. The last one will be about 70 pages and I am hoping to have that published here in London.
And -- but again, I'd be interested in what you said earlier, I'd like to send the manuscript to you and have Stanley have a look at it.
Well, as you said, there is a great market for the life that musicians lead, you know, there's a tremendous interest in it.
Well, Bud, wait a minute, let's -- we're skipping again. It's very easy to do that.
That's all right, we'll go back anyway.
Yes, we'll go back. What I wanted to ask you was, when were you demobbed, in '45?
I came out of the Army in -- I was home on furlough and I was sitting with a very old friend of ours, Stan Warren -- do you remember Stan?
No.
I thought you knew him. Stan was head of Musak for awhile. Was it Stan Warren --
And as a matter of fact, you see, I was in the Army and I was away from '42 until the end of '45 and then I married in '47 and I was over here in England for 12 years. So I was away for quite awhile.
Well, anyway, I could be wrong about his name because as I said earlier, I have always been that way about names, having the uncle with my same name, I forgot his name.
But at any rate, I think it was Stan Warren, but I was sitting in his apartment. We were playing some records and having a drink, and he said, 'Did you hear about the bomb?' and

I said, 'No, I just got back yesterday.' Just back from the Aleutian Islands, came through Edmonton, Canada and then to Chicago and took a train from Chicago -- stood up all the way from Chicago to New York on this train.

So I was pretty tired and hadn't had much sleep, hadn't had any sleep at all. He said, 'Oh, they just dropped a bomb on Hiroshima.' He says, 'It's the most incredible thing.' Of course, this was the greatest secret of all time. So then, of course, Nagasaki right after that and the war was ended while I was home on furlough.

And I went to Fort Dix for a change of station. I didn't know I was going to be let out, but I was 39 years old, you see, and as soon as the war ended, they dropped the age to 38 and as I say, I was 39, which meant that I could get out, so I went there and the three days that I spent at Fort Dix were longer than any of the time I put in the Aleutian Islands, because -- that is, they seemed to be longer because I was in with a paratroop, an airborne outfit, a rough-tough guys who had seen a lot of action and they were getting them out of the service in a hurry and they were tearing down fences, going into town, wrecking saloons, bars and things. They were a wild bunch and set fire to one of the barracks so I slept out in the field for three days.
And I couldn't wait to get out and I finally, after three days, we went into a little church and this little old'
Colonel handed out the diplomas, honorable discharge.
These people got out in three days.

Yes, very, very lucky and I will never forget what a thrilling thing that was. I went home that night and I was married at that time to Escaleda and we looked in the paper and Art Tatum was playing at the, I think, the Three Deuces or the Downbeat on 52nd Street and we went down of course, to hear this great master, this great artist and they brought for me a bottle of champagne and I remember Art coming over and pouring we poured the champagne over one another, what a wild -- one of the great musical experiences of my life, what a great man he was and then, as happy as I was to get out of the Army, I wasn't happy to get out of the uniform.

It took me a month to make up my mind to take it off and my wife got on me, she said -- I didn't have any clothes, you see, I had to buy some new civilian clothes and I remember going to a place called Paul Stewart's, it was like a small Brooks Brothers and I bought a couple of suits, and the day I took off the uniform I got a call from Ray McKinley who was with Glenn Miller in Europe and he said, Budd, there's a chance to do a show, a radio show called Report to the Nation and a lot of important people on it and it's coast to coast, comes from New York all the way to the Coast and we want to do a spot on it and it pays very well, and I'd like to do just --
(Tape 9)
And you were saying it was really the first time the --

The drums and tenor worked together as sort of an act on a show and then we were to later record it for Majestic Records and Ernie Anderson went to the Ex-Mayor Walker, Jimmy Walker, who was the vice-president of the company, Majestic Records, and talked Jimmy into hiring me as a house band. I used a little jazz band and I used such names as Ray McKinley drums, Bob Haggart bass.
A house band for what, Bud?

For Majestic Records. Playing for people like the DeMarco Sisters, there was a well-known, the Carpenter girl, I forget her first name -- Thelma Carpenter, played -- did a lot of dates, were doing a couple of dates a week and it was a great job, and then Walker, as I say, I used people like Yank Lawson, Bob Haggart, Peanuts Hucko, Gene Schroeder, who was playing with Condon -- oh, dear, I don't think Eddie made any of them, but anyway -- I had Lou McGarity, I had some really good players and we did -- had a jazz background for all the singers that came out and then did some jazz things ourselves. Well, anyway, But at any rate, Jimmy Walker sort of resigned and that was about the end of the thing. I don't know what happened to the company. They sold out to somebody and that
was the end of that job, but while it was going on I had a nice thing, because I was playing concerts at schools, playing the off night with an all-star band at Condon's and had that job.
When that ended I then -- let's see --
I just wanted to ask you, isn't that when you were using that pretty theme of your own. Did you broadcast from Condon's occasionally?
There were a few broadcasts from Condon, but I am not sure that I did one.
Well, I used to hear you occasionally on the air from somewhere and you -- what was that theme you used?
That would be, Easy to Get, you mean?
Yes.
That was Brad Gowans' tune.
Oh, I thought it was yours.
Well, I did -- Brad didn't have a complete tune, he did the first part and we developed the thing. But it was actually Brad's tune.
I see. Well, was it from there that you did that.
It was from the Sherman. I never did that at Condon's. I never played it at Condon's.
I see, okay --
That was the Sherman Hotel in Chicago, the Panther Room, which it was a coast to coast broadcast.

Good. Well, now I interrupted you. According to these notes here, so after the Army, from the summer of 1945 that you had your own quartet and you'd be telling the things you did. Then in February '47 took own trio to play residency at the Cocacabana in Rio.

Yes, George, Ginley, one of the wealthiest men in the world and sort of a playboy who loved jazz and we were friends, opened a room called the [Manorchi] (phonetic) which in Portugese means midnight room and they wanted a trio, an American trio and he -- it was a very sort of posh place and he wanted just special musicians and would I get a trio and so I brought Joe Bushkin down, we were talking about that the other night, Joe Bushkin came in this club to see me and a bass player by the name of Herb Warren.

We got down there and realized that we needed a drum and there was a Portugese drummer from Lisbon by the name of BeeBee Miranda, he didn't sticks, he just played with his hands and had little metal things he put on his fingers and he was just a fantastic artist. So we had a fine quartet, bass player --
You didn't record that.
No, we didn't record. I didn't stay

in Brazil long, in fact, I was a little unhappy with it. We were there 14 weeks and actually, although we were on salary all the time, I never did anything, because the Brazilians did a very odd thing. We went into this room where we were a very big success and they decided to close it and decorate it but to pay us. We stayed on and they paid us, until I said, 'I want to do something. I am not going to sit around here and be idle,' so they put me in a show in a big room in the hotel -- I played I Got Rhythm every night where I did five minutes -- and then we played a dance, you know, it was the craziest thing and then after 14 weeks, the climate was so terribly hot -- I don't know, there wasn't enough -- there wasn't any theatre that I wanted to see and I didn't really -- but if we had stayed, we would have got to recording and got into radio.
So we came back and Joe Bushkin married Francese the heiress and I think they were married there. She came down to see him.

And Joe came in the other night in this little club I was playing in London and -- in Hampstead -- and he came in and played a couple of -- played for about a half hour with me. I hadn't seen him in a long time and he's playing beautifully. He's here in London with Bing, they open tonight at the Palladium, and Johnny Smith, the great American guitarist is with him too, and Jake Hannah, the drummer with Bing here.
Which Johnny Smith?

Johnny Smith, the guitarist who lives in Colorado. I think he == I don't know where he was originally from, he has a sort of western accent. He's a fine guitarist and of course, Jake Hannah, and they're with Bing here. They open tonight at the Palladium.
He's just got the three guys with him.
Yes -- well, I think it's a trio. And Bushkin is just playing oh, he's a marvelous pianist and he was so nice. I hadn't seen him in years. I knew Joe when he was 15, 16 years old.
Fancy that. Well, now, Bud, after that, according to this, you know, you had a long residency at the Gaffer Club in Chicago.

That was a very interesting thing there, that was in a little place called, of all things, East South Water Street, that's an odd name. It's a cute little street and it was down below the street level of Michigan Avenue and you walked down a flight of stairs to get there and it was next to the Time and Life Building, and it was a wonderful little old bar that was owned by an ex-bootlegger and we went in to look at a room upstairs.
This Bill Doler I talked about earlier had a friend there who wanted me to see the room with a view to taking the

room over ourselves. Well, we didn't have any money and I looked at the room and thought what an ideal place to run some jam sessions, which I did, but no, the jam sessions were later. We got -- made a deal with this bootlegger -- ex-bootlegger. He said, I'll tell you what I'll do. You supply the music and I'll supply the booze and service and we'll go 50-50.

Well, the first month it looked like we were going to really make a lot of money, it was going to be a marvelous thing. But I had to go out on the road to do my concerts and things, I was into that and I found that when you're away, the bartenders play with your money, so we came back and that sort of collapsed, and we started -- they started some jazz concerts there which were very successful.
Who was running them, do you know?
I started them and then some other people took them over because I had to go away and I think --
Not people like Steiner, or people like that.

John was interested in it, but I don't think he did anything there. Yes, he did have that record label he was quite a guy by the way. It was a great little club though. But you know, after all, I couldn't run a club, what experience did I have.
It was not what you wanted.

You got to watch it and it was depressing being around there late all the time, sort of an after hours place in Chicago and it wasn't what I wanted and then -- I am trying to think what actually happened there. I broke up -- my first wife and I separated and I met another woman who owned a place and I put a band in her place. It was a place called the Fourth Estate, a newspaper men's hangout in Chicago, and we made a -- it was a very successful thing for awhile, but then she had a lot of debts and there were some Chinese people pressuring her to sell and she made some sort of promise to, I think maybe in writing I am not sure, to sell the place, so finally she had to and so she got some money out of it, and we went to New York.

She said, 'Let's go to New York where you can get back into the concerts and things, and we were in New York three days and I got an offer to go to Boston to Mrs. Donahue's place, the Savoy, and you know, very good money and of course, I had to take a band, I got an all-star band and incidentally, Omer Simeon was in that band.
Was he?
And a guy by the name of Kirkpatrick, the pianist.
I know him.
Don Kirkpatrick.
He was with Chuck Webb for awhile.

I can't remember the drummer but Lee Castaldo Catoido, who later became a bandleader and called himself Lee Castle. Well, he's still around of course, I think. It's difficult to remember the names. Oh, Big Chief Russell Moore.
Did you put this band together?
I put the band together just for that gig.
So you brought Simeon in from Chicago.
No, no, he was in New York. They all had to be in New York. We got on a train and went there, and we were there a month.

And then I -- let's see, oh, yes, then I got an offer to go to East St. Louis to play a club that was starting a jazz policy and I took Ruby Braff with me and a fellow by the name of Paul Jordan, who was a wonderful composer, do you remember, pianist-composer, and we didn't have a drummer so we couldn't go on for the opening night until we got a drummer, who turned out to be very good and there again, it's difficult to remember the other people. Oh, Bob Wilbur played clarinet.
He did, some of the earliest times that Bob Wilbur was heard.
Well, Bob Wilbur -- I don't remember
just what Bob Wilber --
He hadn't had too much exposure by then.
I don't think he had had too much, but he was a marvelous player.
At Eddie's.
Yes, he might have played at Eddie's or I think it was later when he played at Eddie's. It's difficult to remember that.
He's very talented, isn't it.

Oh, he's a marvelous musician, yes. And then we were three three weeks and while we were there, my lady friend's mother died and left her quite a sum of money, a fortune, and she said, 'Look, I want to go to Chile to live. I want to have a house on the sea in Vina Del Mar and I think you could -- you'd have enough money to take your time to look around for work if you wanted, and well, I wanted to go because the climate is lovely in Chile and I didn't want to fight the music business anymore in New York so we went down to Chile. We got a house that is a flat, an apartment, a very posh apartment, right on the sea. In, of course, a place called Viña Del Mar.
I didn't take any work there. I belonged to -- I joined because of my mistress' wealth, I joined -- we were invited to join a very private British golf club, had maybe less than

200 members, and I'll never forget sitting around -- of course, many of the people knew me, they knew my name. I was sitting around one night with these British gentlemen with walrus-like mustaches and as you know, Helen, there is nothing more British than an Briton out of his own country, and over there there were -- so we were sitting around one night and they said, 'For God's sake, Freeman, you are such a gentlemen, what's jazz?'

Well, of course, you can imagine how lonely I felt hearing during that, time, but I did stay there. I played golf practically seven days a week and then my wife decided she wanted -- my mistress decided she wanted to see Santiago which had the ideal climate. It was about 70 degrees every day, very dry, so we moved there. We were in Vina Del Mar for about five months and we went to Santiago for five months, and --
Did you pick up Spanish, Bud?

They said that I spoke as a native, but when I went later on to Barcelona I found I was speaking very bad Spanish, you know, because they speak [Spanish] and they don't sound the "s" and mucho gracia, is mucho gracia, and it was so funny, and anyway, I did speak it. I spoke their dialect, as a native, they thought.
She was.
Margo.
Yes.
No, Margo was a graduate of the University of Vienna and she spoke Viennese quite beautifully,

and English, and she was kind of a, I am sorry to say a snob. She wanted servants which we had in Chile and I hated the idea. with them. You know, I wanted to be friends. I just couldn't order them around. I never liked that idea, having servants, and then well, I began to realize that I should get back and get back to and get into music the States, get back to New York -- I was offered a job. We stayed in a hotel called the El Carrera and there was a room a very nice little room in the hotel, [inaudible] it was called, and I had a Chilean quintet, which really wasn't too bad and we did about three short floor shows a night and played for dancing. It was an easy job, and they gave us a suite in the hotel. The salary was quite -- you know, a fantastic salary.

But I stayed there about a month, I don't know there was something lonely about being there and I'd have -- musicians would come late and you know, it was that same old problem of me trying to be a leader which I didn't want to be. So we came back to the States and moved into the Village and she decided she wanted to go to Mexico to live and so we broke up and she went on to Mexico and I got back in the music business and I've been --
It says here that you opened at the Metropole. Is that right?
Yes, I opened at the Metropole and I lived at a little hotel called the Van Rensseler, one of the early Manhattan New York Dutch names and I ran sessions there,

about 15 sessions and they were very successful, and I had The Lion, I had Lips Page, I had Buck Book, I had Bob Wilber, George Wilbur, I had George Wettling, Dave Bowman. I had -- Joe Bushkin, a lot of actors and well-known people used to come down there. They were very successful, but I was --it was taking up a lot of my time. I really wasn't getting anything for it. I mean, I'd give the money to the men and maybe take $20.00 for myself just to meet my liquor expenses.

But they became very successful, they ran a lot of them after I left, and then I went into the Metropole. I was in there on and off for about a year. I had a trail in the afternoon and then I played at night, but oh, those hours were so long. I will never forget. I used to get out of there about 3:30 in the morning, 4:00.
But it got me back into playing again, because I had been out of playing for a year and away from it, and I had been -- It just built up ever since.
Well, according to this, you were regularly featured at major jazz festivals throughout the USA.
Yes, that's right.
That was in the late fifties and sixties.
Well, it was just after that. I did a show called The Tonight Show, which you know, with Steve

Allen. Now, George Wein, a very interesting thing, had not hired me that year for the Newport Jazz Festival. I did 14 Newport Jazz Festivals, 14 years. I was in four riots in those years, and now he had not hired me for the Newport Festival this particular year, but I did the Steve Allen Show and he saw it, and he called me that night as soon as I came off the show -- it was live -- and he said I want you to come over to Newport tomorrow and do the show and I laughed and I thought, oh, dear, I have to be on a television show to get it, but he offered a very good piece of money for it so I went over and did it and that led to other work.

Then I started to go to Europe. I got -- let's see, George Wein gave a party -- George Wein had now moved into New York and in his apartment he gave a party for Gerald Lascelles, the Queen's cousin, and he invited me to the party and I met Gerald Lascelles, and he was all over me, we were very good friends and he said, 'Oh, I have been following your records, ever since I was a young man,' and he said, 'We are going to have a big jazz festival -- now, this was about 16 years ago, we're going to have a big jazz festival in Beulay, outside of Manchester and I would like you to come. I have invited you, Buck Clayton and Dizzy Gillespie,' so we went over and we worked in three different bands.
Dizzy was with Johnny Dankworth and Buck was with Humphrey Littleton and I worked with Chris Barber, and Alex

Welch, it seems to me was on that thing. I didn't work with him but I met him and a year later, I -- oh, no, after I got back about a month later I wrote -- Harold Davidson had come backstage, that's right, and I told him I would like to work there as a soloist, so I sent him a letter and he sent back a very nice letter saying that I should get in touch with his man, Jack Higgins, which I did and so told Higgins I wanted to come over and work with the Alex Welch band as a soloist.
So that caught on and I was coming --
Why do you think that was.
That was -- I'd say that the first time -- well, I came here 16 years ago and this is now -- we're almost into -- '62, yes, you said that. Let's see if that's right. Yes, it has to be '62.
Now, I was coming over two and three times a year, we see. We were because it was very successful, doing a lot of business with the band.
Incidentally, Bud, we saw you in Mexico City with George's festival.
Well, of course, I wasn't staying there. I'd go back to the States after -- the tours were only for a couple of weeks, you see, and then I'd be back in the States.
And you continued to do festivals for George.

Oh, I worked with George with the Newport Jazz Festival for 14 years. And we went -- we did Mexico, I went to Europe a couple of times with George. I can't remember the year, maybe 20 years ago, we went to West Berlin. That was really a big show. I remember there must have been a hundred different musicians on that show.
Wasn't Billy on that?
Billy Butterfield?
No, Billie Holliday.
Billie Holliday, I don't recall Billie --
Did Leonard Feather take--that [for him]
I am quite sure Leonard wasn't with us on that one, nor was Billie, but it was all -- I don't recall any singers. Wait a minute, there might have been one singer.
No, I think the show I am thinking of, Bud, was for Norman Granz probably.

Yes, well, we opened the Philharmonia at the new Philharmonia Hall in West Berlin which was a beautiful hall and I will never forget our audience was all young kids and they gave us a standing ovation. It was a marvelous thing.

And I played with Buck and the people in our group were Buck, Pee Wee, we had a German drummer. I think George played piano. It is difficult to remember the bass player and I remember Hawkins was on the show, Dave Brubeck. Oh, there

was just everybody, and we played all over Europe. I don't know if we -- yes, we did play the U.K. but we did a television show. It's difficult to remember if we played in the U. K. but it just seems that we were on the Continent because I remember we got stuck in the Paris airport for eight hours, couldn't get out, and finally did and went over to Copenhagen and Here we were with maybe 150 musicians of different groups, so we put on a festival there at the Tivoli Gardens that ran eight hours.
We didn't play for eight hours, but it took eight hours to get all that music in and those people sat out there all that time and listened to that.
That's when I realized what a big market Europe was for jazz.
And of course, you were making a good many records here and there.
Oh, yes, I was recording all the time.
All the time [in the markets.] They were being released abroad and so on.

Yes, that's true, anybody who made a lot of records can do very well over here, because people remember the records. In fact, in concerts I do today, they'll come back and say you didn't play it that way on the record. They know, you see.
Yes, they know. You didn't go out for Norman Granz's at all, did you?
I don't recall ever having worked for Grant's, no.
Well, you know, he got his stable one way or another, didn't he?

No, Granz came in, I remember, I was playing -- this is during all this, jumping to Europe, being with George, and we'd go to Canada quite a lot, and I was -- go to Toronto -- I was playing at a place called the Town Tavern in Toronto, which certainly you know, and on the night I opened there, the Jazz at the Philharmonic played Massey Hall and the whole show came over. I'll never forget Dizzy -- these were all younger people and they all seemed to know me, and they came over. It was such a marvelous thing, and Dizzy sat with his pipe down in front looking up and smiling at me and beating encouragement to me.

Just marvelous people in the show and there were -- they sold out the room. Ella came, Sonny Stitt, Joe Jones, Dizzy Gillespie, Gene Krupa, Stan Getz. I had never met Stan Getz and he came up and asked me, 'Well, how do you get that big note out of that horn,' and I said, 'I think it's due to a leak in the horn.' And he was so nice to me, and all of these and Flip Phillips, very nice, and Lester Young, they were all so pleasant. Hawkins, they all came to see me and I remember Flip went to Norman Granz and he said, 'Bud would be great for us.' Norman said or as Flip told me, 'Yes, that's an idea, maybe we

should do something, but we never did get together. I never -- you know, I was doing quite a lot of work with George and we had a little group called the Newport Jazz Festival All Stars, which was Ruby Braff, who has become a brilliant player, Pee Wee Russell, clarinet, George played the piano and well, we would go from one bass player to another and I couldn't remember their names and we would use different drummers in the festival.
And we played -- did a lot of dates around the States, you know, Newport Festival.
You had your own following.

And then, of course, I left George -- I remember the call. I got a call from George to do something. You know, George, I have been with you for 14 years, but I've got a chance now to go into a cooperative band that's going to be financed, that of course, being the World's Greatest Jazz Band which I talked about earlier, and George said, 'Well, that's fine, I wish you all the best.' But Ruby was not very happy with me for having done so because we did have this nice little group.

And anyway, I went into it and I stayed in it for six years, and we played, as I told you earlier, we never spent a winter in the north. We were in Hawaii, we were in San Francisco and Los Angeles, we were in Florida, we were in the Bahamas. We were in the Virgin Islands.
And you traveled well.

We traveled well and we went to Europe two or three times. We -- it was a very good life, I must say, for six years and then as I mentioned earlier, in the piece where you suggested we were getting too far ahead of ourselves, I was here with them in Europe four years ago, almost four years ago, and then got the opportunity, the offer to say and so I am here.
Hold it a minute. Let me see now. Well, when it says toured Europe with Jazz from the Swinging Era.

That still didn't take me away from George Wein. I had done work just before that and went back. You see, all those people in the group called Jazz of the Swing Era, were in the Newport Jazz Festival too. Because we had Earl Hines and Charles Thompson, the two pianists. We had Oliver Jackson, drums. All of these people played in the festival. We had Bill Pemberton, a marvelous bass player. We had Vic Dickenson. We had Roy Eldridge and Buck Clayton, if I didn't mention Buck before. We had Budd Johnson, Earl Warren, myself on saxophones and I believe that was the band.
And so that band used to play together as a band.
Well, we didn't play together as a band, we did 28 straight festivals without a night off, and of course, it was a brutal thing, you've got had to have nights off.
You didn't give me that little joke, that little line, about the head of a pin.

We were talking about greedy agents could be to get their 10 percent and in this particular case, this agent never stopped to think that we were human beings and he just wanted to get his commission so he booked us 28 days in a row, all over the Continent, no sleep.

And I said it reminded me of that wonderful story of Fred Allen, the great American humorist, he -- Fred Allen had a thing about agents, he called them the greedy ten-percenters and he said that you can take the smallest pinhead and inscribe the Lord's Prayer on it, and still have enough room left for an agent's heart.

But again to get back to the band, you see, that band was tied in with the festival, because we all in that band played the festival.
I think we have come to the end of this tape, so we'll turn it over.
I interrupted you there just a moment. You -- well, you were carrying on with that.

You asked me to tell the, we played 28 straight days.

All right. Now, the band went back and I did a tour, Lockjaw Davis was playing at Ronnie Scott's and when he finished, Lockjaw -- Ben Webster I think was living in Holland or

Copenhagen or whatever, and he came over and we had this agent, got together a thing called -- now, Eddie Miller was in Europe, playing with Alex Welch, and I had just finished the 28 straight days with the Jazz of the Swing Era and they went back to the states and Eddie Lockjaw Davis, Ben Webster, Eddie Miller and I went on this thing called Just for Tenor, you know, it was a concert, we did about eight concerts, and then they went back to the States and I went into Ronnie Scott's for the first -- well, I think I went in there for about two weeks, as a soloist and had a very good quartet.

At the end, there was a fellow by the name of Danny Moss, a fine tenor player I played with the other night, and Ronnie Scott, who is a fine player, and at the end -- I did three shows there a night -- and at the end of each show we'd use the three tenors for a finale which was a marvelous thing. People loved it.
Then back to the States and it's difficult to remember what I did, except that I went back to work to do concerts for George.
Did everybody get along nicely together, the three tenor saxophone players.
It was beautiful, yes. They were gentlemen.
Everybody rotated, I mean, it wasn't tonight so and so finished the set .
You see, Danny Moss and his wife had a group there, and I was fronting a quartet, and that was the show. And we had a ball and Ronnie Scott is a fine gentleman.
Yes, that's very nice, isn't it. Bud, I'll tell you one thing you didn't -- about this time, I didn't know that you were in a car smash, in '67 or '68.

Yes, as I said, I had been coming to Europe to the U.K. two and three times a year, and then I got into a -- you see the World's Greatest Jazz Band hadn't begun yet. We were doing -- we had done some things for Gibson, out in Colorado, in Denver and then I was living in New York, I was married, I enrolled at New York University, to take a class in composition. There was a fine Viennese composer by the name of Sussmann Shyman who was into some pretty deep stuff and I wanted to study with this guy just as a non-entity. I didn't --
In composition.
Yes, to study composition, and my first class was to start that night at 8:25 and that afternoon I was in an automobile accident, riding --
How did that happen.
Well, I was riding from Long Island, we were going over the Queensborough Bridge and the man with me

was a good driver and we weren't going very fast, but we were over on the left side and there was traffic coming toward us which was stalled, and a man in a little white truck pulled out for no reason at all and hit us headon, but luckily, we skidded into him, by the time he put the skids we might not have been going more than 20 miles an hour. But you can imagine, it's a headon thing -- I don't know -- I don't know that we had a belt, there weren't seat belts, but I know that I didn't use one and I saw it coming.
