I had maybe two or three seconds warning, and I just instinctively threw my right arm up over my eyes thinking there would be broken glass and all that, and I was thrown into this sharp dashboard and I had a multiple fracture of the right ribcage, broke nine ribs.

I wasn't knocked out. I got out of the car under my own strength and our car looked like an accordion, you should have seen it, it was incredible that we weren't killed, and just then a taxi was going by on the bridge and he took me, 96 th I lived up on 9th Street between Park and Madison, and he got me to my home in 20 minutes, and I had two of my ex-wife's aunts, two old Louisville belles were there, and I said get me a tall straight drink of vodka, which I drank down, got pretty drunk to lessen the pain and call a doctor.
So they got in touch with my wife who was teaching, she was a child therapist, she was teaching down in her office,

and she called her doctor, who came over and he gave me a shot and took me in the hospital wagon to the best, incidentally, best bone hospital, one of the best in the world, 124th and Madison, in Harlem.
What's it called.

I don't remember, I am not very good with names, but it was an excellent hospital. You see, they didn't bind me up, I was just left to heal by myself and I took no -- they said, I don't think you're going to be able to stand the pain, we may have to put you on something. I said, no, I don't want any narcotics, I'll take the pain and found out that I have sort of a high pain threshold, or at least I was able to go through that.
How many ribs?

Nine, a multiple fracture of the right ribcage, and I used to have to rehearse getting in and out of bed every night, because it was so painful, but I did manage to drink. My wife, my ex-wife would send brandy over, and I always had a lot of visitors, and weweren't allowed television, but my brother brought a set in and we watched -- at the time the World Series was going on and the whole ward came in to watch the World Series.
There was a lot of activity around that place, but I must say -- I was there 15 days and my lawyer, who was suing for a tremendous amount of money, was very unhappy because I

didn't want to stay. I said, I am going to get out of this place. I don't care about the money, I just don't want to stay here another day, 15 days in that hospital is just living death, you know, because there are many people in hospitals who identify with death. They make a way of life in a hospital and don't want to come out.

And so as I say, the lawyer sued for a lot of money and because of my name they wanted to get it off the books so they made a settlement out of court for quite a sum of money and I remember the lawyer bringing this money over in an old crumpled check. It was so funny.

So I thought, Well, I'll never go -- you couldn't pay me a million dollars to go through that pain again, it was really something, so I bought some bonds and had them for some time and just sold them when I came over here.
Is that right.

But money doesn't mean anything to me, because I would hate ever to go through that. And incidentally, I have developed a Freudian fear of riding in a car, it's something I can't seem to rid myself of.
Well, you had those seconds of fear.

Before that accident, Helen, I was -- George Wein used to drive 90 miles an hour when we were going up, say, Northern Michigan from Detroit, way up there. I never paid any attention to it. We were always singing or talking, but

now I have a difficult time riding in a car, but I love to fly. I never think of flying, I always never say -- if I say anything to myself, I always say, well, in a plane you crash that's it, there's nothing to worry about or think about, so I am probably not worried about dying but worried about being maimed for life, and I cannot overcome this. I suppose I could go to therapy about it and maybe it would help, but I really do have a difficult time riding in cars.
Well, I think
The point is, it happened to you and if it had been one of those that happened so fast that you didn't know anything about it, but you had a few seconds.

Well, I was very lucky. I had no ill effects from it. The first show I did, I didn't do anything for seven months, and Art Hodes called me from Chicago -- he had that wonderful show, I think it was called Blues Alley. And he asked me if I'd come out. And the doctor said now you might feel some pain when you start to play again, because the expansion and all, but there was nothing. No pain, it was marvelous and I played that first thing and that started me all over again.
You mean you actually hadn't blown, you hadn't played at all.
I hadn't played in seven months. I stayed away from it to let the thing heal.
Stan and I were just talking about
that rib business. You didn't run any risk of pneumonia, then, Bud. You had to be pretty careful.

I could easily have got that and there was a slight puncture of one of the lungs, but never had any -- but I do catch, as much as I love living in England, I do catch colds here, which I have never caught, because I have been taking Vitamin C for about 20 years and Vitamin E, but I do catch colds here, catch chills.

It's too bad because I think it's a lovely country, but it's a damp, damp country. But then you see, I am sitting on top of all the work here, as I told you, it takes me such little time to get to places I have to play. I never know with whom or with what I am going to play, but I work as a soloist and --
Let's just go to about three and a half years ago, where -- did you just come and decide you would stay or did you make up your mind there, that you'd come.

Well, I wasn't too sure. I said, I think I'll try it for about six months and see how it works, but right from the very go, from the first day as I said in Rotterdam airport, this man offered me this Breda festival for a tremendous money. I didn't make that much in a week playing in the World's Greatest Jazz Band, and that was for one hour and that caught on, and now we're getting -- as you know, I am 71, if I can look forward to another ten years, or whatever

the case may be, if my health holds out, I can look forward to a busy life of playing. I want to cut my work down to about six months a year, because I don't want to get sick. My health has been excellent and I want to just do this work, and we're booked up, practically two years ahead.

When I say booked up, we don't have signed contracts for that, but we're signed up six months but we know that the work is there, because we keep -- I have turned down a tremendous amount of work which now I will have to do, and I don't mean again to boast or anything, but I have picked up a tremendous amount of publicity here. I do -- you see, they have radio shows over here now that they pay for, that is, in Holland, and Germany and Switzerland and television is quite a bit thing, you pay quite a sum of money for that, and tied it in with the concert and I work, as I said, with the Dutch Swing Dutchman College Band, I worked with a little group in Holland called Ted Easton's band, and these bands are very good bands.

There is so much work in Holland alone and in Switzerland and in Germany. Germany has 300 jazz clubs, so I say, if I am alive ten years from now, I can be playing these, because I don't have to work hard. I go in, there's a group set up, a trio or quartet or whatever, and they go out and they play about 45 minutes and then they bring me on and I do a half hour, and I do that twice a night.
With the Dutchmen College Band, I do about two 20-

minutes sets a night, and not so long ago I went over to Hanover to do the impressario called and said, would you want to come over and close a show. A big jazz concert with a lot of wellknown people in Europe and I went over and there was 11 minutes left for me. They paid me before I went on, I did the 11 minutes and caught a plane back to London, the same day. It's incredible, but I love the way of life here.

I, of course, the United States is a beautiful country, but I just don't know that the opportunities for a jazz soloist are there because the evidence of all this lies in seeing all the best soloists coming over here to work. But then again I haven't been in the States in three and a half years, so I don't know if the work is there or not.

I think you're probably right, though, you see, because the proximity of so many different countries, which each constitutes a market of its own, and that you don't have, so you go from state to state or you do the West Coast, you do the East Coast, and so on, and it's -- I mean the people that are working steadily or more or less steadily at home certainly fit Europe in twice a year to fill out.

Well, do you want to know an interesting thing, Helen. I see American jazz musician friends more in Europe than ever I saw them in the States because many of them were living in Florida, many in California, you know, spread all over the country, but I see them all, men I haven't seen

in 20 years, maybe in some cases 25 years and they all come over here and we have a marvelous time. Billy Butterfield came today, and I haven't seen him, but he's staying at a hotel I used to stay, at the Century, and he's starting a tour for my agent, Robert Masters.
Is he? How very nice.
And Billy's very popular over here, but all the American jazz players are very popular in Europe.
Who does Masters put back of Billy.
Well, he probably will use a local rhythm section, as I do, you see.
So as a brass player, I mean, how much will Billy's lip stand up to. How much will he do a night.
He will work pretty much the way I do, probably a couple of sets a night. It's easy work and you get a chance to live.
Yes, that's right. Well, of course, in your case it's very much better because you're at home. You know, when you're off, you're at home.

Yes, I have a lot of -- well, I know everybody in London, and I know so many people throughout the U.K. and I played -- I must have played in the 16 years I have been coming here on and off, I must have played 100 cities, you know, and they are all jazz -- you know, you must
realize the British have been supporting American music, that would be dance music and jazz for some 70 years, and the Prince of Wales, Edward the VIII was an amateur drummer.
Yes, I remember, Prince George too.

Yes, and the British really love jazz. I mean, they are quite serious about it. They do turn out for a wellknown American soloist, and the British have some damned good players now themselves. They have been dedicated to music.
Is Bruce Turner still playing?

Oh, very much so. We made an album called The Song of the Tenor and Bruce is on that. The recording company Phonogram asked me if I'd like to do an album and what would I like to use, and I said, I would like to do an all British album, use all British musicians who are exploited too much, and Bob Wilber happened to be here and so we used Bob and it was a fine album, with Bruce, Bob and I on reeds, and a young London pianist by the name of Keith Ingam, plays very well, and he's going to the States by the way, to play, to work, to live, and a fine bass player by the name of -- oh, dear, I'm that way about names again. A drummer by the name of Bobby Orr -- well, as I mentioned Bruce Turner, oh, yes, Roy Williams, who is a very fine trombone player. George Wein used about six British musicians in the Nice festival just last July and they were a big success.
Who were they?
Roy Williams, I don't know all the men, who were on it, but I know they used just six British musicians.
That's very nice, isn't it. Well, who did arrangements on that session or did you use arrangements.
Well, I wasn't on the Nice festival this year.
No, I don't mean that, I mean on the album.
Oh, yes, Bob Wilber wrote out some very nice things.

Well, that's very good, isn't it. Bud, I think what we want to do, we're nearly completed here, and we ought to just talk about -- there are one or two outstanding things we didn't mention. You never mentioned the fact that you studied for awhile with Lennie Tristano.

Well, when I came back from Brazil, I had a sort of breakdown where I lost all confidence and it was a mental thing perhaps and I went to a lot of different teachers and they all gave me the same old thing, you know, getting their individual selves into the act and trying to tell me the mistakes I had been making all these years, playing, but it wasn't helping me any, so I heard about Lennie Tristano and

I thought well, a blind man, he probably would hear something that nobody else heard, so I went to study with him and he heard it immediately. He said, 'Well, you are just all nerves, you are just closing up and not letting the sound ring through, no one else told me, with all the teachers I went to, and so he snapped me out of it and it was very interesting. I stayed with him for a very short period. We just went back to the basics of music. I didn't get into anything because I had to make a living going out on the road, but he was a marvelous teacher, a great musician.
How nice, it was the sort of relationship that you established?

Oh, absolutely, we got along beautifully. As I say, he was able to hear what was wrong, I was all nerves, all tension and I was just closing up and not letting the sound flow, and that was what it was about.
What a great relief.
Yes, And I came out of that and went on to work --
Without any more problems.
Well, another thing we didn't mention was the fact that you were a poll winner on a number of things. It was in '37, of course.
I think that was the first poll wasn't it, the Metronome --
The Metronome Poll and then you won the Downbeat Poll in '38.

'38, yes, but never -- you know, I think those were the first polls and I was getting, you know, a lot of popularity. You notice that the men who did win the polls, with all due respect to their being great players, are pretty much in the limelight, have a big act going or they're with a big band and they're being featured, as I was in those early days, '37 with Dorsey and '38 with Goodman.
Well, what about in Europe. What about Panassie and people like that. They often make awards, the French Hot Tub and so on. Were you involved in any of those?

No, I don't think -- there was a very odd thing about Pernasia (phonetic) he in 1927 wrote a piece about me in the DownBeat, highly praising my playing, but then Mezzrow went over there to see him and told him some funny things, and Pernassie just turned from our group, which he liked very much, the group that made Nobody's Sweetheart and all that, and went along with Mezzrow, and never said another word about me.
Very much unduly influenced by Mezzrow, wasn't he?
Yes, he came to a concert. I remember seeing him when I did the show -- this was in Paris, we played

Freyel La Plaisail (phonetic) with the Jazz of the Swing Era and he was sitting in the front row, but I didn't get a chance to talk to him and I didn't feel that he cared too much for my playing anyway.
That's unfortunate. It seemed to me and I may be wrong, but it seemed to me that he was in New York at the time that Mezzrow formed that band and went into that New York spot, that integrated band.

I remember one time, the only time I think he came, unless I am mistaken. I was playing with Benny Goodman and the producer of the show had Panassie Pernasie, John Hammond Panassie. I think, was not the producer -- he got Pernasian to talk and I remember Mezzrow was with him, had come with him to the show.

That was the only time I saw them. We went out that night, went to a little restaurant in the Village, and I remember that a corny recording of Tiger Rag was being played on the Musak, they had in the restaurant, and we were all laughing, it was a satire on jazz, it was so bad, and Panassie Pernasian, he thought it was excellent, so I began to realize that he might not have known too much about jazz.
I think he was very intuitive, but he was very much influenced by Mezz.
Mezzrow, oh, no doubt. Mezzrow told him, I think, that he taught us all how to play.
Yes, that's true. Look, there are still some other things I want to ask you about.
Now, English TV which is a big thing here, you have been doing -- you had a segment of a feature of your own.

This show, Tony Palmer produced it here, called All You Need Is Love, which is the Beatles title and it was 17 episodes, the history of American popular music and some jazz so I -- as I say, broken up into episodes, and I was in the ninth episode which opens up with Cab Calloway, this is called the swinging episode. Bing's in it. Artie Shaw doesn't play, he talks -- well, I think he does do a little playing.
Was Artie over here then.

No, they went all over the world to find the people for this, and they recorded me in Friberg, Dutch Swing Switzerland. I was playing a concert with the Dutchmen-College Band. It was a great piece of publicity for me, because it showed all over the U.K. and now is showing in Switzerland and Holland, and as I say my episode was the ninth episode and I had three very nice spots on it, and I closed the show, and interestingly enough, when they're showing the credits, the -- my face is stuck on there for 40 seconds, all you can see is this, and it was a fine piece of publicity and I got a lot of work out of that. And now I am going to do -- I am very
much into television in Switzerland and Holland and Germany and I'll be doing, making another film in Copenhagen, about the history of the tenor sax.
Oh, what an interesting thing. Do you have to research that.

Well, I don't, the producer, the man who is producing it and directing it called me recently and asked me if I'd like to make a film and I asked him to put it in the hands of my agent and we're going to do it sometime --
Wonderful. Do you see anything of Yannick Bruynoghe, you know, Yannick who is the film man and he also wrote that book on Big Bill Broonzy! Do you know who I mean.

I know who you mean. I think I did meet him once in -- I played a -- I did a festival one of the summer festivals in Belgium and a very interesting thing happened. I looked out of the wings and there is Buddy Tate and I said, 'How about getting your horn up,' which he did and came up and played a half hour with me, and it was marvelous. He's a great guy and Buddy comes over quite a lot.
Yes, I know he does, and he's worked a lot with Benny too.
He's made a big name for himself in Europe, it's great to see.
Couldn't have a nicer person, and he

right now he's -- he worked with Jay McShann at Michael's Pub recently and they made a session for Atlantic and they also made a session for -- well, while they were live in Toronto, marvelcus, really very wonderful.
I met Jay McShann and for the first time at the Newport Jazz Festival last July. And Buddy was there, too.
Did you, for the first time, isn't that funny. He's a marvelous piano player.
Yes, and Michael's Pub is doing very well, is it?
Yes, it's doing well. It's proving to be quite a showcase for the right kind of music and so on.

Well, now, look, perhaps I was going to speak to you, about Humph and so on, but perhaps you -- we're getting near the end of this and you might just like to tell me what you feel about jazz, how you look at it.

I can say from a therapeutic point of view, it's -- there's something in the music that makes you happy when you're despondent, there's something in the music that makes you well when you're in pain. Of course, this happens to many actors. I have had nights where I had a bad headache or stomachache or maybe my feet might hurt or just some minor ailment and I'd go onstage and play and in just the very act of being on stage and performing and playing this particular kind of music, seemed to take me -- extricate me

from that suffering I thought I was going through, and I am not so sure that this happens with all kinds of music, I think it definitely happens with jazz and then when you finish playing a jazz concert, you're very high and you're excited about what you are playing, and thinking about what you would have liked to play and you have a difficult time going to sleep, so that's why --
You're strung out.

You're strung out, of course, this happens to all people in the theatre, in performing and perhaps in the symphony too. But I think that jazz one day will become a world folk music, it seems to me -- now, I live around the world and it seems to be spreading and the young have really taken it up.
There are thousands and thousands of young people coming to all the jazz concerts. I mean to hear all the American jazz soloists or any soloists, who are dedicated to playing jazz.
And that's a reasonably new development.

Yes, it is. It is fairly new because I should have thought that these kids would still be with rock, but many of them have broken away. Now, when I say broken away from rock, I don't have anything against rock, because I think everything is needed. There's room for everything.

We have had a lot of important jazz musicians who have resented it because they thought it put them out of work, but I don't see that they did, because they're in another world, you see. They're -- it's so much photogenity going on that the young people hardly listen to music, or it's just so loud that you can't --
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.title: Copyright notice, Smithsonian oral history header
segments.summary: Rutgers copyright warning and Smithsonian transcript title pages: Helen Dance interview of Bud Freeman, sides 1-4.

segments.title: Hearing music at home: Kimball piano, Victrola, school daydreams
segments.summary: Freeman says he was aware of music at eight: his mother and her siblings played piano, his father had a Victrola with opera and Whiteman records.

segments.title: Skipping a Junior Olympics interview for a C-Melody saxophone
segments.summary: Winning track events as a boy, Freeman was due to meet an athletic society but stopped at a Wabash Avenue shop window and fell for a C-Melody saxophone; his father was heartbroken.

segments.title: Austin High, the McPartlands and Dave Tough
segments.summary: At Austin High Freeman meets the McPartland brothers, who persuade his father to buy a saxophone, and he first meets Dave Tough at a Friday social.

segments.title: Dave Tough, Hemingway and young musicians who drank
segments.summary: Tough went to Oak Park High, introduced Freeman to Hemingway, and like Wettling and Condon began drinking young; Benny Goodman turned pro at twelve.

segments.title: Frank Teschemacher and the Austin High Gang
segments.summary: Freeman recalls meeting Tesch at Austin High, a year ahead of him, in the Austin High Gang; Dance asks about George Wettling.

segments.title: First professional job at Sheboygan Inn on C-Melody
segments.summary: At sixteen Freeman gets a C-Melody and two years later plays the Sheboygan Inn in Lyman Woods's trio on Dave Tough's recommendation, barely able to play.

segments.title: Dave Tough leaves, Freeman is fired and switches to tenor
segments.summary: Earning $40 a week, Freeman is threatened with murder after Tough leaves, returns to Chicago and takes up tenor, relearning in B-flat by ear.

segments.title: Listening to New Orleans Rhythm Kings and King Oliver's band
segments.summary: The Chicago kids loved the New Orleans Rhythm Kings, then went to hear King Oliver with Louis Armstrong at the Lincoln Gardens, the greatest band Freeman ever heard.

segments.title: King Oliver, Louis Armstrong and the Hot Five records
segments.summary: Freeman thinks Oliver held the young Louis down, praises the Hot Five records, and says young people miss Armstrong's true greatness.

segments.title: Bix, the Whiteman and Goldkette sidemen, and leaving the NORK behind
segments.summary: Freeman says Bix is hard to hear through sidemen who were not true jazzmen, and the Chicagoans never went back to the NORK after Oliver.

segments.title: Who could play jazz: race, talent and Professor James
segments.summary: Freeman argues only a handful of blacks and whites could play jazz, cites a black biochemist who disputed jazz's African origin, and says only individual talent matters.

segments.title: Mezz Mezzrow's feeling for the blues
segments.summary: Freeman and Dance agree Mezzrow's love and feeling for the blues were authentic despite his limited facility.

segments.title: First recording with the McKenzie-Condon Chicagoans and move to New York
segments.summary: Freeman's first record, Nobody's Sweetheart, led to Pollack's offer and the move east to New York after Chicago's jazz players left.

segments.title: Hawkins, black singers and dancers, and the origin of Chicago jazz
segments.summary: Freeman says he learned from Ethel Waters and Bessie Smith, was awed by Coleman Hawkins's tenor, and calls Chicago jazz a white impression of Oliver and Louis.

segments.title: Pianists and clarinetists who influenced him: Lucky Roberts, James P., Fats, Earl Hines
segments.summary: Freeman names Lucky Roberts, James P. Johnson, Fats Waller and Earl Hines, recalls meeting Roberts at the Life photo and touring with Hines in Britain.

segments.title: Dance asks to probe the Chicago picture
segments.summary: Dance explains she will interject questions to draw out an in-depth picture of Chicago's jazz family.

segments.title: Lessons from the McPartland family: Dick teaches chords
segments.summary: Freeman took a few lessons from Jimmy McPartland's father, learned chords from Dick McPartland, and learned jazz from records more than clubs.

segments.title: Black South Side nightclubs and their freedom of spirit
segments.summary: Freeman describes going to black clubs solely for the music and the free spirit of the dancers despite their hardship.

segments.title: King Oliver's decline and the need to read
segments.summary: Freeman knew Louis and Earl but not Oliver, whose last job he heard was racking balls in a poolroom, and notes soloists could not make a living.

segments.title: Learning to read music with Duke Real
segments.summary: Freeman studies with the Chicago Symphony's first clarinetist, Duke Real, and learns to read in five months through hours of practice.

segments.title: Condon and McKenzie's record date and McKenzie's salesmanship
segments.summary: Freeman recalls his first record, made at 21 with Condon and McKenzie, and how McKenzie and Condon could sell to record companies.

segments.title: Family ethnic background, sister and brother Arnie
segments.summary: Freeman describes his multi-ethnic grandparents, his one sister, and his younger brother who became an actor.

segments.title: Where the talent came from and his father's trade
segments.summary: Asked where his talent came from, Freeman says no musicians in the family; his father cut ladies' garments and adored talent.

segments.title: Neighbours complain about the idle Freeman boys
segments.summary: Neighbours pressure Freeman's father to make his sons work; he wakes them at 7:30 and Arnie protests, after which dad leaves them alone.

segments.title: Father and the Ray Noble band film foot
segments.summary: Freeman's father first saw him in a film with the Ray Noble band, recognizing only his foot; Freeman promises the Noble story later.

segments.title: Freeman's mother's illness and death
segments.summary: His mother, a pianist with a lovely voice, died when he was sixteen, never knowing he'd become a musician.

segments.title: Dave Tough and the Cezannes at the Art Institute
segments.summary: Tough takes teenage Freeman to see Cezanne at the Chicago Art Institute and brought him to books, theatre and painting.

segments.title: Dave Tough as a band drummer influenced by Baby Dodds
segments.summary: Freeman calls Tough the greatest band drummer, a Baby Dodds follower who played behind soloists, and says musicians don't use categories.

segments.title: Dave Tough introduces the new sound; Louis's beat
segments.summary: Tough introduced Freeman to the sound of Oliver and Louis, whose beat no trumpet player since has matched.

segments.title: Hearing Jack Teagarden in a speakeasy
segments.summary: While in Pollack's band Freeman hears Teagarden play alone in a speakeasy, and Pollack hires him after one chorus.

segments.title: Jack Teagarden's character and his band
segments.summary: Freeman remembers recording with Teagarden before he died, a man whose life was all music, and thinks leading a band was a mistake.

segments.title: Goodman and Tommy Dorsey as hard bandleaders
segments.summary: Freeman says Goodman and Dorsey were hard men on the bandstand but pleasant off it, and tells how Dorsey kept the drunk Bunny Berigan.

segments.title: Max Roach and Dave Tough on a cold Chicago street
segments.summary: Freeman recalls meeting Max Roach in the Chicago wind and talking for 35 minutes about Dave Tough, who he says influenced avant-garde drummers.

segments.title: Tough's concept of drums as the heart of the band
segments.summary: Freeman and Dance discuss Tough shaping his backing to each soloist and giving Woody Herman's band its sound.

segments.title: Tough's mentality, reading and humor
segments.summary: Freeman describes Tough as an educated, music-reading drummer with brilliant humor, and corrects his arithmetic on how long Tough played.

segments.title: The album From Austin High Comes Jazz
segments.summary: Freeman recommends the 1938 New York Condon-group album with Tough and Teagarden that he fronted.

segments.title: Fronting Condon's Summa Cum Laude band at Nick's
segments.summary: After leaving Goodman Freeman fronts Condon's band at Nick's with Pee Wee Russell and others; Phyllis Condon names it Summa Cum Laude.

segments.title: Why he never wanted a band; Goodman theatre grind with Tough
segments.summary: Disillusioned after years in big bands, Freeman recalls nine-show days with Goodman and Tough that left them working eighteen hours.

segments.title: Dave Tough's family background
segments.summary: Dance asks about Tough's family; Freeman recalls his learned father, mother's death, and Tough's reading from age ten.

segments.title: Dave Tough's influence on Freeman during the bootleg era
segments.summary: Freeman says Tough kept him from the bootleg-era gangsters, shaping him with books, painting and music.

segments.title: Why Tough drank: dipsomania versus musicians' lives
segments.summary: Dance asks what drove Tough to drink; Freeman says musicians don't drink because they are musicians, and Tough and Bix were dipsomaniacs.

segments.title: Dipsomania, childhood and hereditary drinking
segments.summary: Freeman distinguishes a dipsomaniac from a drunkard, says Tough could not handle one drink, and wonders whether childhood shapes later life.

segments.title: His father's view of drink and Freeman's own health habits
segments.summary: Freeman's athletic father disapproved of Tough's and McPartland's drinking; Freeman and his brother kept to health, golf and moderation.

segments.title: Drink as escape for Tough; Freeman's hangovers
segments.summary: Freeman thinks Tough never enjoyed drinking but used it to escape tension, and describes his own horror of hangovers.

segments.title: Tough's first marriage and Paris
segments.summary: Dance asks about Tough's marriages; Freeman tells how Tough's first wife was unfaithful in Paris and how he left them his flat, with Tough's quip.

segments.title: Tough marries Casey Majors after Philadelphia show
segments.summary: In 1937 with Tommy Dorsey at Nixon's Grand in Philadelphia, Tough and Freeman fall for chorus girls and Tough marries Casey Majors, who got him off drink for three years.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: Harlem as a village of great pianists
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Harlem in the 1930s, with Willie the Lion, James P., Fats Waller and Lucky Roberts, safe streets and Sugar Hill.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: Racial misunderstanding and the old man at the Cubs game
segments.summary: Freeman says white musicians were color blind, whites were ignorant not hostile, and an old man at Jackie Robinson's Cubs game told him the cause is misunderstanding.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: No racial prejudice and the luck of making a living in jazz
segments.summary: Freeman says his prejudices were never racial and he never dreamed he could make a living playing this music.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: Success in Europe at age 71 and doubts about the United States
segments.summary: Based in London for three and a half years and booked across the Continent, Freeman says a genuine jazz soloist is valued more as he ages.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: Dexter Gordon's return to the States and being yourself
segments.summary: Dance and Freeman discuss Dexter Gordon's success after years abroad and whether Freeman would do as well at home.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: Tony Palmer's All You Need Is Love film and U.S. profile
segments.summary: Freeman describes his swing-era episode in Tony Palmer's seventeen-part film series and his growing name from abroad.

segments.chapter: Harlem, race and life in Europe
segments.title: Playing with different groups across Europe; Red Norvo
segments.summary: Freeman plays with whoever is booked, avoids leading a group, and flies between concerts; Dance notes Red Norvo does the same.

segments.title: Coleman Hawkins at Freeman's apartment
segments.summary: Hawkins, a loner, visits Freeman and says they are still in demand because they knew their instruments when young; Freeman calls Hawkins the father of tenor soloists.

segments.title: Dance on Freeman's place beside Lester Young
segments.summary: Dance says Freeman was the only white tenor of his kind in Chicago and hears a family relationship with Lester Young.

segments.title: Lester Young's tiny sound and the great tenor players
segments.summary: Freeman says he and Lester shared the Louis beat; Lester swung everything with a small sound, and Freeman praises Ben Webster, Getz and Eddie Miller.

segments.title: Going out as a tenor soloist at Kelly's Stables and the tenor parade
segments.summary: Freeman says he was the first to leave a big band as a soloist, at Kelly's Stables, followed by Lester, Hawkins, Webster and Eldridge in a 'tenor parade'.

segments.title: Storyville drummer Marcus Foster and Lester's 'tiddy-voo'
segments.summary: Following Lester into Storyville, Freeman hears from drummer Marcus Foster that Lester told him only to 'tiddy-voo'.

segments.title: The critic who asked Lester for Bud Freeman records
segments.summary: A critic who refused to play Freeman's records hosted Lester Young, who asked 'You got any Bud Freeman?'; years later the critic apologized.

segments.title: Dance challenges Freeman's view of critics
segments.summary: Dance calls his claim about critics too sweeping and describes growing to hear Charlie Parker; Freeman says the critic idolized only Lester.

segments.title: Lester Young as singing music, and his playing after Basie
segments.summary: Dance hears Lester's creative flow as singing; Freeman says Lester improved after Basie once he had freedom, having begun on alto.

segments.title: What Freeman asks to hear: pianists, Louis, Bix, Lester, Ben
segments.summary: Freeman says he asks for piano, Louis, Bix, Lester and Ben, and that Lester relaxes him where other tenors make him nervous.

segments.title: Louis's alphabet, Hawk's tenor, and Lester telling a story
segments.summary: Dance likens Louis and Hawkins to establishing jazz's alphabet while Lester started at Z; Freeman says Lester told a story about his life.

segments.title: Three Little Words: Lester remembers a Freeman trio record
segments.summary: Freeman tells how Lester asked to hear his Trio album twice on 52nd Street and, in 1946, greeted him saying 'Three Little Words was a bitch.'

segments.title: Gene Ramey's story of Lester on the Southern bus
segments.summary: Ramey told Freeman how Lester, Buck Clayton and Bud Johnson were threatened on a Southern bus and Lester laughed 'Shoot your pistol, baby.'

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Wingy Manone and the Austin sax team with Tesch
segments.summary: Dance asks about Tesch; Freeman recalls playing with Tesch in Wingy Manone's band at the Merry Garden Ballroom while still in high school.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Teschemacher's influences and talent
segments.summary: Freeman says Tesch was influenced by Bix, Jimmy Noone and Omer Simeon, and might have become one of the greats had he lived.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Classical music Bix introduced to the Chicagoans
segments.summary: Freeman recalls listening to Stravinsky, Ravel, Debussy and others through Bix, a fine pianist.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Tesch and Bix living for music; Maugham's beachcomber
segments.summary: Freeman says Tesch lived jazz deeply, young players wrongly imitated Bix's life, and compares them to Maugham's beachcomber killed by beauty.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Teschemacher's death in a car accident
segments.summary: Freeman says Tesch was no drunk and died in a sideswipe on Chicago's North Side while riding with Wild Bill.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Summer resort job with Jess Stacy near Dowagiac
segments.summary: Between top New York bands Freeman joined Jess Stacy at a Michigan lake resort for room, board and tiny pay before a Dorsey telegram.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Mezzrow's interracial band before Goodman
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Mezz Mezzrow's early-1930s black and white band with Benny Carter and Alex Hill writing, which folded for lack of financing.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: End of sides 1-4 and new session header
segments.summary: The first recorded session ends and a new Smithsonian header begins for sides 5-10.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Jess Stacy's Bix influence and the dance marathon
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Jess Stacy's Bix repertoire, a Chicago dance marathon job won by Frankie Laine, and not working with Jess again until Goodman.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Jess Stacy as an overlooked soloist; the Trio records
segments.summary: Freeman says Stacy had the Louis-Bix beat, was overshadowed by Teddy Wilson in Goodman's band, and played on the praised Trio records with Wettling.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Jess Stacy's comeback: Carnegie Hall and the New Yorker profile
segments.summary: At Freeman's 50th anniversary concert Stacy returned, the New Yorker ran a profile, and Stacy said he now felt he was doing something worthwhile.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Bringing Jess Stacy to Europe
segments.summary: Freeman says European pianists imitate Stacy and discusses his agent bringing American stars over and whether Stacy would tour.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Being an idol while still alive
segments.summary: Freeman and Dance discuss how history now brings back musicians in their seventies and eighties, and whether Stacy wants the rat race.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Stacy and Cliff Leeman's duet date and Carnegie Hall ovation
segments.summary: A piano-drums duet session led to Stacy playing Carnegie Hall and getting a standing ovation, while Freeman was still with the World's Greatest Jazz Band.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: A 96-year-old New Orleans bassist and his chick of 78
segments.summary: Freeman tells a story of an elderly New Orleans bassist on a London tour, and jokes about forgetting names.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Earl Hines and the influences that make a style
segments.summary: Freeman credits Earl Hines with introducing the Harlem pianists, and describes his own style as a ball of many influences.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: George Wettling, snare drummer and drinker
segments.summary: Freeman opens with Wettling from his book of anecdotes: a Baby Dodds and Louis devotee who became a berserk drunk.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Wettling's cowboy outfit from Paul Whiteman
segments.summary: Freeman tells the story of Wettling wearing the sheriff's cowboy outfit on drunks in New York gangster bars.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: Wettling the humorist and painter, pupil of Stuart Davis
segments.summary: Wettling wrote the Esquire satire A Night Before Bopmas and painted under Stuart Davis; Freeman met De Kooning and other painters through him.

segments.chapter: Chicago friends: Tesch, Stacy and Wettling
segments.title: George Wettling's last days in hospital
segments.summary: Freeman visits the dying Wettling, jokes about 'critical', and recalls he said he no longer had to carry drums.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Back to the career: Mezzrow's house in the Bronx
segments.summary: Dance steers Freeman back to chronology; he and Floyd O'Brien join Mezzrow's rehearsal band, which does not take off.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Roger Wolfe Kahn's band and the cost of being a millionaire's son
segments.summary: Freeman plays six months with Roger Wolfe Kahn's studio-player band, losing jobs when owners try to sell clubs to Otto Kahn's son.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Joe Haymes's band at the McAlpine Hotel
segments.summary: Freeman joins arranger Joe Haymes's band for about eighteen months at New York's McAlpine Hotel with Pee Wee Erwin and Toots Mondello.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Toots Mondello: session man and a rumour of his death
segments.summary: Freeman and Dance discuss Mondello as a studio saxophonist who studied composition, and Dance's unconfirmed report that he died.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Haymes band personnel and Haymes's stage fright
segments.summary: Freeman names others in the Haymes band, later taken over by Tommy Dorsey, and says Haymes feared the public.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Joining Ray Noble at the Rainbow Room
segments.summary: Pee Wee Erwin, Mondello and Freeman join Ray Noble's American band at the Rainbow Room, with Glenn Miller, Claude Thornhill, Bill Harty and Spivak.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Ray Noble's English and Bud as interpreter
segments.summary: Freeman translates Noble's British phrasing for the band; a musician locked in a closet misses rehearsal and Noble says 'Didn't know, my ass.'

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: We Don't Go Through the Kitchen Any More
segments.summary: Noble's band plays a debutante's party, refuses the kitchen entrance, drinks her champagne and plays only an hour.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Leaving Ray Noble; Glenn Miller's drinking
segments.summary: Freeman spent eighteen months with Noble; a drunk Glenn Miller warned Ray about 'a bad British band', and later stopped drinking with his own band.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Claude Thornhill's exit from the Rainbow Room
segments.summary: Thornhill leaves the Noble band by announcing his departure from the stage with an armload of music cases.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Claude Thornhill's eccentricity and serious music
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Thornhill as a funny, deep musician who dressed carelessly, roomed with the band and drank at Hurley's bar.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Brief stint in Paul Whiteman's Woodbury Soap Hour group
segments.summary: Freeman spends about a month in a small Whiteman radio band with Carl Kress, the Teagardens and Trumbauer, then goes with Tommy Dorsey.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Joining Tommy Dorsey: freedom to solo
segments.summary: Freeman joined Dorsey in 1936 alongside Dave Tough and Max Kaminsky and was happy because Dorsey let him play many choruses.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Recordings, broadcasts and residuals with Dorsey
segments.summary: Freeman says recordings made his name, and tells of a year's broadcast residuals in 1937 after a union rule.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Hard leaders and the regimentation of big bands
segments.summary: Freeman says leaders like Dorsey and Goodman had to be hard, and that sitting in tuxedos in a section felt like jail, offset by his solo space.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Tommy Dorsey's taste for showmanship: Shavers and Lunceford
segments.summary: Freeman says Dorsey valued showy jazz like Charlie Shavers and the commercial Lunceford band, not pure players like Buck Clayton.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Sy Oliver renews Dorsey; bandleaders as institutions
segments.summary: Freeman says Sy Oliver's arrangements gave Dorsey new life and that Lombardo, Herman, Goodman and Miller are institutions.

segments.chapter: New York dance bands and Dorsey
segments.title: Benny Goodman and Glenn Miller on 'the blues'
segments.summary: In Pollack's band Goodman and Miller laughed at Freeman's remark about the blues, later apologizing.

segments.title: Ben Pollack as drummer; Glenn Miller on Johnny Dodds
segments.summary: Freeman calls Pollack one of the first to understand jazz; Miller, who knew no early jazz, took offense at praise of Johnny Dodds in front of Goodman.

segments.title: Goodman's symphonic background versus Freeman's raw jazz
segments.summary: Freeman says the Pollack men went to Harlem only after Bix took him and McPartland there; Goodman's training was classical while his was jazz.

segments.title: How Freeman got into Pollack's band
segments.summary: Dance asks how Pollack hired him; Freeman says Miller, Goodman and McPartland recommended him when Fud Livingston left the Black Hawk band.

segments.title: Fud Livingston's decline and death
segments.summary: Freeman describes Livingston as a marvelous tenor and clarinet player who drank and was found dead on a stairway in New York's Skid Row.

segments.title: Benny Goodman as a young man in the Pollack band
segments.summary: Freeman says Goodman was kind to him at Pollack's but later, running a big band, grew cruel without awareness.

segments.title: Goodman's egomaniacal shell and his family duty
segments.summary: Freeman says Goodman's world is built around himself, but credits him for supporting a large family and kind acts.

segments.title: The gift that comes naturally: Max Farley's question
segments.summary: Dance says Goodman never saw the size of his gift; Freeman tells how saxophonist Max Farley replied 'Isn't that the way it's supposed to be?'

segments.title: How Not to Be a Genius: Goodman and Dorsey worked hard
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Huneker's essay, says Goodman and Dorsey practiced constantly, and that Goodman's symphonic schooling surprised people; Dance asks about Bartok.

segments.title: Pollack's death and playing drums at a 1950 Los Angeles concert
segments.summary: Freeman says Pollack hanged himself, and recalls him still playing marvelous drums at a Shriner's Mosque jazz concert.

segments.title: Judging the artist versus the man: Beethoven's Nephew
segments.summary: Freeman resists discussing Goodman's personality, citing Beethoven, and prefers to credit the good he did; Dance argues biography needs the person.

segments.title: Freeman on reading and not reading jazz books
segments.summary: Freeman says he rarely reads jazz books because he lived the history, but reads a paperback a day.

segments.title: Pollack's unhappy end; leaving for Paris and Zez Confrey
segments.summary: Freeman declines to discuss Pollack's end, then says he left the band after a year in 1928 for Paris, found the music bad, and joined Zez Confrey in Chicago.

segments.title: Muggsy Spanier, faithful to Oliver and Louis
segments.summary: Freeman, not close to Spanier, recalls a few concerts and a Condon record, and says he never changed his style.

segments.title: Longevity, Condon's resilience and Ellington who never stopped working
segments.summary: Freeman muses that longevity may be inherited, jokes about old drunks, and says Ellington kept creating until the end.

segments.title: Recording break; plan to follow the career chronologically
segments.summary: The recording is interrupted, then Dance proposes covering the career in order before digressing and returning to the present.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: Pee Wee Russell, the nervous drinker who became a painter
segments.summary: Freeman says you had to see Pee Wee suffer to play, then recalls his late-life paintings influenced by Stuart Davis that Freeman sold for $700 and up.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: The Black Tie: Pee Wee declines the Australian Ambassador's show
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Mary's death, an invitation to show Pee Wee's paintings, and Pee Wee skipping it for lack of a tuxedo; talent moved into another art.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: Goodman's remark at Juilliard: 'If you want to play like that, don't practice'
segments.summary: Asked about Pee Wee by a student, Goodman said he was a great artist and not to practice, which Freeman finds hilarious and unmeant.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: Sober Pee Wee as a lucid painter
segments.summary: Freeman says painting required Pee Wee to be sober, and phoning him he sounded so articulate that he thought it was a wrong number.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: Ellington the painter; musicians as rebel artists
segments.summary: Dance notes Ellington painted as a teen; Freeman says jazz musicians would have been other artists, rebelling against societal structure.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: An advertising job and finding music a hard life
segments.summary: Freeman recalls dreaming out the window of a Chicago ad agency at 17 and finding music, with nine shows a day, was like factory work.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: Never again for a bandleader: soloist years and the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: After Goodman Freeman vowed to be a soloist, survived lean years, and spent six years in a Colorado millionaire's band of soloists.

segments.chapter: Pee Wee Russell and going solo
segments.title: Declining a College Swing Band tour, then staying in Europe
segments.summary: Haggart persuaded him to decline a tour offer, but at Rotterdam a Dutch promoter offered Festival money and Robert Masters began handling him as a soloist.

segments.title: Dance steers back to the career after Dorsey and Goodman
segments.summary: Dance asks Freeman to cover his thinking in the stretch after leaving Dorsey in 1938 and Goodman in 1939, leading to the Condon band.

segments.title: Fronting a band at the Brass Rail in Chicago
segments.summary: Freeman fronts a band at the Brass Rail, but the men grow late and take advantage of his easy-going style, so he gives notice after fourteen weeks.

segments.title: Bill Doler, the polar bear and the grizzly
segments.summary: Freeman tells of alto player Bill Doler feeding bears at Lincoln Park after hours, his mauled hand, and his golf club revenge.

segments.title: Bill Doler's induction physical
segments.summary: Doler faked a swollen leg and cracked wise to the Army psychiatrist but was still taken and spent four years playing golf in a Florida band.

segments.title: Army service fronting a band in the Aleutians
segments.summary: Freeman went into the Army and spent 22 months in the Aleutians fronting a band, touring islands in the show Take A Break, bored but safe.

segments.title: Dashiell Hammett and the Adakian
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Hammett as a buck sergeant editing the camp paper, lecturing on China and Russia, and politely rebuffing a general.

segments.title: Hammett's jail term under McCarthy
segments.summary: Freeman says Hammett refused to name names and went to jail for six months, dying not long after.

segments.title: Freeman's Army years and Hammett's visit to Condon's
segments.summary: Freeman was 36 when he entered, spent 28 months in, and recalls Hammett and Lillian Hellman visiting Condon's in 1945.

segments.title: Musicians and politics
segments.summary: Freeman says he never got into politics, citing Trumbo and Casals, and that jazz music is political enough.

segments.title: Hammett's kindness as editor
segments.summary: Freeman never saw Hammett do an unkind act; he politely edited staff writers on the Adakian.

segments.title: Writing You Don't Look Like a Musician
segments.summary: Encouraged by food editor Nancy Kennedy, Freeman wrote his first book of anecdotes in longhand, then books published in Ireland.

segments.title: Discharge: news of the bomb and three days at Fort Dix
segments.summary: Freeman hears of Hiroshima on furlough, then is discharged because he was 39, after three wild days at Fort Dix.

segments.title: Art Tatum's champagne and putting aside the uniform
segments.summary: On his first night out of the Army Freeman hears Art Tatum on 52nd Street, who pours champagne with him, and then takes a month to give up his uniform.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: Report to the Nation and the Majestic Records house band
segments.summary: Ray McKinley's call leads to a radio spot, and Freeman leads the Majestic Records house band with Haggart, Lawson and McGarity until the company folds.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: The theme Easy to Get and the Sherman Hotel broadcasts
segments.summary: Dance asks about his radio theme; Freeman says it was Brad Gowans's tune, played at the Sherman Hotel's Panther Room, not at Condon's.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: Residency in Rio with Joe Bushkin
segments.summary: Freeman takes a trio with Joe Bushkin to a posh Rio room owned by a rich playboy; paid but idle for fourteen weeks.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: Joe Bushkin in London with Bing Crosby
segments.summary: Freeman says Bushkin visited the Hampstead club where he played, before opening with Bing at the Palladium.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: The Gaffer Club in Chicago on South Water Street
segments.summary: Freeman and Doler took over a room from an ex-bootlegger on a 50-50 deal; it collapsed when he toured, but concerts followed.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: The Fourth Estate, then an all-star band at the Savoy in Boston
segments.summary: After leaving Chicago clubs Freeman puts a band in the Fourth Estate and later brings an all-star band including Omer Simeon to Boston's Savoy for a month.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: East St. Louis jazz policy gig with Ruby Braff and Bob Wilber
segments.summary: Freeman takes Ruby Braff, Paul Jordan and Bob Wilber to a new East St. Louis jazz club, needing a drummer before opening.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: Chile: Viña del Mar, a British golf club and Santiago
segments.summary: With his lady friend's inheritance Freeman moves to Viña del Mar, plays golf, and is asked by British club members what jazz is.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: Margo, servants and a Chilean quintet before returning to New York
segments.summary: Freeman dislikes having servants, plays briefly with a Chilean quintet, then returns to the States where they separate.

segments.chapter: Postwar clubs, Chile and New York
segments.title: Sessions at the Van Rensselaer and the Metropole
segments.summary: Freeman runs about fifteen sessions at a Manhattan hotel with Lips Page, the Lion and Wettling, then plays the Metropole, getting back into playing.

segments.title: Newport Jazz Festival years and the Steve Allen Show
segments.summary: Freeman says he played fourteen Newport festivals, and George Wein hired him back after seeing him on the live Steve Allen Show.

segments.title: Gerald Lascelles's Beaulieu festival and first solo trips to Britain
segments.summary: Invited to a British festival, Freeman played with Chris Barber, then arranged solo tours with the Alex Welch band, coming two or three times yearly.

segments.title: Newport tours, Mexico and the West Berlin Philharmonic Hall
segments.summary: Freeman recalls tours with George Wein's all-stars, including opening West Berlin's Philharmonie, and a Copenhagen Tivoli festival, showing Europe's jazz market.

segments.title: Records abroad and his European following
segments.summary: Freeman says anyone who made many records does well in Europe because audiences know them.

segments.title: Jazz at the Philharmonic visits the Town Tavern in Toronto
segments.summary: Norman Granz's JATP stars, including Dizzy, Getz, Hawkins and Lester, came to hear Freeman, but he never worked with Granz.

segments.title: Leaving George Wein for the World's Greatest Jazz Band
segments.summary: Freeman leaves Wein for the cooperative World's Greatest Jazz Band, staying six years touring warm places and Europe.

segments.title: Jazz of the Swing Era: 28 festival days in a row
segments.summary: Freeman lists the Newport all-star band and recounts 28 consecutive festival dates booked by a greedy agent, with Fred Allen's joke.

segments.title: Just for Tenors and Ronnie Scott's
segments.summary: After the tour Freeman joins Lockjaw Davis, Ben Webster and Eddie Miller for Just for Tenors, then plays two weeks at Ronnie Scott's with a three-tenor finale.

segments.title: Car accident on the Queensborough Bridge
segments.summary: Heading to a composition class at NYU, Freeman was hit head-on by a truck, breaking nine ribs, and was treated at a Harlem hospital refusing narcotics.

segments.title: Hospital stay, lawsuit settlement and bonds
segments.summary: Freeman spent fifteen days in hospital with nine broken ribs, watched the World Series with the ward, and received an out-of-court settlement.

segments.title: Fear of riding in cars after the accident
segments.summary: Freeman, once unbothered by Wein's fast driving, now fears cars but not planes, worrying more about being maimed than dying.

segments.title: Returning to playing after seven months
segments.summary: Freeman did not play for seven months, then felt no pain at Art Hodes's Chicago show; he mentions lung puncture and catching colds in England.

segments.title: Deciding to stay in Europe: the Breda festival and bookings
segments.summary: Freeman planned six months in Europe, was offered big money for one hour at the Breda festival, and is now booked about two years ahead.

segments.title: The pattern of European work: short sets, quick flights
segments.summary: Freeman describes 20 to 45 minute sets with local rhythm sections, German jazz clubs, and an eleven-minute closing spot at Hanover.

segments.title: American musicians meeting in Europe; Billy Butterfield's tour
segments.summary: Dance and Freeman discuss Europe as a market of many countries where American friends he hasn't seen in 20 years now visit.

segments.title: British support for jazz
segments.summary: Freeman says Britons have backed American dance music and jazz for seventy years and turn out seriously for American soloists.

segments.title: The all-British album The Song of the Tenor
segments.summary: Phonogram asked Freeman for an album and he used British players such as Bruce Turner, Roy Williams and Bob Wilber's arrangements.

segments.title: Studying with Lennie Tristano after the Brazil breakdown
segments.summary: After losing confidence on returning from Brazil Freeman went to the blind Tristano, who diagnosed tension and not letting the sound ring.

segments.title: Metronome and Down Beat poll wins
segments.summary: Dance notes the 1937 Metronome and 1938 Down Beat polls; Freeman says poll winners were those featured with big bands.

segments.title: Hugues Panassie and Mezz Mezzrow
segments.summary: Freeman says Panassie praised his playing in 1927, then dropped him after Mezzrow's influence, and Freeman doubted his knowledge of jazz.

segments.title: Tony Palmer's television series and a film on the tenor sax
segments.summary: Freeman describes his episode in All You Need Is Love, recorded in Switzerland, and a planned Copenhagen film on the history of the tenor.

segments.title: Buddy Tate, Jay McShann and Michael's Pub
segments.summary: Freeman recalls Buddy Tate coming onstage at a Belgian festival, Tate's European popularity, and meeting Jay McShann at Newport.

segments.title: What jazz means: therapy, world folk music and the young
segments.summary: Freeman says jazz relieves pain, leaves you strung out after concerts, and may become world folk music as young people leave rock.
